News.title: DWP £10,000 'trigger' alert as new update given
News.content:
DWP £10,000 'trigger' alert as new update given

Experts have expressed concern behind the headline figures

View 3 Images The DWP published new figures this morning (Image: Alphotographic via Getty Images)

New Department for Work and Pensions figures published today have led to concern from money experts.

‌



Around nine in 10 (90%) of eligible employees in Great Britain were saving into a workplace pension in 2025, continuing the trend of previous years, with 22.6 million eligible employees saving, according to DWP data published this morning. This is an increase of 0.6 million more eligible employees saving and a 1ppt increase in the pension participation rate compared to 2024.

‌



One financial adviser warned that "90% participation is a headline about how many people are in the queue, not how much is in the pot". Another said "Defined Benefit (DB) schemes are creeping towards extinction, which leaves the state pension at up to £12,500 a year and whatever assets/savings you can build up".

‌



The DWP report also revealed that the overall workplace pension participation rate of all employees in Great Britain continued to be around eight in 10 (82%) in 2025, with 24.2 million employees saving. This is a 0.6 million greater number of employees saving compared to 2024.

View 3 Images The State Pension is not enough for many people (Image: John Lamb via Getty Images)

The number of employees saving, the DWP said, continues to increase year on year, something that can be attributed to an increase in the number of employees brought into AE (auto-enrolment) eligibility, as the earnings trigger (currently £10,000) has remained frozen in recent years. However, only around 55% of eligible employees working for a micro employer (those with fewer than five employees) in the private sector are saving into a workplace pension, and just 67% of Pakistani and Bangladeshi eligible employees are saving into a workplace pension.

‌



The DWP observed that the vast majority, 94%, of the 12.9million individuals in receipt of a private pension payment in 2025/26 are currently in receipt of a Defined Benefit or an annuity. However, it said this is slowly changing. When assessing private pensions accessed for the first time, the proportion receiving a lump sum or other Defined Contribution product rose from 37% (280,000) in the 2016/17 financial year to 49% (410,000) in the 2025/26 financial year.

Anita Wright, Chartered Financial Planner at Ribble Wealth Management, said people needed to look beyond the headline figure.

She continued: "90% participation is a headline about how many people are in the queue, not how much is in the pot. Auto-enrolment counts bodies and says nothing about whether the legal minimum contribution buys anyone a retirement and it simply doesn't.

‌



"And look at why the number rose. The £10,000 earnings trigger has been frozen for years, so ordinary wage growth quietly drags more low earners in.

"Almost everyone drawing a private pension today has a guaranteed income. Someone else made the promise. Someone else carried the risk. Among those retiring for the first time, nearly half now take a cash lump sum or a pot they have to manage themselves.

"No promise. Just a balance, a set of choices and the hope that markets behave. That is the transfer, happening in plain sight.

‌



"One generation retired on guarantees. The next retires on a market, a drawdown decision, and whatever inflation leaves behind. Signing people up isn't the same as them saving enough. We find out the difference in 20 years."

Rob Mansfield, Independent Financial Advisor at Tonbridge-based Rootes Wealth Management, also said the end of DB schemes was a cause for concern: "Defined Benefit schemes are creeping towards extinction, which leaves the state pension at up to £12,500 a year and whatever assets/savings you can build up. All the liability has been passed onto the individual with very little education or risk warning.

"We've got a cost of living crisis that limits how much some people can save and then, of those that can, they face a complex system that is constantly tinkered with by governments. Many people are sleepwalking towards a struggle in retirement."

‌



View 3 Images The sums might not add up for future generations (Image: Pexels)

Eamonn Prendergast, Chartered Financial Adviser at Bromley-based Palantir Financial Planning, was ambivalent: "Auto-enrolment continues to be a success story, as getting around 90% of eligible employees saving is a major achievement. But participation is only half the story.

"The real issue is adequacy, as many people are saving at minimum levels, which simply won’t deliver the retirement they expect. The gap among micro employers is also a concern, highlighting that access and engagement still aren’t consistent across the workforce.

‌



"What we’re also seeing is a clear shift toward defined contribution pensions and greater flexibility at retirement, which puts more responsibility on individuals to make the right decisions. The risk is that, without guidance or advice, people could make choices that don’t support their long-term financial security."

Graham Nicoll, financial planner, Chartered FCSI at NCL Wealth Partners, said "automatic enrolment has transformed workplace pension saving, but participation is increasingly shaped by employer culture".

He added: "In smaller firms, where pensions can feel like an optional benefit and opt-out decisions are more visible, participation may be lower. Larger employers often normalise pension saving through stronger communication and workplace culture, making staying enrolled feel like the default. Closing this gap will require greater engagement, not just automatic enrolment."

‌



Nouran Moustafa, practice principal at Roxton Wealth, also cautioned that, while the headline 90% participation figure was positive, "it risks hiding the real pension problem".

She continued: "Getting 90% of eligible employees enrolled is not the same as getting 90% on track for a comfortable retirement. Participation is only the first hurdle, while adequacy is the real test.

"The 55% participation rate among micro-employers is the figure that should worry policymakers most. It shows that the smallest workplaces remain the weakest link, where lower pay, limited HR support and poor pension communication can leave people behind.

‌



"The shift towards lump sums and other defined contribution withdrawals also means more responsibility is moving from institutions to individuals. That offers flexibility, but it also creates greater risk of poor timing, overspending and running out of money.

"We have built a strong enrolment system; the next challenge is making sure people save enough and are supported to turn those savings into a sustainable retirement income."

Kate Underwood, founder of Southampton-based Kate Underwood HR and Training, said it was the eligible employees in the smallest businesses who were missing out the most.

Article continues below

She continued: "For many micro-employers, it isn’t a lack of commitment. It’s the reality of rising employment costs and tight cash flow.

"Auto-enrolment has been a huge success and schemes like NEST have made it much easier for small businesses to offer workplace pensions. But enrolling someone is only the first step. Too many employees believe the minimum contribution will be enough, when in reality it may fall well short of the retirement they hope for.

"The next challenge isn’t getting people into pensions but getting them engaged with their pension. Better education and clearer communication will have a far bigger impact than simply increasing participation numbers."

News.title: Three migrants die crossing the Channel after busiest day this year
News.content:
Three migrants die crossing the Channel after busiest day this year

The group were found dead on a boat off the coast of Dunkirk on Thursday morning, the French coastguard said

View 3 Images Three migrants died on Thursday (Image: Gareth Fuller/PA Wire)

Three migrants have died trying to reach the UK after one of the busiest days for Channel crossings this year.

‌



The group were found dead on a boat off the coast of Dunkirk on Thursday morning, the French coastguard said. It comes after Prime Minister Andy Burnham insisted the Government's plan to curb Channel crossings was "working," but admitted there was "more to do.”

‌



The boat was spotted at around 6am and the three people on board were found unresponsive. They were taken to shore by rescue crews where they were confirmed dead. Wednesday was one of the busiest days for crossings so far this year, with a steady stream of attempts throughout the day due to the sunny weather and calm seas.

‌



View 3 Images The migrants were found unresponsive in the dingy (Image: Anadolu via Getty Images)

Dramatic footage shows arrests as small boat gang disruptions soar READ MORE :

Chilling drone footage shows children and pregnant woman crammed onto small boat as pilot jailed READ MORE :

In a separate incident, a small boat capsized off Hardelot, on France's north west coast, late on Wednesday. The administrative department for the Pas-de-Calais said: "The provisional toll is one man, estimated to be between 30 and 40 years old, deceased, and six people with minor injuries, including a one-year-old child, who were treated by emergency services.” A judicial investigation has been opened to determine the cause of the incident.

‌



Up to 700 migrants are believed to have crossed the Channel in small boats on Wednesday. French police were filmed on Hardelot beach, south of Boulogne, watching on as dozens of people boarded a dinghy destined for the UK. French officers are not allowed to intervene when migrants are in the water and boarding the boats due to the risk of drowning.

The size of the rubber dinghies has increased significantly as smugglers adapt to increased police activity on French beaches. Larger boats now “taxi” around the coast of France and wait to pick up people slightly offshore, rather than launching from the sand. A record 128 migrants arrived in one dinghy this month, up from the previous record of 125 in September last year.

View 3 Images The size of dinghies has increased significantly (Image: Anadolu via Getty Images)

Article continues below

In April, the UK agreed to pay France extra cash to police its shores. A £662m deal was agreed for the next three years, with around £160m of it to be spent on new tactics like policing to stop so-called taxi boats.

The £160m is conditional on the success of the French operation. The UK will pay around £501m for more officers on the beaches of northern France and extra surveillance technology, despite a previous boost in funding failing to bring the number of Channel crossings down. Charities fear the enforcement would push people to flee to the UK and could lead to more deaths.

A government spokesperson said: “We are deeply saddened to hear about these deaths. “Every death in the Channel is a tragedy and a stark reminder of the dangers posed by criminal gangs exploiting vulnerable people for profit. We will continue working relentlessly with the French and our partners overseas to prevent these perilous journeys. The French authorities are leading the response and investigation into this incident.”

News.title: Banks urged to help families pay back cash used by shamed funeral director Robert Bush
News.content:
Banks urged to help families pay back cash used by shamed funeral director Robert Bush

WARNING - DISTRESSING CONTENT: Humberside Police officer Jason Sutcliffe said coming across the dead bodies and foetus at the funeral directors was "probably the worst experience of my career"

Inside funeral parlour where owner gave ashes to wrong families and left bodies to rot

A judge has said it might "be good" if banks help grieving families hurt by shamed funeral director Robert Bush by paying them back the money they have lost.

‌



Mr Justice Hillard shared the comments after hearing heartbreaking evidence from officers and families impacted by Bush earlier this morning. Police officers shared their "disbelief" after finding dead bodies and a foetus in a bag at Legacy Independent Funeral Directors, with one describing it as the "worst experience of his career." James Milligan, the Humberside Police force lead for chemical, radiation and hazardous material, said he was deployed to Legacy in March 2024 with a team of five officers.

In his statement read out to the court, he recalled his team's reaction when they discovered the remains of Jasmine Beverley's baby in a bag. "I remember one of the team saying: 'is this what I think it is?'

"We were all looking at each other in what I can only describe as disbelief. For one of the few times in my life, it knocked the wind out of my sails that this was an unborn human foetus/baby. I can’t remember what was said, but I do remember that the mood within the team became quite dark, even angry."

View 6 Images Robert Bush is due to be sentenced after pleading guilty to several counts of fraud (Image: Humberside Police)

PC Jason Sutcliffe said in his statement to the court: "I class myself as a resilient person. Finding the foetus will never leave my thoughts, and I was disgusted and deeply saddened.

"Luckily, I have had the support of my colleagues at the time, and this has helped me immensely. I am due to retire from the police shortly, and I can honestly say that this was probably the worst experience of my career."

No justice

Maxine Hill told how her parents were conned by Bush after buying funeral plans from the sick funeral director at Legacy in Hull.

Tragically both her mum Margaret, who died in May 2024, and her dad, John who died a year later in June 2025, never got to see the "justice they deserved". Maxine added: “Even though mum was poorly, the added worry of losing the money they had paid to Robert Bush, and how they would pay for their funerals, didn’t help at all.

View 6 Images Family members of the victims have pursued justice with courage (Image: Annabel Lee-Ellis/PA Wire)

"Mum had paid Bush in cash, so the bank has refused to refund the fraud she has been subjected to. Although Dad did receive a refund from the TSB Bank, he still worried that he owed this money to the bank.

"Then, 90 days after receiving the refund, the TSB took the money…back as they said there was no evidence that he hadn’t received a product. Both mum and dad were defrauded of £2,649 each.

View 6 Images Jasmine Beverley son, Sunny, was stillborn and had his funeral arranged by Robert Bush (Image: Andy Commins)

"The stress of this financial worry is something they should not have had to endure and added to the strain on their mental and physical health." She told how she "tried to shield and protect" her parents from what Bush had done "but it upset them both greatly".

"You would honestly think that 'butter wouldn’t melt' in Mr Bush’s mouth. He came across as being just so nice and so placid,” she told the court today. "It hurts me to think that he could go and visit my parents knowing he was going to do this to them after knowing me personally. Although we weren’t friends, I would say we were acquaintances, and I feel very angry and let down. I feel that I can’t trust anyone.

View 6 Images Bush has pleaded guilty to multiple offences (Image: PA)

She added: "I also worry that I even have my husband’s ashes, after entrusting Robert Bush to look after him on his death. There are so many questions, that I feel will never be answered."

Hull Crown Court heard how Bush, 48, defrauded 226 people by charging them for funeral plans he was not authorised to set up, and then pocketing the money. He kept more than half a million pounds over almost 12 years.

'I can't believe he could do this to people'

On the fourth day of his sentencing hearing, Bush sat with his head lowered in the dock as victim personal statements were read by some of the people who had lost their money to his fraudulent funeral plans. Anne Hillerby said Bush had charged her “around £5,000” for two funeral plans but offered to "knock off £100 for paying in cash".

Her statement read: "We have since found out the plans are not in place and I have not received a refund due to paying in cash. Robert Bush has ripped off so many vulnerable people. I can’t believe he could do this to people.

View 6 Images Police carried out a large-scale investigation of Legacy (Image: Danny Lawson/PA Wire)

"He has used lower prices to get the customers in then ripped them off." Several victims said they had other savings and the plans had been intended as a safety net to save their children from worrying about their funeral costs.

In April, Bush pleaded guilty to 30 counts of preventing a lawful and decent burial, and theft from the 12 charities. He had already admitted 30 counts of fraud by false representation relating to bodies found at the site, and four "foetus allegations" of fraud, where he presented ashes to women falsely saying that they were "the remains of their unborn".

View 6 Images Police gave harrowing testimony during the sentencing hearing (Image: PA)

Bush also pleaded guilty to a further charge of fraud, covering the ashes of 57 people between 2017 and 2024, and one of fraudulent trading relating to funeral plans between 2012 and 2024.

Bush is due to be sentenced for 67 offences spanning 12 years.

News.title: New Lidl £7 dress that looks like Next's £156 version coming out on Sunday
News.content:
New Lidl £7 dress that looks like Next's £156 version coming out on Sunday

Shoppers won't have too long to wait for the new range of clothing and accessories in Lidl's Middle Aisle

View 3 Images Lidl updates its Special Buys every Thursday and Sunday (Image: Getty)

Lidl has shared an early glimpse of what shoppers can expect in its upcoming Special Buy deals next month. On Sunday, August 9, the budget supermarket will add a range of clothing items and accessories to its popular Middle Aisle in stores across the UK.

‌



One piece of clothing customers will be able to buy is Lidl's Esmara Ladies' Green Linen-Blend Dress for £6.99. The less-than-£10 dress could be ideal for anyone wanting to keep cool as the warm summer weather continues, as it is made from "l ightweight linen-viscose blend fabric".

‌



Lidl says that the dress features a "relaxed fit in a modern midi length", with a round neckline and a "decorative knot and long side slits." It is 87% viscose and 13% linen and comes in small, medium, or large.

‌



The £6.99 dress could be a budget-friendly alternative for anyone who likes the look of the BOSS Green Erlays Midi Dress, which is available at Next for £159, but would prefer not to spend more than they need to. Both dresses come in khaki green and have short sleeves, a round neckline, side slits, and a decorative side knot.

However, opting for the similar-looking version at Lidl would save shoppers around £152. The £159 dress at Next is made from 95% modal and 5% elastane, and it is available to buy online in sizes eight to fourteen.

View 3 Images Lidl's Esmara Ladies’ Beige Linen-Blend Dress for £6.99 (L) Next's BOSS Green Erlays Midi Dress for £159 (R) (Image: Lidl/Next)

‌



In the product description, Next says: "The BOSS Erlays Midi Dress offers a timeless, elegant silhouette with a flattering midi length and sleek design. Made from luxurious fabric, it’s the perfect choice for both formal occasions and evening outings. Machine washable."

Lidl's £6.99 Ladies' Patterned Linen-Blend Dress comes in three different colours and patterns. Besides the khaki green version, shoppers will also be able to choose from a geometric black-and-cream pattern or a plain beige colourway.

Lidl Special Buys, usually located in the well-known "Middle of Lidl," are temporary, non-food products that feature DIY tools, home gadgets, and toys for children. These items arrive at stores twice a week, with fresh selections debuting every Thursday and Sunday.

‌



View 3 Images The dress will be arriving in stores next Sunday (Image: Lidl)

What other clothing and accessories is Lidl bringing out on Sunday August 9?

Shoppers will also be able to buy a three-pack of Lidl's Ladies' Ribbed Vest Tops With Lace, in either blue, green and grey; or light pink, dark pink and white; or white and black, for £6.99. Sizes vary from small to extra large, and Lidl says the vests are made with cotton for "comfort" and "LYCRA for a superior fit".

Another option is Lidl's three-pack of Ladies’ Green Seamless Ribbed Briefs for £4.99. Or, a pack of ten Men’s Cotton Rich Boxers for £14.99.

Article continues below

For men, there is the Grey Linen-Blend Shirt for £7.99, which also comes in a blue and stripe pattern. Another pick is the Esmara Men’s Dark Grey Linen Blend Trousers for £8.99.

News.title: Suffolk wildfire live: Nuclear plant 'monitoring' huge Dunwich Heath blaze
News.content:
Fire spans 100 hectares as crews from other areas called in

It is understood the fire now spans 100 hectares. Fire services from as far away as Essex are arriving to help with the emergency effort.

The smell of smoke occasionally fills the air with changing wind, as well as the sound of sirens from passing fire trucks and the whirring of a helicopter passing intermittently overhead.

At Westleton Village Hall, locals are banding together to help others, including holidaymakers, who have been evacuated from holiday lets and caravans near the fire.

Volunteers set up the makeshift rescue centre late on Wednesday night after the scale of the fire became clear.

They are helping evacuees to sort accommodation and giving away free food and drinks, including sandwiches, delivered from supermarket chain Waitrose, to the needy, including babies, families, elderly residents and some in wheelchairs.

Volunteers are also handing out pet food to animals evacuated.

Shortly before midday, they anlso unpacked bedding and pillows from a delivery van before moving them into the main hall.

Among the volunteers is Barry Banks, 52, who has lived in the village full-time for the past five years.

He told the Mirror: "We were made aware by the smell of smoke and sirens. We’re lucky we haven’t had too many fires in the past but it’s always in the back of everyone’s minds.

"By the time we got down here to open up there was already a strong team of volunteers ready to help in any way they could.

"We were fully open and operational for refreshments from about 10pm and then we heard that people were being evacuated from the campsites up until about midnight, 1am.

"We managed to get 47 people housed with the village. Everyone that turned up here was successfully housed.

"It was a mixture of accommodation, but I’d say about 80-90 per cent was people’s houses. It was a great effort. We’re very proud.

"We arrived this morning to cook a full breakfast for everyone that was housed overnight."

Barry added: "From the two updates we’ve had this morning, we understand things are still very fluid as far as the fire is concerned.

"The fire service are trying to slow the spread, but with the wind whipping up and due to change direction shortly, according to the forecast, it’s still a bit of the unknown.

"We understand there were possibly 18 to 20 fire appliances at its peak. It was constant through the night with sirens.

"It was amazing to see the response from everyone, emergency services especially."

News.title: Jaguar Land Rover to cut hundreds of UK jobs as car giant issues major statement
News.content:
Jaguar Land Rover to cut hundreds of UK jobs as car giant issues major statement

Jaguar Land Rover will cut up to 300 roles as part of a 'redeployment and displacement' programme underway at the global car giant

View Image Jaguar Land Rover will cut up to 300 jobs in the UK (Image: UK)

Jaguar Land Rover is to axe up to 300 roles as part of a "restructure" following the impact of tariffs and a crippling cyber attack.

‌



Salaried and managerial posts are affected by the programme of 'redeployment and displacement' under way at the global giant, which is based in the West Midlands.

‌



The company said it was part of its ongoing 'transformation' including a focus on next generation and electric vehicles.

‌



Unions have been informed. In a statement, a JLR spokesman said: “As we evolve our operating model to accelerate the growth of our House of Brands and deliver our next-generation vehicles, we are transforming our business to improve decision-making and performance.

“As part of our ongoing transformation initiatives, we have launched a limited redeployment and displacement programme. Impacted colleagues will be supported to find alternative roles wherever possible, alongside the option of voluntary early exit.”

The company expects in all 'less than 300' staff to leave as a result, all in salaried and management grades. Its hourly workforce on the production floors are not included in the programme.

‌



Affected staff will be offered the chance to make an 'early exit' on favourable redundancy terms or to 'explore redeployment opportunities', with redundancy an option if nothing suitable can be agreed.

Jaguar Land Rover’s annual profits, announced in May, had slumped by more than 99 per cent year-on-year as it was hard hit by the cost of US tariffs and a crippling cyber attack last year that disrupted its factories for months.

It reported only £14m in profit before tax and exceptional items in the year to March, down from £2.5bn the year before, according to its financial results.

‌



The manufacturer employs 33,000 people in the UK, including thousands in the West Midlands at plants in Solihull and Castle Bromwich.

It was badly affected by Donald Trump’s automotive industry tariffs that caused turmoil in its important export market to the United States.

The firm was also hit by a hugely damaging damaging cyber attack on the last day of August that forced the company to shut down most of its systems and factories for weeks, causing a dire knock on impact on its local supply chain, with disruption still ongoing.

‌



The 'redeployment and displacement' programme affects staff working in Solihull, Gaydon in Warwickshire, Wolverhampton and Coventry.

At present JLR employs around 10,700 staff at its vehicle assembly plant in Solihull, and another 10,000 at its global headquarters, responsible for product engineering and design, in Gaydon.

It also has a propulsion and battery manufacturing plant in Wolverhampton, employing up to 1,400 people, and an advanced engineering and commercial operations base in Coventry, employing 2,500 people.

Article continues below

The firm said those affected were based across its locations.

Unite national officer Des Quinn said of the redundances: "Any of our members that need support will have the full support of Unite the union."

News.title: Europe wildfires live: Crete inferno rages with warning 'all of continent' at risk
News.content:
Europe's emergency response chief has warned that wildfires could engulf the whole continent as fires ravage parts of the Greek island of Crete

A new wildfire is ravaging the Greek island of Crete as Europe's emergency response chief warned the entire continent could be engulfed.

Wildfires in the Rethymno region in the south of the island are currently burning "out of control on all fronts", and firefighting aircraft unable to be deployed due to strong winds. Two of three firefighters killed in Greece since the wildfires began were tackling flames in Crete with 8,000 evacuated holidaymakers evacuated from a resort village on the island.

Maria Zuber, head of the EU's Emergency Response Co-ordination Centre, said wildfires could engulf "all of Europe" within days. Her warning comes as intense blazes also rage in France, Spain, and Portugal.

"Italy will face risk at the beginning of August, and we will need to see what will happen with the Iberian Peninsula, because if (it is) there as well, we will have all Europe on fire," she said.

News.title: Evil mum and boyfriend who murdered girl, two, in 'campaign of violence' jailed for life
News.content:
Evil mum and boyfriend who murdered girl, two, in 'campaign of violence' jailed for life

Mum Alexandra Walker and her boyfriend Harrison Simpson have been jailed for life after murdering two-year-old Isabelle Welsh, who was also sexually abused by Simpson

Footage released of Isabelle Welsh as mum and partner found guilty of murder

A couple who blamed each other after a two-year-old girl in their care was sexually abused and murdered have been jailed for life after subjecting the tragic toddler to a "campaign of violence".

The girl's mum Alexandra Walker, 26, and her boyfriend Harrison Simpson, 22, denied the horrific abuse of Isabelle Welsh, but were found guilty on Tuesday.

Isabelle collapsed at her home in Thornaby, Teesside, on September 13 last year after suffering a catastrophic head injury. She died in hospital the following day. The toddler suffered 21 broken bones in the weeks before her murder.

At Teesside Crown Court today (Thursday), Walker and Simpson were sentenced to life with minimum terms of 22 and 28 years, respectively.

View 5 Images Isabelle Welsh, two, was murdered by her mum, Alexandra Walker, and Walker's boyfriend, Harrison Simpson (Image: PA)

Dramatic arrest of teenage Norwegian 'hitman' who organised crime gang tasked to kill someone READ MORE :

While Isabelle was dying at her home in Hartington Close, Walker smoked a cigarette in her kitchen and delayed ringing 999, instead Googling "why would my toddler be bleeding".

She first called her stepdad to tell him to come to the house, and it was only on his instruction that she alerted the emergency services.

View 5 Images Alexandra Walker (Image: Cleveland Police)

When paramedics arrived within a minute, they found bruises all over the little girl’s body including to her head, neck, abdomen, back and genitalia. There was also blood in her nappy and vomit on her face.

Isabelle was not breathing and was cold to the touch as medics battled in vain to save her. A post-mortem examination revealed that her skull was fractured, her brain damaged and that she had been sexually assaulted.

View 5 Images Harrison Simpson (Image: Cleveland Police)

Experts told the jury that Isabelle had been shaken and her head impacted against a wall or the floor.

During her short relationship with Simpson, Walker voiced concerns that he might be a paedophile, saying she thought it was "weird" that he preferred to see her and Isabelle at the same time, rather than be alone with his girlfriend. But despite being suspicious enough to check if Simpson was on the sex offenders' register, Walker did not break up with him.

Just 11 days before her fatal collapse, Isabelle was taken to her GP and then to hospital with a broken leg. The little girl was discharged to her mother who had shown aggression towards medics when concerns were raised about what had happened. Walker explained that Isabelle must have hurt her leg when it got caught in her cot.

On that occasion too, Walker had waited two weeks to seek medical help for Isabelle, despite the toddler being in pain and struggling to walk.

After almost seven hours of deliberations, a jury at Teesside Crown Court convicted Simpson and Walker of murder by a majority of 11 to one. They also convicted the pair of child cruelty. Simpson was convicted of sexual assault on the toddler, while Walker was cleared of that charge.

Prosecutor Richard Wright KC told the court: "For weeks this child had been violently assaulted and her death, by that terrible head injury, was simply the end point in that campaign of violence to which she had been subjected."

Videos taken last June - before Simpson came into her life - showed the little girl happily playing.

View 5 Images 'My whole life has been shattered,' Isabelle's dad said

Walker and Simpson had met on Facebook Dating earlier last summer and Simpson became a regular visitor to the house.

Walker had previously been subjected to domestic violence and had installed two cameras in her home, with one overlooking the back of the house that captured evidence reflected in a window.

‌



The camera showed that Walker was a frequent drinker, sometimes downing up to 10 cans of Stella Artois, and Simpson was a habitual cannabis smoker. The couple sold cannabis at times and Walker explained how bouts of self-harm, which were caught on her CCTV, were attempts to get out of selling drugs.

The CCTV footage also proved that Isabelle suffered a broken leg while in the sole care of Simpson. Walker’s concerned mother said “looks like she is being abused” during one visit after Isabelle’s leg was broken.

The night when Isabelle was fatally injured, the couple stayed up late, with Walker drinking cans of lager and Simpson smoking cannabis. The next morning Simpson woke up, claiming to be looking after Isabelle, while Walker stayed in bed.

‌



View 5 Images Flowers and teddies laid at the scene in tribute to Isabelle

One of the nurses who treated Isabelle’s broken leg - and who had concerns about her care - was on duty when she was brought back to University Hospital of North Tees in a state of collapse 11 days later. Simpson and Walker were arrested after Isabelle's death.

Simpson declined to answer police questions and did not give evidence at the trial. Walker gave various accounts of what happened before eventually telling police she believed her boyfriend had been abusing her daughter.

‌



Mr Wright said Walker did not protect her daughter, saying: "On the contrary, she delayed, she deflected and she failed to act when action was most urgently required."

Following the convictions, Isabelle’s father Josh Welsh said: "My whole life has been shattered, my whole family. My sisters and brothers have lost their niece. It means the world to me that we have justice for Isabelle."

Kirstie Devine, from the Crown Prosecution Service, said: "The prosecution presented a raft of evidence including pathology reports, expert medical evidence, CCTV from the home, records of text messages and phone conversations that showed only the two adults who were regularly with Isabelle could have harmed her."

Article continues below

Senior Investigating Officer, Detective Chief Inspector Steve Chatterton of Cleveland Police, said: "Isabelle suffered catastrophic injuries at the hands of the very people who should have loved her, cared for her and protected her. Her life was cruelly taken in the most tragic and heartbreaking circumstances.”

News.title: Joe Root returns as England Test cricket captain with Stephen Fleming named head coach
News.content:
Former New Zealand captain Stephen Fleming has been appointed as England Test coach, with Joe Root returning as captain.

Fleming, 53, has never previously worked as head coach of a national team but he led Chennai Super Kings to a record five Indian Premier League titles during his 17-year tenure as head coach.

Previous Test coach Brendon McCullum was fired earlier this month following a string of poor results and several off-field incidents, but remains in charge of England's white-ball sides.

Root, 35, whose first spell as Test captain was between 2017 and 2022, captained England to a record 27 Test wins in 65 matches.

He has been reappointed captain following the shock retirement of Ben Stokes from international cricket in June.

Fleming said he was "incredibly excited" to be taking on the role as Test coach.

"It's one of the most prestigious coaching positions in world cricket and I am honoured to be appointed," he added.

Fleming will not be in charge for the Test series against Pakistan, which begins on 19 August. Assistant coach Marcus Trescothick will be the interim head coach.

Fleming will spend time with his family in New Zealand before flying to the UK later this summer to begin preparations for the South Africa Test tour in December.

Root said taking on the captain's role alongside Fleming was a "huge motivator".

He added: "[Fleming] has proved over a long period of time that he is an exceptional leader with a great knowledge of the game, and I am looking forward to working with him and helping to build a winning environment."

Fleming will inherit a side that saw its momentum falter after a breathtaking start to the McCullum era.

McCullum won 10 out of 12 Tests in his first year in charge but since then, England have lost 18 and won 17 of 37 Tests.

They have not won a multi-match series since December 2024.

The decision to remove McCullum came after the 4-1 Ashes hammering in Australia was followed by a 2-1 home series defeat by New Zealand, including Stokes announcing his retirement during play in the third Test.

News.title: Israel building new land barriers in Gaza and displacing families
News.content:
"We've been displaced from place to place, and now we have nowhere left to go," says Umm Mohammed al-Shawish.

She is desperately searching for somewhere to live after Israel moved yellow concrete blocks that mark out where it controls in the Gaza Strip.

Families living in al-Tuffah in northern Gaza woke on Monday to find the blocks had been moved westwards into the centre of Salah al-Din road, a key north-south route through Gaza.

Nearby, an Israeli flag was flying on top of an earth barrier around 3m (10ft) tall.

The al-Shawish family home was destroyed during the war. On Sunday, they had to flee again after the Israeli military called to warn of an attack on a nearby building. Their only shelter was a tent, which was torn apart by the strike.

"We are going to die here," Mohammed al-Shawish said. "Death is better than humiliation. No-one is standing with us."

Under the terms of the US-brokered ceasefire deal between Israel and Hamas last October, Israel agreed to withdraw its forces from across Gaza to a designated demarcation - the Yellow Line.

The deal was meant to leave Israel in temporary control of the area behind the Yellow Line - equating to 53% of Gaza's territory. However, the Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu recently said the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) controlled more than 60%. In May, he said publicly that his "directive" was to move to 70%.

Hamas accuses Israel of violating the October ceasefire agreement by moving the Yellow Line westwards. A senior Israeli government official said Israel rejected Hamas's claims outright. The BBC was told: "IDF deployments and security lines are operational measures taken to protect Israeli citizens and prevent Hamas from rebuilding its terror army. Israel will continue to act against any ceasefire violations."

The Israeli military initially marked the Yellow Line with concrete blocks, before moving some markers further into Gaza. But Israel has now constructed a network of barriers, having started soon after the ceasefire. The barriers now stretch more than 42km (26 miles) and cover 85% of Israel's Yellow Line, with the longest section already 13.8km (8.5 miles).

Experts have told the BBC that the earthworks suggest Israel is planning for a long occupation of the strip. In some areas the earth barrier effectively moves the de facto "border" - the Yellow Line - deeper into Gaza, further increasing the deadly no-go zone for Gazans.

One section of the embankment near the al-Mawasi camp is more than 1.5km beyond where the Yellow Line was originally mapped. Another section in Khan Younis is positioned more than 500m over it.

News.title: Olivia Dean nominated and  Lily Allen snubbed in Mercury Prize list
News.content:
Olivia Dean's campaign to collect every major music award in existence continues, with a nomination for this year's Mercury Prize.

The star is among the favourites to win the Â£25,000 prize, which recognises outstanding albums, after her second record, The Art of Loving, won album of the year at both the Brits and the Mobo Awards.

Sir Paul McCartney also receives his first ever Mercury nomination, aged 84, for the nostalgia-laden The Boys of Dungeon Lane, while Suede, Jade, Raye and Nia Archives are also in contention.

But there was a surprise omission for Lily Allen, whose scathing break-up album, West End Girl, was one of the biggest critical and commercial successes of the last 12 months.

The record examines the collapse of her marriage to actor David Harbour in unvarnished detail. Reviews praised its candour and musical invention, calling Allen's work "breathtaking and heartbreaking", external and "a brutal, tell-all masterpiece", external.

Artists submit themselves for the prize, making it impossible to determine whether Allen was snubbed or simply not in contention - but she was previously nominated for her 2018 album No Shame.

Other notable omissions include Harry Stylesâ Kiss All The Time, Disco Occasionally and Gorillazâ sweeping meditation on grief, The Mountain.

News.title: Watch: Giant iceberg turns over near  Greenland's coast
News.content:
A massive iceberg was seen turning over off the coast of Greenland, near Ilulissat.

Video captured by an eyewitness showed the moment the iceberg turned over, creating waves close to the coastal city.

Ilulissat is home to the Unesco listed Ilulissat Icefjord and is located on the west coast of the island.

News.title: Mum and boyfriend jailed for girl's  murder
News.content:
Warning: This story contains distressing details

A mum and her new boyfriend have been jailed for life for the "sadistic" abuse and murder of her two-year-old daughter.

Isabelle Welsh was a "happy and thriving" child before her mother, Alexandra Walker, invited Harrison Simpson into their lives in Thornaby, Stockton, in June 2025, Teesside Crown Court heard.

A judge said Isabelle was the victim of a campaign of violent and sexual abuse at the hands of those meant to love, care for and protect her.

Simpson, 22, and Walker, 26, were both found guilty of murder and child cruelty, with Simpson also convicted of sexual abuse of a child. Simpson must serve a minimum of 28 and a half years and Walker 22 years.

Ms Justice Norton said both were "equally and jointly responsible" for Isabelle's murder and the campaign of cruelty she endured, with the couple putting up a "wall of silence, lies and obfuscation" about the last weeks of her life.

News.title: UK on track for record heat-related deaths this year, UKHSA estimates
News.content:
The UK is on track this year for the highest number of heat-related deaths since records began, according to estimates by the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA).

In a preliminary assessment, it said there were an estimated 2,877 heat-related deaths during the May and June heatwaves, almost double the figure for the whole of last year.

An estimated 753 deaths were associated with the 24-27 May heatwave and a further 2,124 with the one from 21-28 June. Definitive figures are expected in early 2027.

Both spells broke Met Office UK monthly temperature records, with 35.1C (95.2F) recorded at Kew Gardens on 26 May and 38.0C recorded at Lingwood, Norfolk on 26 June.

The current record for heat-related deaths was set in 2022, when 2,985 deaths were recorded.

Report author Dr Ross Thompson, from the UKHSA, said "while the figures are interim, they suggest that, if we experience more periods of hot weather this summer, we could see the highest number of heat-associated deaths on record".

Thompson added: "These figures highlight the significant danger that very hot weather can pose to people's health.

"This is particularly true for those who are more vulnerable including older adults and people with underlying medical conditions."

He said "as the climate becomes warmer, we can expect periods of hot weather to become longer, more frequent and more extreme", adding that it is vital the country is prepared to deal with higher temperatures.

Earlier this week parts of the UK sweltered through another heatwave that peaked on Wednesday, with temperature reaching 35.2C in Writtle, Essex.

Cooler conditions and some rain are on the way for some on Thursday and into the weekend, but likely not in the driest areas.

News.title: Zendaya and Tom Holland's decade-long Spider-Man romance in pictures
News.content:
Holland and Zendaya were just 20 and 19 years old years old when they first met in 2016, on the set of Spider-Man: Homecoming, during the film's casting and initial production.

The film showed British actor Holland as Peter Parker balancing high school life with being a superhero - Spider-Man - for the first time.

It also introduced US actress Zendaya as MJ, his awkward but intellectual classmate.

The on-screen chemistry was clear from the start and the film received good reviews but the pair denied rumours of a romance, insisting they were just close friends while promoting the movie.

They even took to Twitter [now X] to make light of the rumours. She posted: "Wait wait ... my favourite is when it says we go on vacations together HA! I haven't been on a vacation in years! hbu @TomHolland1996 ???"

Holland responded: "Does the press tour count?"

News.title: Beauty Pie founder on how she dropped out of university and built five businesses
News.content:
Kilgore didn't always know she wanted to be an entrepreneur but growing up she saw first-hand the stress that financial insecurity could cause.

"I remember deciding at eight-years-old that when I was my parents' age, I would never want to be stressed about my electric bill," she says.

That desire shaped her approach to work and risk. "I knew that working for other people wouldn't necessarily give me the freedom I wanted and at least when you are an entrepreneur, the risk is your own."

She didn't begin with a grand business plan - she moved from Canada to New York to study at Columbia University and her tuition plan fell through so she had to get a job to support herself.

"You can't sit around thinking: 'What am I going to do? You have to survive. I knew I had to use the skills I had to support myself and then I would figure it out."

She started working as a personal trainer and taking beauty classes in the evening.

"What ended up transpiring was that I was quite good at the beauty industry job," she says and eventually she dropped out of university to pursue a career in it.

News.title: Holidaymakers warned about 'explosive diarrhoea' cyclospora parasite infection
News.content:
UK holidaymakers are being warned about a nasty infectious disease called cyclosporiasis that can cause explosive diarrhoea, after a sharp rise in cases.

The UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA), external said 67 cases have been reported since April, with many of them among travellers returning from Mexico.

It comes amid an outbreak in the US that has infected more than 18,000 people across 45 states. The source hasn't been identified yet and there have been no reported deaths.

The illness is caused by a parasite, cyclospora, that can contaminate food like salads, herbs and soft fruits. It doesn't naturally occur in the UK and there is no risk of spread from person to person, experts stress.

Between 30 April and 15 July 2026, 30 cases have been reported in England, 27 in Scotland and 10 in Wales, according to the UKHSA.

Of the 52 cases with travel information available, 48 reported having travelled to Mexico, with many saying they had stayed in either the white sand beach resort area of Riviera Maya, or slightly north of there in coastal CancÃºn.

The UKHSA said those affected reported staying in "a range of different hotels and consuming a variety of different food and drink within their resort as part of an all-inclusive holiday package".

There are ongoing investigations and monitoring of the situation.

People can protect themselves while away by following good food and water hygiene measures, including drinking bottled water and eating thoroughly cooked food, even when staying in high-end all-inclusive resorts.

Experts also advise people avoid certain foods such as fresh uncooked berries and herbs, unpeeled fruit and salad items.

News.title: Virgin engineer died after traumatic brain injury
News.content:
A Virgin Atlantic engineer died after suffering a traumatic brain injury when he was hit in the face in an incident at Heathrow Airport, a coroners' court has heard.

Aircraft technician Georgie Buxton, 23, was injured on the morning of 11 June and died at St Mary's Hospital on 7 July.

Senior coroner Lydia Brown opened and suspended an inquest into his death at West London Coroners' Court on Thursday, as she is waiting to see if any criminal charges are brought.

Brown said a forensic post-mortem examination found Mr Buxton had suffered a traumatic brain injury â a craniofacial trauma.

She said: "There was an accident at Georgie's place of work. He took a trauma to the face causing him complex and tragically fatal injuries.

"He did undergo various surgeries in hospital but these were not able to save life."

Buxton started working for Virgin Atlantic two years ago, according to his LinkedIn profile, external.

News.title: Former farmer, aged 99, fulfils wish to lead cow at show one more time
News.content:
A 99-year-old care home resident in south-west Scotland has fulfilled his wish to show a cow at his local agricultural show one more time.

Staff at the Belmont Care Centre in Stranraer put a post on social media about former farmer Jackie Brown's dream in the hope of being able to see it realised.

It came to the attention of the organisers of Stranraer Show who organised for Jackie to come along to the farming event on Wednesday.

He showed one of the Ayrshire cows - just as he had done many times across his pioneering career.

News.title: Four people die trying to cross Channel in small boats
News.content:
Four people died trying to cross the Channel in small boats overnight, French officials have said.

One man died after a vessel capsized off France's northern coast late on Wednesday, with a one-year-old child among those injured.

Separately, three people were found dead aboard a small boat early on Thursday after launching from Dunkirk overnight, some 100km (62 miles) up the coast.

French officials confirmed their deaths after several hundred people crossed the Channel into the UK on Wednesday.

The first boat capsized off the coast at Hardelot around 23:30 local time (21:30 GMT) on Wednesday.

The man is thought to have been in his thirties or forties, officials added. Six other people including the child sustained minor injuries.

Local officials said the vessel was a "taxi" boat - vessels which cruise along the coast and pick up their paying customers who are waiting in the sea.

Security officials "neutralised" the boat and an investigation into the incident has been launched.

The second boat launched from the Dunkirk area overnight and was spotted near a breakwater off the coast at 06:00, the French coastguard said.

Search and rescue officials subsequently found three unconscious people on board. Their deaths were later confirmed by emergency medical personnel.

A UK government spokesperson said: "Every death in the Channel is a tragedy and a stark reminder of the dangers posed by criminal gangs exploiting vulnerable people for profit."

News.title: ScotRail apology as passengers unable to book tickets in app launch chaos
News.content:
ScotRail has apologised for the chaotic launch of its new booking app, which has left hundreds of passengers unable to book train tickets.

The operator replaced its existing system, provided by Trainline, with an updated ticketing platform for travellers on Thursday morning.

Complaints on ScotRail's social media channels saw a series of issues with passengers being forced to reset account passwords and journeys not appearing in booking searches.

ScotRail said it was working to resolve the issues and said passengers should continue using the old phone app until midday.

News.title: Suspected Kinahan gang leader faces extradition
News.content:
Suspected crime boss Daniel Kinahan is to be extradited back to Ireland, BBC News NI understands.

He was arrested in Dubai under a warrant issued by the Irish courts in April but has fought attempts to extradite him.

However, his appeals have been unsuccessful and he is due to be flown back to Ireland within weeks.

GardaÃ­ (Irish police) now expect authorities in the United Arab Emirates (UAE) to sign his extradition which will formally commence the extradition process.

GardaÃ­ expect this will take place very quickly.

Bringing the suspected gang leader back to Ireland will now be the subject of a major security operation between the gardaÃ­ and the Irish Defence Forces.

The US government imposed sanctions on him in April 2022 after he and other members of his family were identified as leaders of the Kinahan organised crime cartel.

Kinahan also had ties to the world of sport via his now defunct boxing management company MTK Global, which represented more than 100 boxers including Tyson Fury and Carl Frampton.

However, Kinahan is now expected to face the Irish courts in the coming weeks and has previously been named as the head of the drug cartel.

The Irish authorities are expected to prosecute him for his involvement in leading an organised crime group.

An extradition agreement is in place between the UAE and Ireland and it was used to extradite Sean McGovern, a "senior lieutenant" in the organised crime group.

He was sentenced to 24 years in prison last month for directing the activities of a criminal organisation.

News.title: Victims of disgraced funeral boss 'unable to get refunds'
News.content:
Some victims of disgraced undertaker Robert Bush have not been refunded for fake funeral plans he sold them, a court has heard.

The 48-year-old defrauded 172 people over 11 years to the tune of Â£562,000, Hull Crown Court was told.

He previously admitted 67 offences in relation to his business, Legacy Independent Funeral Directors in Hull, including failing to bury and cremate people, theft from 12 charities, fraudulent trading in funeral plans, and fraud.

On the fourth day of his sentencing hearing, one woman said her parents, who paid Â£2,649 each for funeral plans, were not alive "to see the justice they deserved". Another said she had not been refunded Â£5,000 for two policies.

This story contains details some might find distressing.

Wiping her eyes with a tissue, Maxine Hill told Mr Justice Hilliard the bank refused to refund the money fraudulently taken by Bush, whom Hill knew personally.

Bush visited both her parents, Margaret and John, in their own home and issued a handwritten receipt to her mother who paid him in cash.

The bank initially refunded the amount paid by Hill's father but 90 days later, the bank took the money back saying "there was no evidence that he hadn't received a product", the court heard.

Both have since died - Margaret in May 2024 and John in June 2025.

News.title: Inquiry finds MoD Afghan data breach was foreseeable failure
News.content:
The committee also questioned the decision not to provide confidential briefing to parliamentarians, with then-Defence Secretary Grant Shapps pushing back against plans to tell then-shadow defence secretary John Healey of the breach.

Thursday's report also questioned the government's overarching policy to not comment on special forces matters, describing it as "inappropriate" in the context of the breach.

The committee added that special forces involvement "should not prevent Parliament and the public from understanding how administrative failings occurred".

Dhesi said: "Secrecy has been too easily used as a shield against proper accountability in areas far removed from sensitive operations."

The role of UKSF in the resettlement scheme was also questioned by the committee after reports the breach had been due to their involvement in deciding whether to relocate Afghan special forces.

The committee was unable to establish this connection, due to the "neither confirm nor deny" policy of the government, but it did raise concerns over the handling of these cases.

In February 2024, BBC Panorama revealed that British Special Forces had been given a de facto veto over Arap applications from their Afghan counterparts seeking to relocate to safety in the UK.

Afghan special forces served alongside UKSF on some of the conflict's most dangerous missions and are considered among those at the highest risk of reprisal since the Taliban takeover.

Last year, the BBC obtained internal MoD documents - also cited in the report - showing a British Special Forces officer personally rejected 1,585 resettlement applications from Afghans with credible links to special forces in a matter of weeks, in 2023. The UKSF officer did not approve a single application during that period.

The rejections from UKSF left many in fear for their lives and former members of the Afghan special forces told the BBC they were living in hiding.

One said he had been interrogated and beaten by the Taliban before he went on the run, while another said he had escaped first but had heard the Taliban had gone to his home looking for him.

"I'm living in a very bad situation. I am in hiding and mostly my family can't live together and we cannot go out and we cannot work," he said. "I feel I have been left alone in the midst of hell."

The government had to announce a review in 2024 and since then 884 former members of Afghan special forces, who served alongside UKSF, have since had their rejections overturned.

The defence committee report outlined that the "proportion of decisions subsequently overturned demonstrates the seriousness of that failure".

The UK government closed Arap to new applications in 2025, but the report said the government had a "special responsibility" to the Afghan special forces it had wrongly rejected. Many of them had made their applications in 2021, but were still living in fear due to "government delay or error".

The defence secretary currently faces a legal challenge at the Royal Courts of Justice from former Afghan special forces who are unable to escape to the UK.

In a hearing on Wednesday, the court heard one family had "$200 left to survive".

A MoD spokesperson said: "This incident should never have happened and we acknowledge the significant impact it has had on many people.

"Thousands of eligible Afghans have already been safely relocated to the UK, where they can rebuild their lives and we are committed to ensuring that we conclude the Afghan resettlement programme by the end of this Parliament.

"We are learning the lessons from this incident and important reforms are already in place, including improved data protection standards, strengthened case-working processes and better programme governance.

"We welcome the public and parliamentary scrutiny of our actions, so we can learn more and be held to account, and we'll continue to work closely with the committee on this issue."

Pubs in Britain are facing shortages of Old Speckled Hen weeks after the ale brand was sold to a Spanish beer giant.

Estrella Damm acquired the business from Greene King earlier this month, which included Old Golden Hen, Old Crafty Hen, Old Master Hen, and Low Alcohol Old Speckled Hen.

A spokesman for the Spanish company said the beer was still being brewed and temporary issues resulting from the change in ownership had created distribution problems.

Pressure was also piled on from hot weather and the football World Cup, the company said.

While supplies are coming, pub landlords would feel the wait as a “shortage”, the company admitted. It added it was working with Greene King to “minimise the impact as much as it can”.

The shortages, first reported by The Morning Advertiser, came after the beers were transferred into Estrella Damm’s supply network.

However, the transition is now “broadly complete” so customers should soon receive stock.

Pubs in Britain are facing shortages of Old Speckled Hen ( Greene King )

Old Speckled Hen was first brewed in 1979 by Morland Brewery in Abingdon.

It was sold to Estrella Damm in May, and the deal was completed on 1 July.

The deal forms part of a broader strategic realignment for Greene King, which aims to concentrate more intently on its pub estate.

The Suffolk-based firm had said it was moving away from producing beer to be sold in retailers including supermarkets.

Old Speckled Hen brands accounted for more than half of Greene King’s beers sold in UK shops.

It was taken on by Greene King in 1999, soon becoming one of Britain’s best-selling premium ales.

TV channel Dave sponsored the beer in 2009, bringing it further publicity.

Greene King, which runs 2,500 pubs, restaurants and hotels, continues to make cask ale and craft beer including Greene King IPA and Abbot Ale.

The group said it will push ahead with the strategy from summer 2027 with the opening of a new £40 million brewery in Bury St Edmunds.

Estrelle Damm has been contacted for a statement.

Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey has a fan in author Joyce Carol Oates, who has defended it from “inappropriate” criticism levied by acclaimed translator Emily Wilson.

It is Wilson’s version of Homer’s Odyssey that inspired Nolan’s blockbuster film, but earlier this week, she said she “would be ashamed to have written any part of its script” and described its writing as “abysmal”.

In a now-viral article on the film for the London Review of Books, she argued that Nolan’s film loses the complexity that defines Odysseus (Matt Damon) and its women characters, including Penelope (Anne Hathaway), and described its narrative structure as gimmicky.

open image in gallery Joyce Carol Oates has defended Christopher Nolan's 'The Odyssey' ( Getty Images / Universal Pictures )

Blonde and We Were Mulvaneys author Oates condemned Wilson for having “a tone of dismissal and haughty superiority” that “strikes a sour note”.

She added that “rather than disagreeing with interpretations of Homer in a collegial manner, this person, who has benefited enormously from Nolan’s film, speaks in the crude language of MAGA folks attacking someone with ideas that differ from hers.”

Oates continued: “Within the world of translators, this seems all the more surprising since all translations are, presumably, subjective & not equivalent to the original text.

“One would expect a translator, of all people, beholden to a text, in service to a text, to be just a wee bit more thoughtful & respectful of others who are acting in good faith just as (she would claim) she is.”

Oates defended Nolan’s attempt to “reimagine a classic hero through the prism of his own invention”. The author levelled that she doesn’t think The Odyssey “will be considered a great classic”, but that “whatever Nolan did, it would disappoint hordes of people”.

“Most moviemakers/creators just try the best they can – it seems odd that this director has drawn such angry criticism,” she said.

open image in gallery Translator Emily Wilson launched a now-viral criticism against ‘The Odyssey’ earlier this year ( Universal Pictures )

Wilson became the first woman to publish a complete English translation of The Odyssey in 2017. In an interview with Empire magazine in November 2025, Nolan said it was the opening line of Wilson's translation – “Tell me about a complicated man” – that unlocked his approach to Odysseus.

“The genius of the character, the cleverness, the inventiveness of him, that was a huge part of what interested me. He’s not just a soldier. He’s an amazing strategist, a very wily person,” he said.

Wilson seized on that in her review, writing: “As they say at the awards shows, I was humbled to learn that Nolan has read at least the first line of my translation of The Odyssey into iambic pentameter. But I would be ashamed to have written any part of this script.”

Oates is best known for her 1999 novel Blonde, which reimagines the life of Marilyn Monroe. It was adapted into a movie in 2022, starring Ana de Armas.

News.title: Final texts sent from phone of British woman found dead in suitcase in Athens revealed
News.content:

A string of text messages was sent from the phone of a Scottish woman in an apparent attempt to cover up her death before her body was found in a suitcase in Athens, police say.

The body of Elisabeth-Jane Ross, 38, was discovered in a derelict building in the Kypseli area of the Greek capital on 18 July.

Ms Ross is believed to have died between five and seven days before she was found. However, investigators said that her phone remained highly active following her death, The Times reports.

The content of messages sent during that period has not been revealed by Greek police, the newspaper said, but the authorities believe they were sent in an attempt to cover up Ms Ross’s death and stopped once her body was discovered. No suspect has yet been identified.

open image in gallery Elisabeth-Jane Ross had been staying with a Greek friend ( Supplied )

According to local media in Greece, texts sent from Ms Ross’s phone to her family on 15 July said that she “needed some time to herself” and that she “wanted to be alone for a while”.

The Daily Mail reports that another message was sent from her phone, after police believe she had died, to a Greek friend she had been staying with days before she was found. It read: “I need some time – I’m going to a Greek island.”

The newspaper reports that investigators say the phone remains missing but was active in the area of Athens until approximately 24 hours ago.

Speaking on BBC Reporting Scotland on Thursday, The Guardian’s Athens correspondent Helena Smith said Ms Ross had been in Greece for about two weeks before she died.

The journalist said messages were then sent from Ms Ross’s phone in an apparent attempt to put those looking for her off the scent.

“She had been staying with a Greek friend here in the capital, and then she disappeared,” Ms Smith said.

“It would seem that someone had control, and I use that word very deliberately, over her mobile phone after she died, and was sending messages clearly to distract from the scent, to distract the authorities and her close friends from trying to track her down.”

Ms Ross had travelled to Greece via Cyprus from the United States, where her fingerprints were registered.

It has been reported that her identity could not be established at first because there were no signs of identification.

But Ms Ross was identified by Greek Police after Interpol examined fingerprint data.

Greek and Cypriot authorities are reportedly working together to exchange information as they try to track down the person who abandoned the suitcase containing her body.

They are also reviewing security camera footage, witness statements and other evidence in an effort to identify people who may have interacted with her and to find out more information on the circumstances surrounding her death.

A spokesperson for Greek police said: “Further details have been requested regarding when she arrived in Greece, how, and with whom.

“We cannot provide further details at this stage, as the investigation is fully under way.”

The Foreign and Commonwealth Office said: “Our thoughts are with Elisabeth’s family during this difficult time. We are providing consular support and are in contact with the local authorities.”

A Police Scotland spokesperson said: “We are aware of the death of a Scottish woman in Athens and are liaising with authorities in Greece.

“Officers are providing support to her family in Scotland.”

Stephen Fleming did always seem to possess a wonderful sense of timing. It was on 12 July that England made the decision to stand down Brendon McCullum as Test head coach and, in serendipitous circumstances, on 13 July that the man they would come to anoint as his successor began his search for a new job. It was nothing more than mere coincidence that the Chennai Super Kings and Fleming mutually parted ways so soon after his former teammate’s departure, but within three days he was expressing interest in the England role in a newspaper interview, and within three weeks impressing the ECB interview panel sufficiently for a hasty appointment after Andy Flower had withdrawn himself from consideration for the role.

Not that Fleming will arrive with undue hustle or hurry; Marcus Trescothick will take interim charge of the three Tests against Pakistan this summer before the 53-year-old begins a four-year deal ahead of the tour to South Africa in December. While Fleming has expressed a desire to spend time with his family, it is a curious situation that again highlights the mistake made by the ECB in not taking the opportunity for a clean break after the Ashes.

open image in gallery Stephen Fleming has not worked in the red-ball game as a coach ( Getty )

One might term this, then, a marriage of convenience – a coach in search of a new challenge taking over a team in need of new direction. On the face of it, Fleming’s credentials are modest: there is no red-ball coaching whatsoever on his CV, nor any past suggestion of a desire to turn away from a franchise T20 circuit he was perhaps the first coach to truly master. He had even turned England down in 2009, feeling it was too soon into his coaching career.

open image in gallery Fleming proved highly successful with Chennai Super Kings in the IPL, however ( Getty )

But this is not necessarily another jamming of a square peg into round, vacant hole. The truth is that requiring past experience of a role like being England Test coach would limit the pool to only past occupiers of the position – particularly with the complicating factor of one’s predecessor remaining as a colleague and, at times, competitor.

McCullum remains, of course, as white-ball coach, which could cause conflict; to slot in a man sufficiently close to his former teammate to have gone into business was surely a key factor in Fleming’s appointment. A similar ethos may be implemented differently with a younger side in need of fresh messaging.

“Stephen Fleming is one of the most highly respected figures in cricket, and we are very fortunate that someone of his calibre is willing to take on the challenge of being the England men’s Test head coach,” Rob Key, the ECB’s managing director of men’s cricket, said. “I believe he is the best person to guide a team stacked full of potential and turn that talent into a world-class outfit that cannot only achieve success but sustain it.”

Past stints in the County Championship, particularly at Nottinghamshire, will be cited, too, though it is tough to find an individual of Fleming’s generation who did not enrich the English game with their visiting presence. Instead, one should look to his work at CSK – in the fractured, fractioned and faction-filled world of modern cricket, a 17-year stint laden with trophies is to be commended. It will, too, have provided some insight into the scrutiny he will now come under; the symbiotic relationship forged with MS Dhoni, a laid-back but highly intuitive leader, is one that Key will hope the oft-understated Fleming can strike with Joe Root.

open image in gallery England are looking to recapture their best form in the Test arena ( Getty )

Even within the statement announcing his appointment were hints that Root’s return as captain is likely to be a temporary arrangement, though, with Fleming pointedly making reference to his excitement to work with Harry Brook. The vice-captain’s time will surely come. The ECB must, however, reflect on the paucity of choices that have forced them to go back to a 35-year-old left worn-down and worn-out by the captaincy his first time around; Root really should have been left in the ranks. But with Brook carrying a significant burden already, a reinstallation was the better of two bad options.

open image in gallery Joe Root returns as England Test captain ( PA Wire )

Fleming hopes that he can provide a more pleasurable experience for his right-hand man. “I know what it feels like to have the weight of leadership and international cricket take their toll, and when that happened to me, my love for the game was rekindled by going to Notts and winning the County Championship,” the head coach said with reference to Root. “English cricket gave that to me and it is a privilege to have this chance to give something back.”

There are other issues, mind, to be solved. Where McCullum’s task to revitalise and rejuvenate was clear on his arrival, Fleming’s assignment is tougher. England are unsettled in the top three, with Jacob Bethell a doubt for the start of the Pakistan series and Emilio Gay yet to cement his spot, and inevitably unbalanced by Ben Stokes’ retirement. There is no like-for-like replacement as a seam bowling all-rounder, which has ramifications elsewhere; it may be hard to pick a specialist spinner, for example, or build a bowling attack around an array of seamers that can sometimes feel at its best in bursts. It has felt like a team inexorably on the slide.

open image in gallery The seam-bowling, all-round prowess of Ben Stokes (right) must be replaced ( PA Wire )

Fleming may thus see a blank canvas; others, a jumbled puzzle of pieces that may not fully fit. By the time he commences his role, he will have a matter of nine months to prepare for an Ashes series that – McCullum will attest – will form a large part of his overall appraisal. England’s new head coach took on Australia 14 times during his Test career and did not once taste victory – turn their trajectory around before next summer and he will have proven a very shrewd appointment indeed.
