World.title: 'Woke' Smithsonian exhibit lionizes embattled Fauci amid conservative scrutiny of museum's messaging
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

The embattled former face of the United States' COVID-19 response is prominently displayed and heroically framed at the Smithsonian's National Museum of American History — as the network of Smithsonian institutions faces scrutiny over woke messaging from government officials.

Dr. Anthony Fauci, formerly the head of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID), has a prominent place at the museum's "Entertainment Nation" exhibit.

"As a deadly pandemic ravaged the nation, major sports leagues found themselves at the center of a debate over 'reopening' the country," a placard dedicated to Fauci says.

FAUCI'S NEWLY RELEASED COVID DIARIES REVEAL BIZARRE FIXATION ON FAME AS PANDEMIC DEATHS MOUNTED

"Amidst a cacophony of misinformation and denial, advice from Dr. Anthony Fauci, the nation’s leading epidemiologist, urged leagues to make decisions about resuming play 'based on scientific evidence and public health judgment,'" it continues. "When baseball became the first league to retake the field, Fauci threw the ceremonial opening pitch—wearing a facemask in a stadium empty of fans."

A diary kept by Fauci while the pandemic raged, recently exposed by Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., shows a man fixated on his own fame, who acknowledged answers to controversial questions in private, but said the opposite in public.

One of those controversial questions dealt with the origin of the virus. COVID-19 may have originated in a National Institute of Health (NIH) funded facility in China. While Fauci recognized privately that the virus may have accidentally escaped a lab, he stalwartly maintained the opposite in public. Fauci critics who suggested otherwise, including other doctors, were castigated. Fauci also insisted that the government was not conducting controversial gain-of-function research. That was later proved false.

FAUCI PRIVATELY TOOK CREDIT FOR COVID-19 LOCKDOWNS DESPITE PUBLIC DENIAL, NEWLY EXPOSED DIARY ENTRIES REVEAL

Alongside the Smithsonian's heroic characterization of Fauci as a man of science, the museum prominently features that Washington Nationals baseball cap, signed by the doctor, that he wore while throwing out the first pitch when MLB resumed play after lockdowns.

Fauci also repeatedly denied that he was behind the damaging pandemic-era lockdowns, but acknowledged in his diary that mayors and health officials in the country's largest metropolitan areas, including New York City and Los Angeles, were taking his advice to shut their municipalities down.

Diary posts also show that the doctor, often framed as a humble lifelong public servant, was obsessed with the attention he received during the pandemic. He extensively documented flattering news stories about himself, bragging in May 2020 that his "national and international fame is explosive and really unimaginable" and that it was "not hyperbole" to say he was "the most famous and talked about person in the country."

TRUMP ORDERS SIGNS OUTSIDE SMITHSONIAN MUSEUM AMID ROW OVER ITS DEPICTION OF AMERICAN HISTORY

The pandemic claimed 1.2 million American lives.

Fauci was grilled on Capitol Hill Wednesday before the Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs, chaired by Paul. He invoked his Fifth Amendment right against self-incrimination 111 times, failing to answer a single question.

The Smithsonian is dealing with government scrutiny of its own, both from Congress and the White House.

The American history museum's director, Anthea Hartig, was grilled before Congress last week over sexually explicit imagery, Mickey Mouse being linked to racism and a museum toolkit discussing "objectivity" as a feature of White supremacy.

The museum's MASS Action Toolkit is a mid-2010s anthology for museums that references the 2014 Ferguson, Missouri, police shooting of Mike Brown and subsequent Black Lives Matter protests. It links politeness and being on time to White supremacy.

The White House chastised the taxpayer-funded museum for pushing "one-sided, divisive political narratives."

"American taxpayers should not be funding institutions that undermine our country or promote one-sided, divisive political narratives," White House official Lindsey Halligan told Fox News Digital. "The Smithsonian Institution should present history in a way that is accurate, balanced, and consistent with the values that make the United States of America exceptional."

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The White House also released a report on July 4 that criticized the Smithsonian's portrayal of American history, and more recently, President Donald Trump ordered the National Park Service to place signs outside the museum directing visitors and passersby to an online resource that he says portrays an "accurate" version of American history.

He also blasted the museum as "woke" and "OUT OF CONTROL" on Truth Social.

Fox News' Charles Creitz and Jasmine Baehr contributed to this report.

World.title: New audio released following Nolan Wells disappearance doesn't show 'anything nefarious': retired FBI agent
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

A retired FBI agent says that new audio released following Nolan Wells' disappearance and death doesn't show "anything nefarious."

Wells, 18, went missing July 4 after a boat trip with friends to Horn Island, a barrier island off Mississippi's Gulf Coast. Crews searched the area for two days before a National Parks Service ranger found his remains on the island's northwestern tip on July 6.

Wells' friends returned to the mainland that afternoon without him. Jackson County Sheriff John Ledbetter has said investigators believe Wells chose to remain on the island, and it wasn't until later that night that his mother learned from one of his friends he was missing, prompting her to report it to authorities.

Fox News Digital obtained a recording of a call made to Sea Tow on the evening of July 4 by someone aboard the boat, who said the vessel was taking on water as it prepared to return to the mainland. The individual said there were seven people on board.

SEARCH CALLED OFF AFTER BODY MATCHING MISSING TEEN NOLAN WELLS FOUND OFF MISSISSIPPI COAST

"Hey, we’re at the west tip of Horn, and our bilge pump stopped working. We’re sinking. Can y’all please come?" an individual can be heard saying to the Sea Tow dispatcher.

When the dispatcher asked how far the water is coming inside the boat, the individual replied, "It’s coming up... we’re just sinking. I don’t know. We’re going down though."

"And is everyone on board and in good health otherwise?" the dispatcher asked.

"Yeah, everyone is on board," the individual on the boat responded.

The man heard talking to the Sea Tow dispatcher requested someone to come help un-sink the boat and get it towed back to the Fort Bayou launch in Ocean Springs, Mississippi.

NOLAN WELLS INDEPENDENT AUTOPSY DOESN'T POINT TO FOUL PLAY, FORMER MEDICAL EXAMINER SAYS

The dispatcher then spoke with a captain, who said he was already on the phone with a man who owned the boat, a relative of the teen who called, and said those on the boat were in a "panic" because the boat wouldn't crank.

SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS

"It sounds like a bunch of kids on board on Horn Island," the dispatcher told the captain. "He’s saying the boat is sinking and he’s on Horn Island. It’s just unfortunate, he’s just a kid. It’s a lot going on.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE

"He wants you guys to go out there and un-pump the boat and then tow it in," the dispatcher said.

The captain said the boat's owner told him the teens didn't "need any help right now, but if something changes, he'll call me back."

FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X

Sea Tow didn't end up towing the boat.

Former FBI agent Jonathan Gilliam told Fox News Digital he doesn't believe the Sea Tow audio points to any signs of foul play, as some people on social media have claimed.

WATCH: Retired FBI agent says nothing 'nefarious' in newly released Nolan Wells boat audio

GOT A TIP?

"I don't hear anything nefarious... it just sounded like there was a lot of stuff going on, that they were taking on water — not panic as much as this young person was trying to resolve a situation in a party atmosphere."

Gilliam also pointed out that the call itself undercuts the idea of a cover-up.

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

"By the way, they're taking on water. They're going to be calling for assistance, which could lead to authorities. If they had done something, that'd be a very bad time for a person who'd done something nefarious to call out people and for them to get away with something. So I don't think it added anything to the conspiracies of something having occurred knowingly in a nefarious manner."

Several of Wells' friends told authorities he "chose to remain at the island" with an unidentified female rather than return to the mainland with the group he arrived with, according to a Mississippi Department of Marine Resources police report obtained by Fox News Digital.

GET BREAKING NEWS BY EMAIL

According to the police report, authorities "did not have reason to believe there were any water related exigencies or emergencies and he believed the most likely scenario was Nolan rode in on another vessel but did not have his phone in his possession to make contact with family."

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

During a July 22 news conference, attorney Ben Crump revealed that an area of "red discoloration" was found on Wells' head, but said Dr. Roger Mitchell, who performed an independent autopsy, couldn't come to a conclusion on a cause or manner of death "pending further investigation." An official autopsy into Wells' death hasn't been completed.

Wells was a wide receiver at Southwest Mississippi Community College and had hopes to play at the Division 1 level, according to Crump, an attorney for his family.

World.title: Trump accused China of an 'election security nightmare' but then undercut his own warning
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Less than two weeks after accusing China of carrying out an "unprecedented election security nightmare," President Donald Trump has not changed his posture toward Beijing and is moving ahead with plans to host Chinese President Xi Jinping in September.

"This data loss presents an unprecedented election security nightmare," Trump said in a July 16 address. "The intelligence even shows that China assigned a data exploitation unit specifically to this new project."

Intelligence officials, he said, "worked to actively suppress and downplay information about the extent of China’s sinister election meddling."

TRUMP’S UPBEAT CHINA MESSAGE COLLIDES WITH DEEPENING BEIJING RIVALRY

Trump did not claim China changed votes or altered election results. Instead, he argued Beijing engaged in an influence campaign aimed at shaping U.S. public perceptions.

But within days of the address, Trump undercut the urgency of his own warning. Asked whether China would face consequences, he said the alleged activity "took place a long time ago" and suggested it reflected the broader intelligence rivalry between the two countries.

"They do things, and we do things to them," Trump said July 21 in remarks to reporters. "I’ll be honest, we do things to them, too. It’s not a one-way street."

So far, the fallout has been directed almost entirely inward. Trump ordered investigations into U.S. officials who handled the intelligence, while his trade and diplomatic engagement with Beijing has continued largely unchanged.

Trump’s posture toward TikTok has undergone a similar shift. He sought to ban the platform during his first term over national-security concerns tied to its Chinese ownership but joined it during the 2024 campaign. Five days after Trump’s address, most Cabinet members launched official accounts after the Justice Department cleared federal employees to use TikTok under its new U.S.-controlled ownership.

It also remains unclear when Trump first learned of the intelligence or whether he knew about it before traveling to Beijing in May. A White House official confirmed Xi's Sept. 24 visit will proceed but did not answer questions about when Trump was briefed or whether anyone accused of withholding the intelligence remains in government.

The Chinese embassy could not immediately be reached for comment on the planned visit.

Newly declassified records released by the administration provide fresh details about China’s alleged collection and analysis of American voter information and reveal an internal intelligence debate over whether Beijing’s broader activities amounted to election interference. But the documents also establish less than some of Trump’s rhetoric appeared to suggest.

CHINA DISMISSES TRUMP ELECTION INTERFERENCE ACCUSATIONS AS 'ENTIRELY FABRICATED,' THREATENS COUNTERMEASURES

During the July 16 address, Trump said China had acquired 220 million U.S. voter files containing names, addresses, phone numbers and political affiliations. He said Beijing assigned a unit to exploit the information which had the potential to use it to register voters or engage in other "nefarious activities."

Trump called the findings "stunning" and the broader vulnerabilities "a cyber threat aimed at the very heart of our democracy."

The president accused intelligence officials of working to "actively suppress and downplay" China’s "sinister election meddling." He cited an internal message saying officials had "deliberately massaged" a pending President’s Daily Brief and another in which an FBI official described "running a shadow government."

'SHADOW GOVERNMENT': TRUMP CLAIMS INTEL COMMUNITY BRAGGED ABOUT HIDING CHINESE MEDDLING

Trump directed the Justice Department, FBI, CIA and Office of the Director of National Intelligence to investigate. He said those responsible should be fired and potentially prosecuted.

The roughly 270 pages of released records show that Chinese entities amassed and analyzed large quantities of American voter information.

The figure at the center of Trump’s announcement appears to come from a record showing that a Chinese entity possessed an unspecified dataset containing approximately 204.8 million American voter records. The document does not identify its source or explain how it was obtained.

Other records describe China analyzing registration information from 18 states and a Chinese actor downloading publicly available historical voter information from six states. The documents do not show that China altered voter rolls, changed ballots or penetrated vote-counting systems.

The documents also include a raw FBI report alleging that China planned to manufacture fraudulent U.S. driver’s licenses that could be used to cast mail ballots for Joe Biden. The allegation came from a single uncorroborated source, and the report was recalled the day it was distributed and never reissued.

There was no evidence that any fraudulent votes were actually cast.

Emily Harding, director of the Intelligence, National Security, and Technology Program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, wrote that China "likely gained little advantage" from voter records that were largely publicly available or available for purchase.

Harding wrote that the internal exchanges showed "an honest, and valuable, analytical debate" rather than a cover-up. She noted that the recalled FBI report relied on unreliable third-hand information and said references to the election were removed from one briefing so a specialized election-security team could address the issue.

Trump did not explain which American activities he considered comparable to China’s collection and analysis of voter information.

There is some public record behind Trump’s suggestion that the intelligence competition runs both ways — but China does not hold free national elections.

Trump authorized the CIA in 2019 to conduct a covert influence campaign against China, Reuters reported in 2024. According to three former U.S. officials, operatives used false online identities to circulate damaging but fact-based information about Xi’s government and attempt to shape public opinion inside China.

The CIA declined to confirm the program. Documents leaked by former National Security Agency contractor Edward Snowden also showed the National Security Agency penetrating Chinese networks, including the systems of telecommunications giant Huawei.

Trump expressed a similar view during his May visit to Beijing, although he was speaking then about Chinese espionage more broadly.

"They spy on us," Trump told Fox News host Sean Hannity during the trip. "We spy on them too, I guess."

Trump otherwise used the visit to promote closer economic ties. He traveled with leading American executives, called Xi a "great leader" and said it was an "honor" to be his friend.

The White House later announced that the two countries had agreed to establish boards of trade and investment. China also committed to purchase 200 Boeing aircraft and at least $17 billion in American agricultural products annually through 2028, according to the administration.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Preparations for Xi’s visit continued after Trump’s address.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio met Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi July 22 to lay the groundwork for what he called a "very positive" visit but said Trump’s election allegations were not discussed. Rubio added that it would be "reckless and irresponsible" for the two powers not to maintain a relationship.

China has denied interfering in the 2020 election. Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Lin Jian called the allegations "entirely fabricated" and urged the United States to stop using China as an election issue.

World.title: Daily eating habit linked to better brain health in older adults, new research suggests
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Eating within a shorter daily window could help support brain health as people age, according to new research.

Preliminary findings presented at NUTRITION 2026 — the American Society for Nutrition’s annual meeting in Maryland — suggests that older women who ate within eight to nine hours per day saw slight cognitive improvement compared to those who spread their meals over about 12 hours each day.

The small six-month trial included 47 postmenopausal obese or overweight women aged 50 to 79. They were each advised to reduce their daily food intake by about 500 calories.

INTERMITTENT FASTING'S REAL BENEFIT MAY COME AFTER YOU START EATING AGAIN

Study findings

The participants were divided into two groups. One ate in a time-restricted window within an average of 8.2 hours, usually from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. The other group ate across a 12.3-hour window, according to a news release.

Both groups lost about 15 pounds over six months, but those in the shorter eating-window group performed better on cognitive tests measuring spatial planning and problem-solving.

The shorter-window group also showed fewer errors on memory and learning tests, but no meaningful differences in reaction time or multi-tasking ability.

PEOPLE LOST WEIGHT WHILE EATING SIGNIFICANTLY MORE FOOD — HERE'S THE SECRET

"These outcomes suggest a better ability to remember information during everyday tasks and reduce mistakes related to memory, attention and problem-solving," lead researcher Sue Shapses, Ph.D., a professor at Rutgers University and Rutgers-RWJ Medical Center, said in a press release. "Reductions in the eating window predicted greater improvements."

Although the pilot study included only a small number of participants, the researchers believe that time-restricted eating may support brain health by regulating circadian rhythm, reducing inflammation and improving metabolic health.

"Think of meal timing as one potential piece of the puzzle rather than a magic bullet."

Losing weight alone can help "ward off some of the aging-related cognitive decline," according to Shapses.

"And these data suggest there may be additional benefits if you stop eating four hours prior to going to sleep and reduce food intake to eight to nine hours per day, compared to the usual eating window of 12 hours per day."

Women, as well as adults who are overweight or obese, tend to face a higher likelihood of developing Alzheimer’s disease and other forms of dementia as they age, according to the researchers.

How might meal timing help the brain?

Lauri Wright, Ph.D., director of nutrition programs and associate professor at the USF College of Public Health, who was not involved in this research, reflected on these findings in an interview with Fox News Digital.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"This is an interesting study because it suggests that when we eat may matter in addition to what and how much we eat," she said. "That suggests meal timing itself may have played a role, not just weight loss."

"The results are promising, but we need larger, longer studies before recommending time-restricted eating specifically to improve brain health."

Experts are still learning about how intermittent fasting affects the brain, although "several biological mechanisms are being considered," Wright noted.

"Giving the body a longer overnight break from eating may improve insulin sensitivity, reduce chronic inflammation, support healthy circadian rhythms and allow cells more time for repair and maintenance," she said. "Those processes are all linked to healthy brain aging."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

From a practical standpoint, eating within a shorter daily window often leads people to consume fewer calories, which can promote weight loss, according to New York-based certified holistic nutritionist Robin DeCicco.

"We know that maintaining a healthy weight helps with virtually everything," she told Fox News Digital. "Eating within a restricted window helps people cut calories."

"When you fast or... have periods of time where you're not just eating throughout the whole day, it does help to lower markers of inflammation and certain sources of oxidative stress."

CLICK HERE TO 

Many people have reported "feeling better" when fasting, DeCicco noted — especially those who have inflammatory conditions, which can include neurological disorders like Alzheimer’s and dementia.

"When you're fasting, you're giving your organs a chance to rest, you're giving the digestive system a chance to ‘rest and digest,’" she added.

Intermittent fasting isn’t the only way to support cognitive health, Wright countered.

"Regular physical activity, adequate sleep, controlling blood pressure and blood sugar, avoiding smoking, maintaining social connections and following an overall healthy dietary pattern, such as the Mediterranean diet, have much stronger evidence for protecting cognitive function over time," she said. "Think of meal timing as one potential piece of the puzzle rather than a magic bullet."

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Intermittent fasting "isn’t appropriate for everyone," Wright warned, adding that she would advise against it for children and teens, pregnant or breastfeeding women, anyone with a history of an eating disorder, and people with diabetes who are taking insulin.

DeCicco agreed that fasting should be recommended and monitored by a medical professional, especially for those who take certain medications or have certain conditions.

World.title: Trump tells foreign students: Overstay your visa, face the consequences
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Amid all the noise in Washington and simultaneous lack of legislation coming out of Congress, there have been some quiet wins for accountability in our visa system.

One recent win is an administrative final rule that requires foreign students to comply with their visas. Administrative rules govern how the government implements the law in practice.

Most foreign students who qualify get an F-1 visa, which allows them to study at the undergraduate or graduate level. Some get a J-1, which is for international exchange visitors.

RUBIO PUSHES BACK ON INDIA'S CONCERNS OVER US VISA CURBS, SAYS POLICY MUST BE 'AMERICA FIRST' UNDER TRUMP

When student visa holders arrive here, they are given permission to enter under what’s called "duration of status." That means that as long as they are full-time students, they can stay.

An earlier rule allows students, while still on their student visas, to work in "Optional Practical Training" for a year, with another two years if they have STEM degrees. The definition of STEM is 16 pages long and generous. Because foreigners on OPT are working using their student visa (remember – "duration of status") their employers are not required to pay into Social Security and Medicare. That’s a discount of up to 15% for hiring foreign workers instead of Americans.

"Duration of status" combined with OPT incentivizes marginal students not to complete their degrees in due course and, as they originally claimed they would, go home.

TRUMP ADMINISTRATION ORDERS GREEN CARD APPLICANTS TO LEAVE THE US, APPLY FROM THEIR HOME COUNTRIES

The education-migration complex is desperate to keep the foreign student gravy train on the rails. They make the new rule seem as if it is cutting off opportunity. Quite the opposite: it’s about asking for responsibility.

It’s not hard to complete a bachelor’s degree in four years, especially for foreign students. Americans can apply to college knowing they’ll need to work or apply for aid and grants. Foreigners, meanwhile, are required to show consular officers in their visa interview that they can afford the entire course of study, including tuition, lodging and incidental costs. They are not, in theory, supposed to work.

If they decide to earn a master’s after their bachelor's, or even a Ph.D., the new rule just means they have to go home, apply for a new visa, and show the consular officer they are credible students, can afford the entire course of study and intend to return home when done.

TRUMP PUTS ASYLUM LAWYERS ‘ON NOTICE’ WITH NEW FRONT IN WAR ON FRAUD

That’s what is really freaking out the edu-crats. Many foreign students intend to stay in the U.S. Some never go to school at all; these get dropped from the Student and Exchange Visitor Information System (SEVIS) maintained by DHS. They should then be deported, but many make frivolous asylum claims to remain.

Others do go to school, but drag it out over many years, taking minimal classes to maintain status while working, often illegally. Schools don’t mind, as long as the fees keep coming.

But we should mind. America doesn’t need to import this type of low-motivation student.

The education-migration complex is desperate to keep the foreign student gravy train on the rails. They make the new rule seem as if it is cutting off opportunity. Quite the opposite: it’s about asking for responsibility.

What America needs even less are students who come here pre-programmed with hostility to the United States, Western civilization and capitalism, who spend their time protesting on campus.

Some foreign students on campuses across the United States have been here for years, spending far too much time and energy protesting Israel, capitalism, ICE and Western civilization instead of hitting the books and getting a degree. These permanent students aren’t adding to our national prosperity, security or unity.

America wants students who come, study and finish their degrees. The left will tell you that foreign students are all the best of the best. Not so. As a consular officer, I did thousands of student visa applications in Africa, Asia and Europe. I’ve seen everything from applicants with full scholarships at MIT and Harvard to those wanting to study English at a community college near their uncle, who just happens to own a motel or gas station.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

America welcomes legitimate students. We will always have room for the most talented and entrepreneurial to stay. But our universities are not there to facilitate mass economic migration.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The unemployment rate for recent American college graduates is 5.7%, higher than the national average. They need our support, not millions of foreign graduates to compete with.

The new rule on student visas is timely and welcome. Future presidents would be wise to keep it instead of caving to the education and migration lobby.

World.title: Senate committee postpones vote on Todd Blanche’s nomination over disagreements with GOP senators
World.content:
WASHINGTON — The Senate Judiciary Committee postponed its vote on whether to advance Todd Blanche’s nomination to be attorney general after two Republican senators said they did not receive written assurances they were seeking from the Justice Department surrounding a settlement between President Donald Trump and the IRS.

The GOP-led committee was scheduled to vote Thursday morning on sending Blanche’s nomination to the full Senate, but Republican Sens. John Cornyn of Texas and Thom Tillis of North Carolina, both of whom have clashed with Trump and neither of whom faces re-election in November, have complicated Blanche’s path to confirmation with their demands from the Justice Department.

Cornyn and Tillis met with Judiciary Committee Chair Chuck Grassley, R-Iowa, on Wednesday afternoon as they said they were continuing to negotiate with the Justice Department.

A spokesperson for the committee said Wednesday evening that the vote would not happen Thursday.

“Chairman Grassley works to set President Trump’s nominees up for success in committee, not failure,” the spokesperson said in a statement. “Senators Cornyn and Tillis want written assurances from the Department of Justice regarding the Trump-IRS settlement. Tomorrow’s markup is postponed as work continues to secure sufficient support in committee to favorably report Attorney General-nominee Todd Blanche, who is highly qualified for the job.”

A Justice Department official said Wednesday night that the Justice Department has transmitted new language to Cornyn and Tillis and that conversations to resolve their concerns continue.

Much of Cornyn and Tillis’ negotiations with the Justice Department has been around the “anti-weaponization” fund that was established under a purported settlement between Trump and the executive branch, which he controls, over a lawsuit he filed over the disclosure of his tax records. The suit led to a five-year prison sentence for a former IRS contractor.

A federal judge in Virginia indefinitely blocked the fund after a former Jan. 6 prosecutor sued. A federal judge in Florida found that Trump’s IRS lawsuit was brought in “bad faith” for an “improper purpose” and ordered sanctions against several people involved, including Blanche.

But the settlement agreement also had provisions that offered Trump — along with his family members and companies — some protection from IRS audits.

Tillis said Wednesday that his demands to the Justice Department have been consistent: kill the anti-weaponization fund and narrow the settlement with Trump involving IRS audits.

“Get whoever the president’s lawyers are the parties to the agreement to sign off on that, we’re good to go,” Tillis said before the vote was postponed.

He said he has been in “constant daily contact with the DOJ” and that it was “working on a draft right now.” After the meeting with Grassley and Cornyn, Tillis said that it appeared the Justice Department has agreed to his terms on the anti-weaponization fund but that he still needed clarification on who is protected against IRS audits through the settlement.

Cornyn, who lost his primary race to Trump-endorsed Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, said Wednesday that it is Grassley’s decision when the vote is held.

It was not immediately clear Wednesday evening when the vote would take place.

Cornyn told reporters that Blanche’s team had failed to provide written proposals to modify the document release that was signed in the tax dispute with Trump and his organization.

“I haven’t seen a single piece of writing that is responsive to what I’ve requested,” Cornyn said.

He later said Trump’s claim that he is holding up the vote because Trump didn’t endorse him in the GOP primary is “a convenient excuse for not cooperating with the Judiciary Committee’s appropriate role in judicial confirmations.”

As the talks continued Wednesday night, the administration was pointing the finger at Cornyn, making some of the same accusations from earlier in the day.

According to a senior administration official, people familiar with the conversations described the senator as continually moving the goal posts, canceling meetings and refusing to communicate — no matter what the Justice Department offered.

Cornyn’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment Wednesday evening.

Blanche, who previously was Trump’s personal defense attorney, had served in the key No. 2 position at the Justice Department until Trump fired Pam Bondi as attorney general in April amid frustrations with her leadership.

After he took over as the acting attorney general, Blanche told NBC News in April that Americans should be “happy” that Trump was so involved in Justice Department matters. Less than two weeks later, the Trump administration brought a case against former FBI Director James Comey, a longtime Trump foe, over an Instagram photo of seashells.

Following the Comey indictment, Trump was said to be happy with Blanche’s performance and ultimately ended up nominating him for the job permanently. Comey’s legal team argued in a court filing this week that the seashells case came about because Blanche was seeking to “please President Trump” during his “audition” for the role.

During his confirmation hearing this month, Blanche said he was not a “yes man” for Trump.

World.title: Trump’s Iran war frustration and on the frontline of France’s wildfire: Morning Rundown
World.content:
Without a clear endgame for the Iran war, Trump is growing frustrated. The president adds another D.C.-area renovation to his list of projects. And why some former MLB players feel the league is turning its back on them in retirement.

Here’s what to know today.

Trump is ‘exasperated’ on Iran as top officials can’t agree on a strategy

Iran vowed to “punish” the United States today after the American military said it had completed a “heavy wave of strikes” overnight. It was the latest retaliation for an attack by Tehran on U.S. forces in the Middle East. The renewed fighting came hours after President Donald Trump threatened to escalate the war as it enters its sixth month.

This is Morning Rundown, a weekday newsletter to start your day. Sign up here to get it in your inbox.

As the president weighs what to do next, he has grown frustrated, according to people familiar with discussions, because his top aides and allies can’t agree on a goal of the war — whether it has to do with a nuclear threat, the Strait of Hormuz or Iran’s missile and drone program — and therefore can’t plan for an endgame.

Last week, Trump erupted during a meeting with some of his top national security officials and yelled expletives, two sources familiar with the discussion said. Two others familiar with the White House discussions on the war said the president and his top aides are not pleased with the status quo.

“The president is exasperated,” according to a Trump ally. “I don’t think he believed it was going to be this difficult to get the Iranians to agree to a deal.” They added that “there was not a real strategy for how long or what they should do to get to the endpoint.”

The disagreement raises the possibility of whether the U.S. is trapped in an increasingly unpopular conflict against an adversary that has proved to be resilient.

Where things stand and what Trump allies have said.

Senate committee postpones vote on Todd Blanche’s nomination

00:14 Senate committee postpones Blanche attorney general vote 00:00 00:00

The Senate Judiciary Committee canceled a vote on Todd Blanche’s attorney general nomination over concerns from two Republican senators. It’s not clear when the committee vote to send Blanche’s full nomination to the Senate, which had been scheduled for this morning, would take place.

The hold up stems from Sens. John Cornyn and Thom Tillis, both of whom have clashed with Trump, as they demand written assurances from the Justice Department that it will kill an “anti-weaponization” fund and narrow who is protected from IRS audits — both related to a settlement between Trump and the IRS earlier this year.

How the Justice Department has responded.

More politics news:

Sen. Rand Paul said he will call for a vote to hold Dr. Anthony Fauci in contempt of Congress after the former head of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases invoked his Fifth Amendment right more than 100 times during a GOP-led Senate hearing about the origins of Covid.

For subscribers: Sens. Bernie Sanders and Chuck Grassley are calling on the Defense Department to perform a full-agency audit — or face penalties — as it requests more funds for the Iran war.

For subscribers: A Democratic Senate primary in Michigan will test voters’ appetites for leftward-driven populism versus a moderate establishment platform.

On the frontline battling France’s huge wildfire

01:22 NBC News’ Raf Sanchez with firefighters and volunteers in France as they battle the flames 00:00 00:00

The fire erupted seemingly out of nowhere. On the side of the road in France’s wine region, as waves of firefighting planes passed over a charred forest, flames burst out at the edge of the tree line.

Two white pickup trucks, manned by volunteers, sped toward the small fire, tackling the flames with hoses. A few minutes later, another blaze erupted just a few yards from the first.

“These small fires are like little candles,” Commander Matthieu Jomain, a fire service spokesman, told NBC News. “If we don’t put them out, we can’t win this battle.”

The encounter illustrates the challenge facing French fire crews as they battle one of the country’s largest-ever fires, four times the size of Paris. The fire has threatened the historic city of Bordeaux and forced 220,000 people from their homes, according to authorities in the region.

Read more from the heart of the blaze.

Trump adds a new D.C.-area renovation to his list or projects

Trump announced a sweeping makeover at Washington’s Dulles International Airport. The renovations include replacements of two concourses and a “magnificent” parking garage, Trump said at an Oval Office event. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the plans also include a “horseshoe rail system” to transport travelers through terminals.

The project is estimated to cost $22 billion, but it won’t be federally funded, Duffy said. That’s because “the airlines who participate in the project are going to pay for it,” he said. The administration is hopeful the project could begin next spring and be completed in two years.

What travelers at Dulles think about the airport’s current condition.

Pope Leo says his ancestors included immigrants, enslaved people and slaveholders

Pope Leo XIV discussed his family’s connection with slavery and his love of America in a one-on-one encounter with “NBC Nightly News” anchor Tom Llamas after the pontiff led a “Concert for Peace.”

In the Borgo Laudato Si’ papal gardens southeast of Rome, Llamas asked the Chicago-born pope what he loved about America. He replied, “So many things. In a sense, speaking about principles, what America stands for, the sense of freedom, the sense of opportunity, the sense of having invited for generations people from around the world to be part of America.”

Leo said his grandparents were immigrants. On his mother’s side “we have people who were both slaves and slave owners,” he said. Earlier this year, he apologized for the Catholic Church’s involvement in legitimizing slavery.

What else Pope Leo said about what it means to be an American.

Staff Pick: Aging ex-MLB stars say the league is turning its back on them

During my high school years in southwestern Ohio, I loved going to Cincinnati Reds baseball games. So I was all-in when Johnny Bench, the Reds Hall-of-Fame catcher and All-Star, called earlier this year suggesting I research inequities in retirement benefits for Major League Baseball players.

I found that retired players, who made a fraction of what current stars do, get benefits that are far less generous than what more recent players receive. They don’t receive cost-of-living increases like younger players do. They have to pay up for healthcare. And their wives get only half their pensions when they pass, versus modern players’ spouses who get 100%. Even worse, some players have identified errors in their service records, meaning they may be owed back pension pay.

The MLB generated $12 billion in revenues in 2024, but the league and players association won’t level the playing field, the men say. One retired player I spoke with told me he thinks the league is waiting for the guys to pass away. And, tragically, another retired player I spoke to for the story — Bob Lacey, a pitcher for the Oakland A’s — died before we published. Now, his widow will receive half his pension. — Gretchen Morgenson, senior financial reporter

World.title: Iran vows to ‘punish the aggressor today’ after U.S. unleashes ‘heavy wave’ of strikes
World.content:
Iran vowed to “punish” the United States on Thursday after the American military said it had completed a “heavy wave of strikes” overnight, the latest retaliation for an attack by Tehran on U.S. forces in the Middle East.

The renewed fighting shattered a brief period of calm that had seen the two sides engage with a push to revive diplomatic efforts and stave off dramatic new escalation.

But President Donald Trump said the U.S. would hit the Islamic Republic hard after its attack on an American base in Jordan. And the powerful Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) signaled the flare-up would not end there, warning early Thursday that “the aggressor will be punished today” following the U.S. strikes.

Jordan said it intercepted a new barrage from Iran, while Kuwait said an Iranian strike hit a building belonging to a Chinese company, killing one worker.

There were also signs that the war was again expanding and drawing in new countries, raising the stakes for the region and the global economy.

After Saudi Arabia joined the U.S. in striking Iran-backed militants, Egypt confirmed Thursday that a drone ignited fires on two natural gas vessels at the port of Damietta.

It was not immediately clear who was behind the drone strike — on a U.S.-owned floating storage facility and a Greek-owned tanker — but an attack there by Iran would mark a significant new expansion of the conflict to a key U.S. ally and mediator. It would also highlight the broader risk to the world’s energy supplies from the difficulty in resolving the conflict.

Asked if it was Iran during an Oval Office event on Wednesday, Trump said he had been briefed on the incident and that “it’s a little more of the same.”

“It’s going to be straightening out,” he added, without expanding on what exactly he meant. “In the meantime, we’re going to be hitting them very hard because it’s our turn to hit them.”

Trump also vowed on Wednesday to “beat the f---ing s--- out of” Iran after its Tuesday attack on American forces, according to Fox News, which cited a phone call with the president.

World.title: Deodorant for kids: Derms talk the right age for deodorant and the best ones for young skin
World.content:
We don’t always have the answers, but we have some people on speed dial who do — which is why we present to you our series FYI where we have experts explain if lip balm is actually bad, how often you should wash your hair and more.

It used to be that as kids approached their teen years, they’d start incorporating deodorant into their routine. But these days, lots of kids are reaching for it before they’ve even turned 10 years old. Because of this, brands have poured into the kids’ deodorant space in recent years, with gentler formulas aimed at tweens and even younger children.

Dermatologists say the shift tracks a real biological change. “This reflects the fact that many children are entering puberty earlier than previous generations,” says Dr. Kristina Collins, a board-certified dermatologist specializing in Mohs micrographic surgery, as well as surgical and cosmetic dermatology in Texas. “Body odor is often one of the first signs that the apocrine sweat glands are becoming active. If a child is experiencing body odor that affects their comfort or confidence, using a gentle deodorant can be appropriate.”

But is it safe for kids to wear deodorant? And if they’re going to, what should you look for in a formula? To get the answers to these questions, I spoke with Collins and another board-certified dermatologist.

Is deodorant safe for kids?

Deodorant is generally safe for kids to use, including during those early tween years when body odor first shows up. That said, kids’ skin tends to be more sensitive than adult skin, so the formula matters more than it might for a grown-up reaching for whatever’s under the sink.

“Heavy fragrances may trigger irritation or allergic reactions and alcohol-heavy formulas can sting or dry out the skin,” says Collins. “If your child has sensitive skin, even ingredients that are ‘natural’ can trigger allergic reactions.”

Translation: It’s worth paying closer attention to labels and doing a bit of trial and error to find something that works for your child’s skin, rather than assuming any deodorant will do.

At what age should a kid start wearing deodorant?

There’s no universal starting line for deodorant use and it really comes down to your child’s own body, not a birthday on the calendar. “It is based on when the sweat glands become active, which is different in everybody,” says Dr. Debra Jaliman, a board-certified dermatologist in New York City. “Most kids can start once body odor becomes noticeable, typically between the ages of 8 and 10.”

The easiest way to know it’s time is if you or your child start noticing a change in smell, especially after gym class, recess, or a hot day; that’s usually the signal that their apocrine sweat glands (ones located in your armpit that secrete oily sweat) have kicked in. At that point, introducing a gentle, kids’ deodorant can help with odor, comfort and confidence.

The best deodorants for kids

To come up with a list of the best deodorants for kids, I used expert guidance (find it below) to select options safe for younger skin. I also focused on trusted brands or products with at least a four-star average rating from hundreds of shoppers.

I regularly use Tubby Todd products and love how gentle they are, so their Deo Stick is an easy pick for sensitive skin. It’s aluminum- and baking soda-free, using tapioca starch and magnesium hydroxide (ingredients our experts say are gentle enough for kid skin) to absorb wetness and fight odor-causing bacteria. According to the brand, it is gentle enough for kids ages 6 and up.

Level Up Boys Deodorant is made specifically for young, sensitive skin. It has an Ocean Fresh scent and is free of aluminum, alcohol and parabens. Similar to the Tubby Todd option, it uses natural tapioca starch to absorb wetness. Reviewers note that the scent is pleasant without being overpowering, and say that it’s effective for 24 hours.

Evereden’s deodorant has an aluminum-free formula that’s made without baking soda or silicones. It contains vitaminsE and B5 to nourish skin and it is dermatologist-tested, according to the brand. It also has a sweet scent of rose, strawberry, and vanilla.

This deodorant is free of aluminum, parabens, phthalates, dyes and baking soda and contains shea butter to keep underarms soft and hydrated. It’s dermatologically tested and vegan, with a sweet watermelon and peach scent. The bright packaging is also appealing for younger kids.

This deodorant delivers 24-hour odor protection without aluminum, parabens or phthalates, according to the brand. It’s hypoallergenic and dermatologist-tested for sensitive skin, glides on clear without white marks, according to parents who’ve bought it, and it comes in a playful gummy burst scent. Parents also say it helps kids who get sweaty and stinky in gym class or on the playground, and that they like that it isn’t irritating.

Want more from NBC Select? 

How to shop for deodorant for kids

Both Collins and Jaliman recommend starting kids with deodorant rather than antiperspirant, since most children simply need help with odor rather than sweat reduction (which is what antiperspirant does — more on that below). Beyond that, they suggest looking for gentle formulas with minimal, recognizable ingredients rather than long lists of additives.

For kids with sensitive skin in particular, both dermatologists recommend opting for fragrance-free options or those with only light fragrance, since heavier scents and unnecessary extras are more likely to cause irritation on young, developing skin.

Do kids need antiperspirant?

Deodorant and antiperspirant often get lumped together, but they do different jobs. Deodorant works by masking and reducing odor, while antiperspirant actually blocks sweat production, typically using aluminum-based compounds.

“For most children, deodorant alone is sufficient because it helps reduce odor without affecting the body’s natural sweating process,” says Collins. “Antiperspirants contain aluminum salts that temporarily reduce sweating and are typically only necessary if a child has excessive sweating that interferes with daily life. If excessive sweating is present, it’s worth discussing with a pediatrician or dermatologist to determine the best treatment.”

In other words, reach for deodorant first, and don’t feel pressure to introduce antiperspirant unless your child is dealing with sweating that goes beyond the normal, everyday kind. And even then, talk to a doctor before you add aluminum and other ingredients to their body care routine.

Frequently asked questions Is there a difference between kid and adult deodorant? Not as much as the packaging might suggest. “The biggest differences are usually in the fragrance and marketing,” says Collins. “Children’s deodorants often use milder fragrances and are more likely to be formulated for sensitive skin. But from an ingredient standpoint, many are very similar to adult deodorants.” In many cases, the kid-focused branding is less about a fundamentally different product and more about making an everyday routine feel approachable for a first-time user. Is there anything else you can do to help prevent body odor in kids? Deodorant alone isn’t the whole equation. Both Collins and Jaliman emphasize that good hygiene habits are just as important, if not more so, in keeping body odor in check. That means taking daily showers or baths, especially after sports or physical activity, and wearing clean clothes and breathable fabrics that don’t trap sweat and bacteria against the skin. Building these habits alongside deodorant use can go a long way in helping kids feel fresh and confident as their bodies go through changes.

Meet our skin care experts

At NBC Selected, we work with experts with specialized knowledge and authority based on relevant training and/or experience. We also ensure all expert advice and recommendations are made independently and without undisclosed financial conflicts of interest.

Dr. Kristina Collins is a board-certified dermatologist specializing in Mohs micrographic surgery, as well as surgical and cosmetic dermatology in Texas.

Dr. Debra Jaliman, is a board-certified dermatologist in New York City and author of “Skin Rules.”

Why trust NBC Selected?

I am a commerce editor at NBC Selected and a journalist who regularly covers wellness, beauty, home and lifestyle. I have written about whether deodorant concealer really works, if beauty pillows actually ward off wrinkles, the benefits of tranexamic acid and more. I’m also a mom of two who is studying up for the days when my kids hit puberty. For this story, I spoke with two board-certified dermatologists on what you should know about kids’ deodorant.

World.title: Montana man, impaled by trekking pole, hikes out of mountains to get help
World.content:
Billings, Montana — David Cifaldi and his two hiking companions were crossing Montana's ominous Froze-to-Death Plateau and approaching the top of the state's highest peak when their adventure took a bizarre and dangerous turn: Cifaldi slipped and impaled himself on his trekking pole as he fell.

The 44-inch steel-tipped pole passed through the flesh beneath Cifaldi's left arm, missing any vital organs, and protruded from his back. After conferring with his friends - and considering the high cost of a helicopter rescue - Cifaldi knew who would save him: himself.

"I was like, 'We've got to get off this mountain.' And they're both like, 'I don't know about that,'" Cifaldi said of his friends' initial reaction. "I'm pretty confident this is outside my chest wall. 'Tis but a flesh wound."

This photo provided by David Cifaldi shows Cifaldi after he impaled himself on a trekking pole while attempting to climb Montana's highest summit, Granite Peak, on July 20, 2026. David Cifaldi via AP

The 32-year-old nurse, who works in wound care at a Billings, Montana, hospital, did a self-assessment. He was alert. There was little pain or blood. And the pole wasn't moving. The group used a satellite-based communication device, a Garmin inReach, to contact local authorities and inform them of their plan to self-rescue.

Then they started hiking out. They carefully descended from the plateau along an unmarked route, navigating through boulders and snowfields before bushwhacking their way to an established trail.

After more than six hours in which they traveled about 10 miles and descended roughly 5,000 feet, the group reached a trailhead where one of them, Cifaldi's friend Jesse Ross, had parked a vehicle.

"The only reason it was possible at all was his confidence," Ross recalled. "Who are we to say anything? He's the medical person. Our job is just to support at that point."

Cifaldi had long wanted to climb Granite Peak. At 12,800 feet, Montana's tallest mountain is prone to unpredictable weather including dangerous lightning storms and bitter cold. Hundreds of people annually try to reach the rocky summit; many come up short. In 2019, authorities said a 65-year-old Minnesota man who was an experienced climber fell about 150 feet to his death after reaching nearly the top of Granite Peak with his son.

As Cifaldi and his companions started hiking out, the pole awkwardly sticking out of his side, Stillwater County Search and Rescue team commander Ty Williams monitored the group's progress via a dispatcher who took calls from the group.

The first call came in at 9:44 a.m. on July 20, right after Cifaldi impaled himself. At 1:30 p.m. the trio said they were getting closer to the trailhead and to let the nearest hospital know they were coming, Williams said.

"There was no danger to anybody else. He didn't want our help and so we're not going to essentially violate his rights or go against his wishes by forcing our help on him," Williams said.

By about 3:30 p.m., the hikers were in Ross' vehicle, headed to the nearest clinic, Cifaldi said.

When they arrived, they were told Cifaldi needed more advanced treatment, in Billings. So they got back in Ross' truck and kept driving to the hospital where he works, St. Vincent Regional Hospital.

Doctors removed the pole, bandaged him up and Cifaldi was back at work this week.

"I think 99 times out of a hundred I would make the same decision," Cifaldi said as he sat in Ross' front yard in Billings. "Search and rescue coming to help you is free. The flight's not. That was a factor in me deciding to self-rescue. But the fact that I had two experienced great friends with me and we had the ability to contact search and rescue if something went wrong made that a lot more of an easy decision."

World.title: White House levels new allegation that China swept up voter data
World.content:
The Trump administration on Thursday reiterated its view that China's alleged efforts to collect millions of American voter registration files constituted election interference — an allegation leveled by President Trump in a primetime address two weeks ago.

The White House said the voter files that were swept up by China "included non-publicly available data," in a fact sheet approved by the CIA, National Security Agency, Department of Homeland Security and Office of the Director of National Intelligence.

The fact sheet did not specify what private information was obtained or which states were impacted. An administration official told reporters the U.S. intelligence community believes China purchased, stole or hacked files, but it cannot confirm what percentage was taken through those methods.

The White House also said Chinese cyber actors "acquired voter registration data stored on commercial websites" in 2022.

The allegation that China collected 220 million U.S. voter registration files first emerged earlier this month, when Mr. Trump declassified a trove of intelligence records that he presented as evidence the U.S. election system falls "catastrophically short."

The president has sought for years to challenge the results of the 2020 election, which he lost to former President Joe Biden and has alleged — without evidence — was rigged. Intelligence agencies assessed in 2021 that China and other foreign countries did not try to interfere in technical aspects of the 2020 election, including voter registration processes.

Mr. Trump earlier this month called China's collection of voter rolls "the largest compromise of election data in history." That drew pushback from election experts, who noted that voter registration files are public and easily accessible in many states, and obtaining voter rolls would not necessarily allow foreign actors to interfere with the voting process.

Every state has slightly different rules for what voter data is public. For example, some states freely release the phone numbers and dates of birth of registered voters, while others keep them confidential.

China's effort lasted several years, the administration official said, with China obtaining tens of millions of files from 18 states in 2020 and 220 million files by 2023.

The official said the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Administration discussed whether the government should release victim notifications for Americans whose files were accessed.

Exactly how China intended to use the voter data is unclear. A 2020 assessment by the National Intelligence Officer for Cyber Issues (NIO-Cyber) said Chinese intelligence "analyzed multiple US states' … election voter data" and intended to "conduct public opinion analysis on the 2020 US general election." The document was declassified four years ago but is heavily redacted.

The White House argued Thursday that foreign powers could also carry out "malign activities" with voter data. Its fact sheet pointed to another newly released 2020 memo by NIO-Cyber that warned adversaries with access to voter registration systems could "alter data" to "prevent individual voters or groups of voters from voting." That memo said it wasn't clear whether any countries had "specific plans to manipulate election-related systems." Election experts have said public voter files cannot be used to modify registration records.

After the 2020 election, the National Intelligence Council assessed that no foreign actors — including China — attempted to alter voter registrations, the casting of ballots, vote counting or any other "technical aspect" of the 2020 election process.

There was some debate, however, over whether China tried to influence the election to help one side win. Most intelligence agencies believed China stayed on the sidelines, according to the National Intelligence Council's assessments, but the NIO-Cyber offered a minority view that Beijing tried to undermine the Trump campaign through efforts like social media posts.

China, for its part, has denied attempting to meddle in U.S. elections.

The Chinese Embassy in Washington, D.C., told CBS News earlier this month it has "all along adhered to the principle of non-interference in others' internal affairs."

World.title: Possible Russian missile crashes in Poland during Russian attacks on Ukraine
World.content:
Kyiv, Ukraine — A Russian ballistic missile and drone barrage across Ukraine overnight into Thursday killed at least eight civilians, including children, and wounded dozens of others, officials said.

The blitz expanded Russia's almost daily bombardment of Ukrainian cities as Moscow apparently looked to exploit Kyiv's critical shortage of Western-supplied anti-ballistic missile defenses.

NATO member Poland, meanwhile, was looking into Ukrainian reports that a Russian cruise missile entered its airspace during the onslaught.

The barrage spanned regions across Ukraine, including areas by the border with Poland that are far from the front line in the east of the country and where Ukraine is believed to store and manufacture weapons for its fight against Russia's more than 4-year-old invasion. Its long-range drones and missiles have battered Russia's oil sector, causing a fuel crisis there.

The attack came two days after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy met in Washington with President Trump and representatives of American defense companies, as he pleads for swifter and bigger deliveries of Patriot air defense systems that are the best way to stop Russia's ballistic assaults.

Local residents react outside a residential building partially destroyed as a result of Russian missile strikes in the western Ukrainian city of Lviv on July 30, 2026. YURIY DYACHYSHYN / AFP via Getty Images

The Iran war has drained stockpiles of the American-made interceptors. Trump has promised to grant Ukraine licenses to build its own Patriots, but production could take a long time to set up.

"Given the critical shortage of air defense missiles from our partners, our warriors are accomplishing truly incredible things, demonstrating a very high level of professionalism," Zelenskyy said on social media.

"This Russian terror once again proves that protection against the Russian missile threat is the most important task when it comes to saving the lives of our people," he said.

Zelenskyy said at least 10 Ukrainian regions were attacked, with dozens of homes, businesses and infrastructure facilities destroyed or damaged.

Russia launched more than 70 missiles, a significant number of them ballistic, he said, along with more than 280 attack drones, of which more than 260 were intercepted.

Polish airspace violated by Russian missile?

A Russian Kh-101 cruise missile crossed into Poland overnight, violating NATO airspace, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said on X.

Sybiha called it a clear demonstration that strengthening Ukraine's air defense is urgent and serves as a guarantee of wider European protection.

Polish authorities didn't immediately confirm Sybiha's comments.

But the Operational Command of the Polish Armed Forces said on X that an unidentified object flying westward in the middle of the night was tracked in Polish airspace and an F-16 fighter jet was launched to identify and intercept it.

The object disappeared from radar screens before it could be identified, the command said. A helicopter flew to its last known location, where the crew discovered a probable impact site in an undeveloped area near the village of Tarnawa-Kolonia in the Lublin province, the command wrote.

Polish authorities haven't confirmed what, if anything, crashed. Prime Minister Donald Tusk traveled to the area Thursday morning to inspect the site. Later, he said it appears the object was a Russian missile, the Reuters news service reported.

"All the indications are that it was a Russian Kh-101 ballistic missile, but we want to be 100% certain about the type of missile and who launched it," Reuters quotes Tusk as telling an emergency meeting. "There was no direct threat because the missile landed in an uninhabited area; we were ready to shoot it down had it continued its flight."

Details on Russia's strikes in Ukraine

The Russian Defense Ministry said it aimed at Ukrainian air bases, arms factories and military telecommunications and logistics facilities.

The targets included drone production factories and storage depots, a missile plant, an aircraft repair plant, a factory making electronic components, and a chemical plant, it said.

In the Dnipropetrovsk region, the Russian attack killed six people and wounded 10, Oleksandr Hanzha, head of the regional military administration, said.

Children were among the dead, he said on Telegram - a 6-year-old girl and boys aged 11 and 17.

The children's parents were killed in the same attack, but two more children were pulled alive from under the rubble, Zelenskyy said.

"It was an ordinary home, blown (to) smithereens by a ballistic missile," he said on X.

World.content: Why is FIFA Forward Enterprise met with negativity from soccer organizations around the world? A little more than a month after a very successful World Cup, FIFA, the world governing body of soccer, is cooking up something new.
