Despite all the changes aimed at discouraging asylum applicants from staying in the U.S., advocates like Cruz said it's unlikely many will leave the U.S.

"Asylum seekers don't have a choice. If they're safe here, they're likely going to stay here rather than risk their lives" by going back to their home country, Cruz said.

World.title: Here's how 'parasite' went from a laughing matter to a serious biological threat
World.content:
Here's how 'parasite' went from a laughing matter to a serious biological threat

toggle caption Brandon Bell/Getty Images

Cyclospora and Christopher Nolan's nearly three hour adaptation of The Odyssey have something in common — parasites.

For Cyclospora, that connection is easy to make. The microscopic parasite causes cyclosporiasis, the intestinal illness that has sickened thousands of Americans.

And while Odysseus does not face an intestinal parasite on his long journey home — though his voyage was still quite miserable — he encountered another kind when he returned to Ithaca. Those were the suitors who had taken over his home, courting his wife Penelope. They embodied a popular character trope in ancient Greek writing: one that originated as a form of comic relief.

Sponsor Message

As part of NPR's "Word of the Week" series, we're explaining how the word "parasite" started as a joke and became anything but funny.

A witty dinner guest in ancient Greece

The original definition of parasite or "parasitos" comes from Greek, literally translating to "alongside of (para) grain or wheat (sitos)."

The ancient Greeks used the word to describe someone, usually poor, who would entertain a wealthy person for food. The sentiment became an "institution" in ancient Greece and Rome, said Richard Martin, a classics professor at Stanford University. It turned into a comedic stock character, he said.

"You should always expect the parasite to come on stage and do crazy stuff," Martin said.

The parasite is a jokester figure who tries to derail the main character and cause confusion, with comedic names like "Bread-Chewer," Martin said. The character could also lean towards the "sleazy" side. The character was big in "New Comedy," he said, a "kind of domestic sitcom style" humor that started in fourth century B.C., specifically from the Greek playwright, Menander.

For a modern example, Martin points to the comedy duo Abbott and Costello from the 1940s and '50s. They're known for the classic "Who's on First" comedy sketch.

Sponsor Message

Craig Jendza, an associate professor of Ancient Greek and Roman Studies at Denison University, said that to audiences, the humor of the parasite laid in their uncanny ability to do anything they possibly could for food. Take, for example, plucking dandruff off another person's head, he said.

In The Odyssey, the freeloading suitors in Odysseus' home are also considered parasites — without the "comedic overtones," Jendza said. That's also implicit in the repetition of breaking "Zeus' law" that's often cited in the Nolan movie. "That's what's going on with the parasite," Jendza said. "He's exploiting those social obligations… and he's doing it for his own self-interest."

In that sense, Martin said, The Odyssey was ahead of his time: "[The suitors] are parasites in the modern sense: They give nothing, but they take everything."

A biological threat

Today, most people know of a parasite as a tiny organism, one that needs a host to live. "A parasite is something that is preying on something else," Craig Hedberg, a professor in the School of Public Health at the University of Minnesota.

There's a plausible linguistic pathway from ancient Greece, said Brian Joseph, a distinguished university professor emeritus of linguistics at The Ohio State University, since they also saw the parasite character as a "freeloader."

Martin, the Stanford professor, said doctors up until at least the 20th century understood Greek and Latin — so he can see how the ancient definition could come to describe "the kind of bug that feeds off another one." This new definition just loses the humor.

"Bring back the funny parasite," Martin said.

That brings us to the microscopic gastrointestinal parasite that's wreaking havoc right now: Cyclospora, which has caused outbreaks in at least nine states. It infects the small intestine and causes excessive diarrhea, fatigue and cramping for several weeks, said Gerardo Lopez, an associate professor of food safety and environmental microbiology at the University of Arizona.

Sponsor Message

Like the Greek parasites, Cyclospora does like to eat: "They are gaining nutrients from us," Lopez said. And their ability to attach to foods like iceberg lettuce and live inside humans is "brilliant," he said.

But unlike the literary figures, "there's nothing funny about it," Lopez said. Hedberg, the University of Minnesota professor, agrees.

"We have a lot of fun talking about diarrhea, but diarrhea isn't a fun thing to actually experience on a personal level," Hedberg said.

World.title: CBC identifies Canadian woman accused of spying at NATO military HQ
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The Canadian woman recently arrested by Belgian authorities on suspicion of spying appears to have worked for multiple government agencies before her NATO internship.

A CBC News investigation has identified the woman as Biwei Zhang, a systems engineer with a background in economics whose online resume suggests she previously worked for the Canadian Space Agency and Statistics Canada.

Zhang's public and professional profiles match the information Belgian prosecutors provided, which described the suspect as a "Canadian national of Chinese origin" who was an intern at Supreme Headquarters Allied Powers Europe (SHAPE), the military headquarters of NATO in Mons, Belgium.

The suspect's home and workplace at SHAPE were searched last Thursday, according to a media release from the Federal Prosecutor's Office. She was reportedly arrested a day later on charges of "espionage and participation in a criminal organization."

WATCH | CBC identifies Canadian woman accused of spying at NATO military HQ: CBC News identifies Canadian intern accused of spying on NATO | Duration 3:14 A CBC News investigation has identified Biwei Zhang as the Canadian intern at NATO who is facing espionage charges. She previously held positions at the World Trade Organization, the European Space Agency, the Canadian Space Agency and Statistics Canada.

Belgian courts do not publicly identify defendants in criminal investigations until the trial. As such, the Belgian prosecutor's office would not confirm the identity of the alleged spy or her counsel, telling CBC News it "never disclose[s] the identities of individuals suspected in ongoing investigations," an approach aligned with its "respect for the presumption of innocence, which must be guaranteed under all circumstances."

However, using open-source investigative techniques, CBC matched the description of Belgian authorities with identifying information on Zhang's LinkedIn, Facebook and Threads profiles, as well as her graduate thesis and a federal court case.

While Biwei Zhang appears to be her legal name, she uses the name Claire Zhang professionally, and goes by Catina Zhang on her Facebook profile.

In posts to two separate Facebook groups in July 2025, Zhang said she was looking for a room to rent in Mons as she began her internship. She also sought housing in Geneva in 2023 right before an internship at the World Trade Organization — dates that line up with her work experience on her LinkedIn profile.

The details also match information reported by Reuters earlier this week, which identified the woman as Claire Z. A security source told Reuters she was working in SHAPE's IT department, which is consistent with Zhang's background in computer science and systems engineering, for which she completed a master's degree at the University of Ottawa in 2022.

The source also described her as "not a student" and "in her 30s," information that matched Zhang's professional profile. Her Facebook username, "biwei.zhang.93," also suggests she may have been born in 1993, which would make her 32 or 33 years old.

In a July 2025 post to a Mons, Belgium, Facebook group, Zhang identified herself as an incoming intern at SHAPE, NATO's military headquarters, and said she was looking for a room to rent for the next six months. (Catina Zhang/Facebook)

Similar identifying details were reported by independent European investigative news outlet Follow the Money and its media partners on Tuesday.

Zhang did not immediately respond to CBC's requests for comment on her LinkedIn and Facebook profiles.

Belgian officials say the alleged spy will remain in pretrial custody for at least another month as the investigation continues.

National security concerns

The case has also raised concerns around the efficacy of Canada's security screening processes, prompting Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree to commit to investigating whether the person in question worked for any Canadian agencies.

"Ultimately, we need to get to the bottom of this, and we need to ensure that these types of incidents do not occur in the future," Anandasangaree said.

WATCH | Canada investigating alleged spy: Minister commits to 'get to the bottom' of Canadian NATO intern spying allegations | Duration 1:26 As a Canadian woman who was an intern at NATO's military headquarters in Belgium is facing 'quite serious' spying charges, Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree said that Canada would investigate its security screening processes and 'get to the bottom of what happened.'

According to her LinkedIn profile, Zhang has held a range of positions at federal agencies, including as a data scientist for the National Research Council for six months in 2017, an economist for StatsCan from April 2018 to October 2022, and then as a systems engineer at the Canadian Space Agency (CSA) from May 2022.

She also lists experience as a policy analyst for the European Space Agency, and the economic research and statistics division of the World Trade Organization, as well as positions on "mirror committees" of the Standards Council of Canada, a Crown corporation that acts as "Canada's voice on standards and accreditation on the international stage."

In an emailed statement, the European Space Agency said it applies standard screening procedures for positions that do not require security clearance, and relies on "the relevant national security authority [to] conduct a comprehensive vetting process of the individual concerned" when classified information is involved.

In a LinkedIn profile with the name 'Claire Z.,' Zhang claims over five years of experience working as an economist for Statistics Canada and a data scientist for the National Research Council. (Claire Z./LinkedIn)

The CSA acknowledged CBC's request for comment but did not provide a response by publication time.

A spokesperson for Global Affairs Canada told CBC News that the Canadian government "makes the final decision to grant, deny, or revoke security clearances for Canadians seeking positions with international organizations, including NATO" following Canadian Security Intelligence Service (CSIS) security assessments.

Global Affairs refused to comment on the specific case "as it is the subject of an ongoing investigation."

Zhang also requested a judicial review of a Public Service Commission of Canada finding that she committed fraud in an application for a position at the Canada Border Services Agency by applying under two different names and emails and failing to later clarify whether she had submitted multiple applications.

A federal judge dismissed the case in August 2024.

Intern positions an 'Achilles heel': ex-spy

Former CSIS intelligence officer Dan Stanton told CBC News that while he does not have direct knowledge of the case, he can see why NATO would be concerned about possible intelligence breaches.

He says intern positions are an "excellent in-road" that he likened to "an Achilles heel" for an organization like NATO.

"Most of the biggest secrets in espionage aren't as a result of stealing files or accessing data banks. It's conversations, it's hearing things," said Stanton, now the director of the national security program at the University of Ottawa's Professional Development Institute.

Dan Stanton, a former CSIS intelligence officer, told CBC News that intern positions are an 'excellent in-road' for intelligence gathering at an organization like NATO. (Jean-François Benoit/CBC)

Still, the former spy sees the investigation as a "good news story."

"In the world of counter-espionage, these types of things happen," he said.

"It's proof that our processes work."

World.title: At least 8 killed in Ukraine after Russia hits several regions
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A Russian ballistic missile and drone barrage across Ukraine overnight into Thursday killed at least eight civilians, including children, and wounded more than 50 others, officials said.

The blitz expanded Russia's almost daily bombardment of Ukrainian cities as Moscow apparently looked to exploit Kyiv's critical shortage of Western-supplied anti-ballistic missile defences.

The barrage spanned regions across Ukraine, including areas by the border with Poland that are far from the front line in the east of the country and where Ukraine is believed to store and manufacture weapons for its fight against Russia's more than four-year-old invasion. Its long-range drones and missiles have battered Russia's oil sector, causing a fuel crisis.

The attack came two days after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy met in Washington with U.S. President Donald Trump and representatives of American defence companies, as he pleads for swifter and bigger deliveries of Patriot air defence systems that are the best way to stop Russia's ballistic assaults.

The Iran war has drained stockpiles of the American-made interceptors. Trump has promised to grant Ukraine licences to build its own Patriots, but production could take a long time to set up.

"Given the critical shortage of air defence missiles from our partners, our warriors are accomplishing truly incredible things, demonstrating a very high level of professionalism," Zelenskyy said on social media.

"This Russian terror once again proves that protection against the Russian missile threat is the most important task when it comes to saving the lives of our people," he said.

Deadliest attack in Dnipropetrovsk

Zelenskyy said at least 10 Ukrainian regions were attacked, with dozens of homes, businesses and infrastructure facilities destroyed or damaged.

Russia launched more than 70 missiles, a significant number of them ballistic, he said, along with more than 280 attack drones, of which more than 260 were intercepted.

The Russian Defence Ministry said it aimed at Ukrainian airbases, arms factories and military telecommunications and logistics facilities.

First responders operate at a residential building partially destroyed as a result of Russian missile strikes in the western Ukrainian city of Lviv on Thursday. (Yuriy Dyachyshyn/AFP/Getty Images)

The targets included drone production factories and storage depots, a missile plant, an aircraft repair plant, a factory making electronic components, and a chemical plant, it said.

In the Dnipropetrovsk region, the Russian attack killed six people and wounded 10, Oleksandr Hanzha, head of the regional military administration, said.

Children were among the dead, he said on Telegram — a six-year-old girl and boys aged 11 and 17 in the area of Kryvyi Rih, Zelenskyy's hometown.

The children's parents were killed in the same attack, but two more children were pulled alive from under the rubble, Zelenskyy said.

In Kyiv, Russian forces struck the capital with ballistic missiles, killing a 31-year-old man and wounding two others, the National Police press service said.

A cruise missile attack struck the western city of Lviv, wounding 34 people, including three children aged six, 13 and 15, according to Maksym Kozytskyi, head of the Lviv regional military administration. Emergency crews were still searching through rubble.

In the Poltava region, a drone hit company warehouses, killing one person, regional military head Vitalii Diakivnych said.

Russian forces also dropped three powerful glide bombs on an industrial zone in the southern city of Kherson on Thursday morning, killing a 56-year-old man, local officials said.

Meanwhile, Russia's Defence Ministry said that air defences downed 258 Ukrainian drones overnight.

A depot belonging to Wildberries online retailer was set ablaze in Russia's Penza region southeast of Moscow, in the latest strike on the company's warehouses, Penza Gov. Oleg Melnichenko.

WATCH | Why Ukraine is targeting a Russian firm: The facts about Ukraine striking Wildberries, Russia’s Amazon | Duration 1:36 Ukraine has been hitting warehouses for the online shopping giant Wildberries in Russia. The drone strikes have killed night shift workers and destroyed the merchandise of many sellers. Here are the facts about Wildberries — and why Ukraine is targeting these sites.

One person was injured and 200 workers fled the area, he said.

The Russian online news outlet Astra reported that another Wildberries depot in the Perm region in the Urals was also set ablaze by a Ukrainian drone strike.

Ukraine accuses Wildberries of supplying goods that can be used by the Russian military.

Poland investigates airspace incursion

NATO member Poland, meanwhile, was looking into Ukrainian reports that a Russian cruise missile entered its airspace. A Russian Kh-101 cruise missile crossed into Poland overnight, violating NATO airspace, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said on X.

Sybiha called it a clear demonstration that strengthening Ukraine's air defence is urgent and serves as a guarantee of wider European protection.

Firefighters and military police work at a site in Poland on Thursday, near Lublin, after an errant missile reportedly fell. (Jakub Orzechowski/Agencja Wyborcza.pl/Reuters)

An unidentified object flying westward in the middle of the night was tracked in Polish airspace and an F-16 fighter jet was launched to identify and intercept it, the Operational Command of the Polish Armed Forces said on X.

The object disappeared from radar screens before it could be identified, the command said. A helicopter flew to its last known location, where the crew discovered a probable impact site in a farming area in the Lublin province, the command wrote.

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk, who recently met with Zelenskyy, travelled to the area Thursday morning to inspect the sites.

World.title: U.S. FCC approves giant space mirror to deliver 'sunlight on demand,' but what are the legal implications?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Despite hundreds of public comments opposing a giant space mirror that would shine a beam of light roughly five kilometres wide back down to Earth, the U.S. Federal Communications Commission (FCC), has given it the green light.

The company building the space mirror, Reflect Orbital, is touting its proposal as "sunlight on demand," which could be used for any number of reasons, it says, such as agriculture, solar farms or for search and rescue.

Astronomers and other groups are sounding the alarm about the project, citing numerous reasons, including the threat to species dependent on a pristine night sky, the threat to important astronomical research and more.

"This harm could include damage to sensitive research telescope equipment, potential flash-blinding of pilots and drivers and — as Reflect Orbital stated in its own FCC filings — potential permanent eye damage to anyone looking through a mid-sized telescope," the American Astronomical Society said in a statement .

The FCC said that those concerns are beyond their scope, as they only regulate communications by radio, television, wire and satellite.

So who does regulate where, how and when a giant five-kilometre swath of light can be used? What's stopping someone from paying potentially tens of thousands of dollars for an hour of reflected sunlight at their home? Does that mean neighbours have to endure disruption to their sleep or nightly routines?

Reflect Orbital aims to have more than 50,000 satellites in orbit by 2035. (Screenshot/Reflect Orbital)

While the Reflect Orbital approval is for one satellite, the company proposes launching a whopping 50,000 by 2035.

And this is on top of the millions of satellite proposed by SpaceX and other companies like Blue Origin, which will add to the thousands of satellites already crowding Earth's orbit.

'Far from unregulated'

Internationally, the United Nations Office for Outer Space Affairs (UNOOSA) deals with all aspects related to space, including its applications and space law.

More than 115 countries (referred to as "states") have signed the 1967 Outer Space Treaty. There are several articles in the treaty, but overall the message is that countries are responsible for the peaceful use of outer space and that countries must take into account other "corresponding interests of all other States Parties," a UNOOSA representative told CBC News via email, when asked about Reflect Orbital's project.

"So the honest answer to 'how legal is it' is that it is not a yes or no question. Nothing in the treaties prohibits placing a reflective object in orbit (Article I, freedom to use outer space). But such an activity is very far from unregulated," UNOOSA said. "It is subject to due regard and consultation obligations owed to every other State. And any State that considers itself affected is entitled to raise it."

LISTEN | A company wants to sell sunlight after dark. Here's why astronomers are worried: Quirks and Quarks 8:35 A company wants to sell sunlight after dark. Here’s why astronomers are worried A company called Reflect Orbital plans to launch thousands of mirrors into space starting with its first as early as next year, to provide customers with extra sunlight at night. The company says the additional light could help power solar arrays, aid in search and rescue missions, and more. But astronomers are concerned that this practice will interfere with their work, and may also be harmful to human health, animals, and the environment.

International space law expert Cassandra Steer said that it could be up to countries to make some sort of laws around the type of reflected sunlight service that Reflect Orbital is aiming to provide.

"I think that there are environmental protection regulations within Canada where the federal government could say, actually, we are not going to allow anybody in Canada to legally purchase and use these services, because we're going to say it's harmful to their environment," Steer said. "How are we going to enforce it is a different question."

Ram Jakhu, professor emeritus at McGill University's faculty of law, agreed that regulations are needed.

"I think, in five, 10 years, you will see something done about it, not only talk and talk," he said.

"The whole issue of night sky, light pollution, these things, they are being addressed, but nothing has been decided yet. But I think there will be serious concerns and discussion, something we can see in the near future. The night sky is very important. But … astronomers are not a major player in geopolitics."

The UNOOSA also said that of the 193 member states that roughly 50 have their own national space legislation, and that, as Steer said, it could be up to individual countries to set their own regulations.

In response to a question about potential regulations, a spokesperson for Reflect Orbital said, "we recognize that responsible deployment at scale requires clear rules. We welcome oversight and want to play an active role in shaping it. We believe it is our responsibility to work alongside governments, scientists and regulators rather than ahead of them."

'Dark and quiet skies'

UNOOSA's Committee on the Peaceful Uses of Outer Space (COPUOS) is already working with International Astronomical Union (IAU), and other international observatories on the "protection of dark and quiet skies," and space-based illumination is included in that, UNOOSA said.

Piero Benvenuti, director of the IAU's Centre for the Protection of Dark and Quiet Sky from Satellite Constellation Interference (CPS), said that they have been speaking with Reflect Orbital from the outset.

The company says on its website that they "maintain strict exclusion zones for astronomy and sensitive environments." But Benvenuti said that, once the CPS showed Reflect Orbital a map of all the observatories contributing to astronomical research, they seemed surprised.

"They probably didn't know that the number of telescopes, including the amateur astronomer telescopes, are huge and are dispersed everywhere in the world," he said.

In the email to CBC News, the company spokesperson said, "We’re an industry member of the International Astronomical Union’s Centre for the Protection of the Dark and Quiet Sky, and feedback from the astronomical community has materially informed the design of our spacecraft and operational plans."

They also noted that they are "committed to ongoing dialogue with scientists, astronomers, environmental researchers and other interested stakeholders."

CPS doesn't have regulatory oversight, but is working with astronomers and satellite providers on reducing the impact satellite constellations will have on the night sky.

WATCH | Light pollution is getting noticeably worse, study confirms: Light pollution is getting noticeably worse, study confirms | Duration 4:16 A new study that analyzed more than 50,000 crowdsourced observations over 12 years has confirmed that light pollution is getting noticeably worse, brightening the night sky by roughly seven to 10 per cent each year.

"The other thing they didn't consider is that it is not just the direct illumination of the telescope," Benvenuti said. "They are shining through the atmosphere, their reflected sunlight, and that is illuminating the atmosphere, and the light, obviously, is diffused by particle and by scattering."

He also noted that they are working with Reflect Orbital to study the effects of the first satellite, Earendil-1.

"What we are negotiating with them is a campaign of observations. So, we want to quantify the effect of this prototype. And then once we have these measures, these data, we will verify the simulation and, you know, check if the simulations are correct."

And if they are?

"They're saying we want to launch 50,000 mirrors by 2035," Benvenuti said. "That would be catastrophic for astronomy, that is clear."

World.title: WestJet flight attendants' union serves 72-hour strike notice
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The union representing 4,400 flight attendants at WestJet says it has issued a 72-hour strike notice, paving the runway for a possible strike during a busy summer travel season.

The Canadian Union of Public Employees says the two sides remain far apart on key issues.

"We have been clear about what needs to change, and we have worked hard to reach a fair deal," Alia Hussain, chair of the union's WestJet contingent, said in a news release early Thursday.

"There's still time to avoid a strike," Hussain added. "We will continue to bargain around the clock until this is resolved."

WestJet, in a statement, said the airline responded to the union's strike notice by issuing a 72-hour lockout notice.

Job action could begin as soon as Sunday at 12:01 a.m. MT if the two sides don't reach a deal. (Jeff McIntosh/The Canadian Press)

The air carrier — the second-largest in Canada — said it is still actively negotiating to reach a deal.

"The decision to issue a lockout notice, in response to the actions taken by the union, was not one that was made lightly. We sincerely regret the inconvenience and uncertainty this continues to cause for our guests," said WestJet CEO Alexis von Hoensbroech in the statement.

"We greatly value the work and contributions of our cabin crew, and it is our responsibility to ensure the integrity of our network and to minimize the risk of stranding our guests, crew and aircraft."

While serving notice does not commit the union to a strike, job action could begin as soon as Sunday at 12:01 a.m. MT if the two sides don't reach a deal.

WATCH | Canada's second-largest airline could see a summer strike: : WestJet preps shutdown ahead of possible flight attendants strike | Duration 2:27 Despite ongoing talks, WestJet and its flight attendants have signed off on a plan to wind down operations ahead of a possible long-weekend strike. Some 4,400 union members could walk off the job this Sunday.

Unless a tentative agreement is reached, some flights could start to be grounded by Friday.

WestJet has been allowing passengers with flights scheduled any time between July 30 and Aug. 4 to make a one-time change or cancel it with no fee.

Travellers booked on its regional WestJet Encore service or code-share flights run by an airline partner such as Delta Air Lines will not be affected by a strike, the carrier said.

Should flight delays or cancellations occur, the airline said impacted guests will be refunded or reaccommodated, "as applicable."

The two sides this week also inked an agreement that lays out how to ground planes and get cabin crew home in the event of a work stoppage.

Unpaid ground duties key issue for union

Cabin crew working a flight when any job action kicks off would complete the trip to its destination. Those who can't immediately return to their home city would receive hotel accommodation for up to a week or a plane ride back to another Canadian city, "subject to seat availability," according to the deal.

The union has said key issues include unpaid work for tasks such as ground duties, while WestJet has said all duties are compensated through a "credit hour" system rather than an hourly rate.

John Gradek, who teaches aviation management at McGill University, has said even a brief shutdown would cost the carrier millions of dollars during the height of summer travel — on a long weekend across much of Canada.

The airline says it operates more than 600 flights per day carrying legions of passengers — more than 70,000 on some days.

World.title: Kids' birthday parties are getting more expensive. Should guests help pay for them?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Kids' birthday parties are a big business these days pretty much any way you go about it.

At best, there's the price of food, cake and balloons. Maybe you rented a bouncy castle to keep the kids entertained, or hired Elsa to sing Let it Go, or paid for the reptile zoo to come to you.

Perhaps, at worst, you booked a party package at the soft play/arcade/ball pit/laser tag/loud indoor theme park. Or maybe you're taking six pre-teens for manicures, or a dozen kids to make splatter art and friendship bracelets at your local pottery studio/craft shop/artisan sandwich cafe that — did you hear?! — just started booking birthday parties.

Big or small, the costs add up. But does this mean the hosts should ask other parents to help cover the expense?

That's the debate currently raging across the internet amid reports some parents are asking guests for tips. And we don't mean advice. We mean cash in a jar, a contribution, or paying to attend.

"Have you seen this on an invitation yet? I bet you will," a cake decorator said in a viral TikTok video last year. In the video, she claims at least three families she'd worked with included requests for tips on their party invitations to help cover costs.

"If you are inviting my children to your child's birthday and you asked me to pay for them to come, nine out of 10 times they're probably not going to be attending," a U.K. parent and financial advisor recently posted.

"I've seen it … the mom invoiced people," a parenting podcaster said in a video posted in March.

In the comments online, most people argue you shouldn't be throwing a party you can't afford, while others defended the practice given costs for everything are skyrocketing.

But it also opened up a bigger conversation: when did the expectations for kid parties get so, well, bananas?

"When it's financially difficult for families to do this to the extent they have to ask other families to pitch in, we are really getting out of hand," Vanessa Lapointe, a parenting consultant based in Surrey, B.C., told CBC News.

An Instagram post from Kim Kardashian from May 14 shares details of her son's Pokemon birthday party. (@kimkardashian/Instagram)

'The pressure is real'

According to recent media reports, the average parent spends at least $445 for a party, at least one in five parents spend more than $700, and a third of parents go into debt for it. Event planners have described wealthy parents willing to spend upward of $42,000 to throw extravagant parties for their children.

Other reports have suggested over two-thirds of parents polled think planning their kid's birthday party is more stressful than their day job. And nearly half of a thousand U.K. parents polled last year admitted they felt competition with other parents to throw the best party.

Meanwhile, parenting blogs and websites encourage "enchanted garden" party themes (complete with fairy doors and pixie dust) and advise that "farmcore" parties — in which the children churn their own butter — are trending. Elsewhere, celebrities like Kim Kardashian are posting photos of their children's bashes, including, in her case, a giant Pikachu.

"There’s definitely a pressure to make sure your kid has a memorable party," Ottawa mom Gaelan Jaffray told CBC News.

"You’re measuring yourself against what you’re seeing on social media and what your friends are doing and you don’t want to be the one with the lame party. The pressure is real and mostly self-inflicted."

Gaelan Jaffray's son opens a present at a dinosaur-themed party she hosted in Ottawa that she jokingly says was 'Pinterest-worthy.' (Gaelan Jaffray)

It's also incredibly expensive no matter which route you take, Jaffray says. She estimates parties for her son, 10-year-old Everett, average about $400, and even hosting at home becomes pricey once you factor in food, cake, decorations, entertainment and loot bags.

For instance, five years ago, Jaffray threw Everett a dinosaur-themed party at home that she jokingly describes as "Pinterest-worthy." There was a balloon arch, a mural, custom cupcakes, a dinosaur bouncy castle and a loot bag for each guest.

"That said, I don’t think the rising cost of hosting justifies asking invited guests to subsidize the party," Jaffray said.

"To me, bringing a gift is already the guest’s contribution."

Warning over 'culture of comparison'

Expectations for modern parenting have become so all-consuming that researchers now have a term for it: the intensification of parenting.

Even the U.S. surgeon general has acknowledged these pressures, issuing a public health advisory in 2024 about the impact on parents' mental health. Part of modern parenting's unique struggles are what he called our "culture of comparison," propagated by influencers and online trends that create unrealistic expectations.

You know, like ombre balloon arches, professionally designed cakes and loot bags that could rival the swag bags at the Oscars.

"Comparison is the thief of joy," said Lapointe, the parenting consultant.

And it's not like the quality of a birthday party is going to make or break their childhood, she added. Kids will look back on the experience and how they felt, not how splashy it was.

Still, said Jaffray, as kids get older and start having specific requests, it's hard to say no.

"It’s the only time they’re going to turn that age," she said. "You want it to be special."

World.title: The web is being redesigned for AI. What does that mean for human readers?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Artificial intelligence is fundamentally reshaping how humans use the internet. For The National, CBC’s Nora Young breaks down the future of search and what happens to information when bots do most of the reading online.

Say goodbye to the internet as you know it

Deb Perelman has seen a lot of change online.

The food blogger's popular site Smitten Kitchen turns 20 years old this summer.

"I've always had the philosophy that I would just meet people where they were," Perelman said, which is why she established a presence on social media platforms from Twitter to Instagram to TikTok — but always took readers back to the recipes and stories on her website.

Now, she faces a new challenge: AI summaries.

Deb Perelman, creator of the food blog Smitten Kitchen, has seen AI summaries eat into her website's traffic. (Submitted by Deb Perelman)

Perelman said she's seen "a summary or a chunk of my own recipe in the AI blurb that you have in the top of search results."

"It's honestly shocking to me that somebody can publish my work ... without my permission," said Perelman, who is now pursuing AI-limiting protections for her site.

Google recently reimagined the search box for the first time in 25 years, with "AI Mode," a conversational back-and-forth that's similar to using ChatGPT or other AI chatbots. This Google function has surpassed a billion monthly users .

This screen grab shows the landing page for Google's AI Mode. (Nora Young)

Beyond that, Google is also prioritizing extensive AI summaries over links to websites — the result being that people increasingly don't need to leave Google's main page to get an answer.

Similarly, you can rely on Claude, ChatGPT or other LLM chatbots to provide answers, recommend products or take on more complex tasks, like creating an itinerary for a trip.

It's convenient, but it means big challenges for site creators who rely on human traffic. The web is being fundamentally reoriented to accommodate the bots that scrape websites for the information we seek.

Websites for machines as well as humans

Human web traffic is declining. Data from Cloudflare, a U.S. company that provides a range of internet services for websites and apps, found declines in human traffic across retail, software, IT and finance websites. Some hardest hit categories declined by up to 40 per cent between June 2025 and April 2026.

"The biggest impact is … machines going to read your content," said Hamzah Khadim, co-founder of Toronto-based internet marketing service Logik Digital .

Khadim argues that as search has moved "from keywords to conversations," the main goal for any website is not turning up in a list of links but being part of an AI's answer.

Logik Digital has long specialized in SEO (search engine optimization), so that websites turn up in search results, but it's now also focused on GEO (generative engine optimization). That means adding specific information that both indicates a site's credibility and answers the questions a user is likely to ask AI.

Sometimes, that means adding a lot of text to a website — for example, in its "About Us" section.

"People aren't gonna necessarily read all of that, but AI definitely will," Khadim said. "And it'll help establish trust."

The AI chatbot ChatGPT is shown on a smartphone in Mulhouse, eastern France. (Sebastien Bozon/AFP/Getty Images)

Getting paid for content and for the cost of scraping

While many independent content creators monetize their content on social media apps, through moves like brand partnerships, a lot of websites rely on selling ads or subscriptions to fund their content. So what happens if website visitors are AI bots and not humans?

Mark Surman, the president of Mozilla, best known for the Firefox browser, is concerned that "if those incentives to create original, creative, independent content disappear, does content just come from big and powerful companies, or from governments, or from AI itself?"

Even if a publisher is content to let AI have content for free and doesn't rely on advertising, there are real costs associated with AI accessing web content.

Wikipedia is one of the most-visited websites in the world. Lane Becker is president of Wikimedia Enterprise, which makes Wikipedia content accessible to organizations at scale. From an access-to-information perspective, Becker is enthusiastic about AI spreading Wikipedia's content.

Wikipedia articles are free for anyone to access, but the server infrastructure providing that content costs Wikipedia (or any website) a tiny bit of money. The sheer volume of requests from bots means that can really add up.

Lane Becker, president of Wikimedia Enterprise, which operates Wikipedia, says just one bot can click on 50 articles in under a second. (Submitted by Wikimedia Foundation)

Becker says just one bot can click on 50 articles in under a second.

"It's easy for one robot to show up and say, 'Hey, I want to scoop every single page out of every single Wikipedia [edition] and every single language, and I'm going to do it in under half an hour.'"

So Wikimedia Enterprise has deals with a number of AI companies — including Google, Microsoft, Amazon and Meta — to pay for direct, bulk access to Wikipedia's data.

A new deal for the AI-native web

Other media companies may start pushing back, too, if the decline in web traffic continues. According to reporting by the Wall Street Journal , Reddit and some other prominent publishers are considering cutting off or changing their relationship with Google.

USA Today's CEO recently said the "traditional Google search business model is dead … that traffic is declining … so we are going to be in a position soon where we have to block Google." He seemed to signal a willingness to forego showing up in Google search results at all.

But hope remains for a model that would preserve the open web and its diversity of voices.

For Deb Perelman, AI summaries miss something you can only get from the individual perspectives of creators.

"The context of a recipe is really important," she said, arguing "you're not going to get that from a blurb on top of a search result that has been extracted, perhaps correctly, perhaps incorrectly, from the actual recipe."

World.title: Kuwaiti worker killed as U.S.-Iran conflict widens
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The United States and Iran each fired barrages of missiles Thursday, as the pattern of back-and-forth strikes took hold again and hope dimmed for any quick resolution to the war.

An Iranian strike hit a Chinese firm's building in northern Kuwait on Thursday morning, severely damaging the structure and killing a worker, Kuwait's military said, hours after Jordan's air defences shot down five missiles launched from Iran.

The attacks came after the U.S. military said it had completed "a heavy wave of strikes against Iran," conducted in response to an earlier Iranian missile attack on a U.S. base in Jordan.

The U.S. military's Central Command said online that it had struck "dozens" of targets belonging to Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps, including military command centres as well as missile and drone facilities, and coastal surveillance and defence sites.

The first strikes from the U.S. in five days came after U.S. President Donald Trump vowed to hit Iran "very hard" after it targeted a base in Jordan that hosts U.S. troops.

Iran's official IRNA news agency said three people were killed and two were wounded in a strike on the island of Qeshm, which lies just off the Iranian mainland in the Strait of Hormuz, the crucial waterway for global energy supplies that Iranian attacks have again effectively closed.

No casualties were reported from Jordan's interception of the missiles, Jordan's state-run Petra news agency said, quoting the spokesperson for the country's armed forces.

WATCH | More countries drawn into war: CBC's Aarti Pole speaks with Retired U.S. Major General Randy Manner on Iran-U.S. strikes | Duration 7:17 Get the latest on CBCNews.ca, the CBC News App, and CBC News Network for breaking news and analysis.

U.S. partners with Saudis

The latest barrage came after the U.S. partnered with Saudi Arabia to strike Iran-backed militias in neighbouring Iraq, the Popular Mobilisation Forces, killing at least 20 fighters and six Iranian advisers on Wednesday.

Iraqi men in the subsequent hours shouted Shia sectarian slogans and "Death to America" as they carried the bodies of slain fighters in body bags.

Elsewhere, British maritime security firm Ambrey said drone strikes ignited fires on two natural gas vessels at the Egyptian port of Damietta on Wednesday. It was not immediately clear who was responsible for the strikes on a U.S.-owned floating storage facility and a Greek-owned tanker, the GasLog Salem. No injuries were reported.

The office of the Egyptian prime minister said initial investigations showed the fires on the two vessels had been caused by a drone.

Egypt, a close U.S. ally and regional mediator, is one of the only countries in the Middle East to have been spared direct military action during the war. A strike by Iran or its allies, if confirmed, would mark a significant widening of the conflict.

Saudi Arabia had accused the Iraqi militias of firing drones against its oil facilities over the past days. An umbrella group of Iraqi militias initially denied the allegations.

A view of the Gaslog Salem vessel is shown in a file photo, off the coast of South Korea. The Greek-owned tanker was reportedly hit by a drone in recent days. (Submitted by Vladimir Tonic/Reuters)

Saudi Arabia is also locked in a renewed conflict with the Houthis. The rebels have declared a blockade of Saudi shipping that could choke off another crucial Middle East trade route, the Bab el-Mandeb strait from the Red Sea into the Gulf of Aden.

Planet Labs satellite imagery from Monday analyzed by The Associated Press showed damage to Saudi Aramco's Abqaiq oil-processing facility. The massive facility is capable of processing approximately seven million barrels of crude oil per day.

Saudi Defence Minister Khalid bin Salman met separately on Wednesday with Trump and U.S. Vice-President JD Vance, according to two people familiar with the matter who were not authorized to comment publicly about the private meetings.

An interim agreement struck in June that was to see Iran and the U.S. pause fighting for 60 days — in order to negotiate issues including maritime transit in the Hormuz as well as Iran's nuclear program — collapsed in recent weeks over renewed fighting in the Strait of Hormuz.

WATCH | Concerns about U.S. stockpiles: Pause in U.S. attacks on Iran prompt questions about weapon supplies | Duration 2:30 A sudden pause in attacks by the U.S. and Iran has prompted questions about whether the break is to allow for peace talks or because the U.S. has largely drained its weapons supply.

It also underscored the difficulty of winding down a five-month conflict started by the U.S. and Israel that has jolted the world economy and is unpopular among Americans.

The fighting was likely to add to concerns in Washington that the U.S. is further drawing on already diminished stockpiles of sophisticated munitions in the five-month-old conflict it started with Israel on Feb. 28.

Since the war began, 18 U.S. service members have been killed, with the Trump administration recently accused of seeking to obfuscate those numbers.

About two-thirds of U.S. adults say the war with Iran has not been worthwhile in the latest monthly poll from the Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research. That includes the vast majority of Democrats and independents, as well as about 37 per cent of Republicans.

Roughly 61 per cent of Republicans surveyed approve of how Trump is handling Iran. The result from the same question in June's poll was 71 per cent.

The AP-NORC poll of 1,165 adults was conducted July 23-27 using a sample drawn from NORC's probability-based AmeriSpeak Panel, which is designed to be representative of the U.S. population. The margin of sampling error for adults overall is plus or minus 3.7 percentage points. The margin of sampling error is plus or minus 6.0 for Republicans overall and plus or minus 5.4 for Democrats overall.

World.title: 40 years, no floods. Now her Montreal home's been hit 3 straight years. What's changed?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Wooden studs are exposed where finished walls once stood and construction tools are scattered across the concrete floor as Arlene Thompson-Maclaren works to rebuild her basement.

For nearly 40 years, the homeowner in Dollard-des-Ormeaux, a suburb in Montreal's West Island, never had to worry about flooding.

Today, she’s rebuilding the space for the third time in as many years.

“It’s three years in a row. August of 2024. July of 2025 and June of 2026,” she said.

Each time, the cleanup has meant tearing out insulation, drywall and flooring — "completely rip it all out and start again," she said with a bitter smile.

Thompson-Maclaren is one of dozens of residents in Dollard-des-Ormeaux whose homes have flooded during heavy summer rain over the past three years.

Until recently , many say they never experienced flooding and are now asking the same question: What changed?

WATCH | What's with the frequent flooding?: Why are Montreal’s West Island residents facing repeated flooding? | Duration 2:26 Dollard-des-Ormeaux resident Arlene Thompson-Maclaren has faced three home floods since 2024 — a problem she had never experienced in nearly 40 years. Civil engineering experts say adapting older neighbourhoods to withstand heavier rainfall remains a significant challenge.

More intense storms

One part of the explanation, experts say, is climate change.

“We do see events now in the Montreal area and around the world that are more intense than they used to be,” said Alexis Berg, a climate science professor at the Université de Montréal.

“That’s a direct consequence of a warmer atmosphere.”

Heavy rain on June 20 caused massive flooding in Dollard-des-Ormeaux. (Bruno Lavoie/Radio-Canada)

Jean-Luc Martel, a professor of construction engineering at École de technologie supérieure who studies urban flooding, says a warmer atmosphere holds more moisture, leading to heavier downpours.

“With respect to climate change, these are now more frequent events,” he said. “We should be ready to see these events more and more.”

But he says heavier rainfall is only one piece of the puzzle.

Aging infrastructure faces a changing climate

Martel says many municipal drainage systems were never expected to handle the kind of rainfall cities are now experiencing.

“The infrastructures were not designed and will never be designed to deal with those extreme rainfall events,” he said.

Jean-Luc Martel says the city's infrastructure was not designed to deal with extreme rainfalls. (Aatefeh Padidar/CBC News)

Susan Gaskin, a professor of civil engineering at McGill University, agrees. She also says residents who say nearby development has changed the way water moves through their neighbourhoods are not wrong.

“They are correct. The more somewhere is built up, the more impermeable surface you have,” she said.

More pavement and rooftops mean less water can soak into the ground, sending larger volumes of runoff toward storm sewers.

However, Gaskin says newer developments are generally designed with systems that temporarily retain some of that runoff before it reaches municipal infrastructure.

The bigger challenge, she says, is adapting older neighbourhoods that were built decades ago for a different climate.

'It's not 1 solution'

Experts say adapting cities will require a combination of approaches.

Some involve upgrading infrastructure. Others focus on changing how neighbourhoods handle rainwater before it reaches storm sewers.

“It’s not one solution,” Martel said. “Every single area will have a different solution that will be helping them more than another area in particular. Depending on the impact that you have, you need to find the right solution.”

WATCH | Residents in Dollard-des-Ormeaux consider legal action after flooding: Dollard-des-Ormeaux residents consider class action after repeated flooding | Duration 2:18 Weeks after flash flooding damaged homes across the suburb in Montreal’s West Island, some residents say the financial and emotional toll has become too much. Residents are backing a proposed class action alleging the city failed to adequately prepare for repeated flooding.

He says homeowners can also reduce future damage by rebuilding flood-prone basements with more resilient materials and limiting expensive finishes in spaces that are likely to flood again.

One approach gaining traction is bringing more nature into urban environments.

Chaïma Ben, executive director of the Centre d’écologie urbaine, says cities have traditionally been designed to move rainwater away as quickly as possible.

“We say bring nature back," she said. "To remove the asphalt, to depave and plant, add more greenery, add areas that can retain the water."

Trees, gardens and other green spaces help absorb rainwater while slowing the amount of runoff entering storm sewers during heavy rainfall.

Ben says these nature-based solutions can complement larger infrastructure projects, which often take years and cost millions of dollars to complete.

She also encourages homeowners to prepare their own properties by maintaining backwater valves and gutters, installing sump pumps where appropriate and replacing paved surfaces with greener alternatives whenever possible.

Thompson-Maclaren's basement in Dollard-des-Ormeaux is undergoing yet another rebuild after a third flood. (Aatefeh Padidar/CBC News)

Back in her basement, Thompson-Maclaren continues the repairs herself.

After three consecutive floods, she says she isn’t looking for someone to blame; she wants to know what comes next.

“We want to know when and how and what so we can set certain expectations,” she said.
