A Cultural Programme Built Around Collective Memory

The state government has confirmed a multi-venue programme that places collective memory at the centre of the city’s summer calendar.

The lineup spans generations and genres, from the hip-hop of Audrey Funk to the punk-inflected sounds of Yucatán A Go Go and the veteran folk voice of Gabino Palomares.

Literary and historical voices carry equal weight, with writer and activist Paco Ignacio Taibo II and historian Francisco Pérez Arce leading discussion panels.

Three Iconic Venues Anchor the Festival of Memory

The festival spreads across three landmarks that already define Puebla’s cultural geography.

The Zócalo, the city’s vast main square at the heart of Puebla’s UNESCO-listed historic centre, will host open-air concerts and large public gatherings.

Indoor events move to the Centro Cultural de San Roque and the Casa de la Cultura Profesor Pedro Ángel Palou, both intimate spaces suited to theatre, film screenings and panel discussions.

What the Festival of Memory Means for Puebla’s Cultural Economy

Free public festivals are not merely civic gestures in Mexico; they are economic multipliers for historic centres.

Hotels, restaurants and informal vendors in the cuadrícula around the Zócalo typically see a measurable uptick during multi-day cultural events, even when admission costs nothing.

For Puebla, a city that competes with San Miguel de Allende and Oaxaca for the North American expat and digital-nomad market, a well-programmed festival reinforces the quality-of-life narrative that drives relocation decisions.

The Expat and Investor Read-Through

Puebla has spent the past decade quietly building a reputation as a lower-cost, less-touristed alternative to Mexico City, just two hours away by road.

Events like the Festival of Memory signal that the local government is investing in the soft infrastructure that retains foreign residents and attracts cultural tourists with disposable income.

For anyone holding or considering residential property in the Historic Centre, a full August calendar adds rental-season ballast and supports the long-term case for Puebla’s appreciation relative to pricier Mexican colonial markets.

How to Navigate the Festival of Memory

The Secretaría de Arte y Cultura has published the complete programme on its official digital channels, and visitors should download it before arriving because printed schedules can run out quickly.

Most events require no registration, but panel discussions at the Casa de la Cultura may fill up, so arriving twenty minutes early is prudent.

The three venues are all walkable from one another within the compact Historic Centre, and August evenings in Puebla are mild enough for moving comfortably between an afternoon panel and a night concert on the Zócalo.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is the Festival of Memory free to attend?

Yes, all events across the four days are free and open to the public. No tickets or advance registration are required for most activities, though indoor panel discussions may have limited seating.

Where can I find the full Festival of Memory programme?

The complete schedule is available on the official pages of the Secretaría de Arte y Cultura de Puebla. It is advisable to check the digital programme before heading to the venues, as printed copies are limited.

What is the best way to get to the festival venues in Puebla?

All three venues sit within the pedestrian-friendly Historic Centre. If you are arriving from outside the city, Puebla is a two-hour drive or bus ride from Mexico City, and ride-hailing apps operate reliably within the metropolitan area.

Criolo Takes the Stage at Porão do Rock Fortaleza

São Paulo rapper and singer Criolo will close the second weekend of Porão do Rock Fortaleza on Friday, 22 August 2026. The performance marks a high point for the long-running independent festival, which has championed Brazilian rock, rap, and alternative music since 1998.

Criolo, born Kleber Cavalcante Gomes, has built a career spanning samba, MPB, and politically charged hip-hop. His appearance at Porão do Rock highlights the festival’s commitment to booking artists who move fluidly across genres and generations.

The Full 22 August Lineup

Criolo does not perform alone. The 22 August bill also features Rodox, the influential Brazilian hardcore band that returned to stages after a long hiatus.

Porão do Rock 2026: Two Weekends of Music

The 2026 edition of Porão do Rock Fortaleza spans four days across two weekends: 14–15 August and 21–22 August. According to local listings, all performances take place at Praça Verde, the open-air square within the Centro Dragão do Mar de Arte e Cultura.

Dragão do Mar is one of Fortaleza’s most recognisable cultural landmarks, drawing visitors for its museums, cinemas, and live events. Hosting Porão do Rock there places the festival at the centre of the city’s cultural life.

Criolo’s Broader Fortaleza Connection

Criolo’s separate “Criolo 50” anniversary tour — marking his fiftieth birthday and two decades in music — also runs additional indoor dates in early August, per the tour’s official schedule.

Porão do Rock has long been a driver of cultural tourism in Ceará, drawing visitors from across Brazil’s Northeast and beyond. Booking a nationally recognised name like Criolo strengthens the festival’s draw for out-of-town audiences.

For investors and expats watching Brazil’s creative economy, the festival’s endurance — nearly three decades — signals the resilience of Fortaleza’s independent cultural sector. The city has steadily built a reputation as a live-music destination, complementing its established beach-tourism profile.

How to Attend and What to Watch

Porão do Rock has historically offered free or low-cost entry, in keeping with its independent ethos. Organisers typically announce ticketing details and full schedules closer to the festival dates via official social-media channels.

Visitors should monitor the festival’s verified Instagram and website for lineup additions, set times, and any access policies. Praça Verde is centrally located and well served by Fortaleza’s public-transport and ride-hailing networks.

When does Criolo perform at Porão do Rock Fortaleza?

Criolo performs on Friday, 22 August 2026, as the headliner of the festival’s closing night. The event takes place at Praça Verde in the Centro Dragão do Mar de Arte e Cultura.

Who else is playing at Porão do Rock on 22 August?

The 22 August lineup includes Rodox, Lucas Inutilismo, Guizão, and Conti alongside Criolo. The festival runs across two weekends, with additional acts performing on 14, 15, and 21 August.

Is Criolo playing any other shows in Fortaleza in 2026?

His separate “Criolo 50” anniversary tour has additional August dates; check the official tour schedule to confirm cities and tickets.

World.title: Brazil Agribusiness Bankruptcies Surge 33% in Q1
World.content:
Brazil · Business

Key Facts —Q1 2026 filings Agribusiness judicial recovery requests reached 517 in Q1 2026, a 33% jump versus Q1 2025, per Neot. —2025 annual record Serasa Experian recorded 1,990 agribusiness recovery requests in 2025, up 56.4% from 1,272 in 2024. —Profile of filers Rural producers (individuals and companies) made 305 of the 517 Q1 requests; input resellers accounted for 83. —Hardest-hit states Goiás led with 113 filings, followed by Mato Grosso (98), Rio Grande do Sul (62), Minas Gerais (56), and Paraná (54). —Top affected crops Soy cultivation (243 companies) and beef cattle raising (89) are the largest segments in judicial recovery, per CNN citing RGF.

Brazil agribusiness bankruptcies are accelerating at a pace that could make 2026 the worst year on record for the sector, as judicial recovery requests by farmers and agricultural companies jumped 33% in the first quarter compared to the same period in 2025.

Brazil Agribusiness Bankruptcies Surge 33% in Q1. (Photo internet reproduction)

A Record-Breaking Trajectory

Agribusiness judicial recovery filings in Brazil totaled 517 in the first three months of 2026, according to data from credit analytics firm Neot published by Folha de S.Paulo on July 29. The figure represents a 33% increase over the first quarter of 2025 and keeps the sector on pace to surpass the annual record set just last year.

For context, Serasa Experian – a separate credit bureau with a different methodology – reported that the broader agribusiness sector logged 1,990 recovery requests in all of 2025. That was a 56.4% surge from 1,272 in 2024 and the highest annual volume in Serasa’s data series dating back to 2021.

The two data sets differ in scope. Neot’s Q1 count of 517 includes a wider range of filers, while Serasa’s Q1 2026 indicator counted 139 recovery processes specifically within the agropecuária category. Both sources, however, point to the same conclusion: rural debt stress is intensifying rapidly.

Who Is Filing and Where

Rural producers – both individual farmers and agricultural companies – accounted for 305 of the 517 first-quarter requests, according to Neot. Input resellers and distributors made up another 83 filings, a spillover effect that Neot directly linked to producer delinquency cascading through the supply chain.

The geographic concentration is stark. The central-western state of Goiás, a major grain and livestock hub, led the country with 113 filings. Mato Grosso, Brazil’s top soybean-producing state, followed with 98 requests. The southern state of Rio Grande do Sul recorded 62, while Minas Gerais and Paraná posted 56 and 54, respectively.

By agricultural activity, soy cultivation dominates the distress picture. Data cited by CNN Brasil from consultancy RGF showed 243 soy-producing companies in judicial recovery. Beef cattle operations ranked second with 89 companies. Corn producers also form part of the stressed grain complex, though the reporting emphasizes soy and beef as the leading segments.

The Drivers of Rural Debt Stress

Low global grain prices sit at the center of the crisis. Soybean and corn prices have weakened considerably from the highs of previous years, squeezing farm margins just as many producers face elevated costs. Brazilian farmers are particularly exposed because many expanded operations aggressively during the commodity boom, taking on dollar-linked or high-interest debt to finance land, machinery, and inputs.

Brazil’s benchmark Selic interest rate remains at an elevated level, making credit expensive and debt service costs punishing. When combined with high input costs for seeds, fertilizers, and agrochemicals, the math becomes unsustainable for leveraged producers. The result is what analysts describe as a structural liquidity crisis – or “crise de liquidez estrutural” – across the sector.

Weather has compounded the problem. Drought and adverse conditions, especially in southern Brazil, worsened cash-flow stress for farmers who were already struggling with thin margins. A poor harvest not only reduces revenue but can trigger loan covenants and accelerate creditor pressure, pushing more producers toward court-supervised restructuring.

What Judicial Recovery Means for Creditors

Judicial recovery in Brazil functions similarly to Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in the United States. It allows debtors to freeze collections, renegotiate obligations with creditors, and present a restructuring plan under court supervision. For foreign investors holding Brazilian agribusiness debt or equity, the process introduces significant uncertainty.

The immediate impact is a delay in debt collection. Creditors, including international banks, commodity traders, and input suppliers, cannot enforce guarantees or seize collateral while the stay period is in effect. Negotiations can stretch for months or years, and approved restructuring plans often impose haircuts on principal and extend maturities.

Neot’s data showing 83 input distributor filings underscores the contagion risk. When farmers default, suppliers of seeds, fertilizers, and crop protection products face their own liquidity crunches. This interconnectedness means distress in the farm sector can quickly migrate to agribusiness service providers, trading houses, and ultimately to the financial institutions that fund them.

The Outlook for Foreign Investors

The pace of filings through March 2026 suggests the full-year total could eclipse the 2025 record. If the first-quarter trend holds, the sector is on track for more than 2,000 judicial recovery requests by December. That would mark a dramatic escalation from the 1,272 filings recorded in 2024 and confirm that the credit cycle has turned sharply against Brazilian agriculture.

For foreign portfolio investors holding Brazilian agribusiness bonds or equities, the rise in judicial recoveries raises the risk of write-downs and delayed payments. Multinational commodity traders who extend pre-export financing to Brazilian farmers may need to increase provisions for doubtful accounts. Private equity and direct investors in farmland or agribusiness platforms should stress-test their assumptions about counterparty credit quality.

The crisis is not uniform. Producers with low leverage, diversified crop mixes, and access to subsidized credit lines from Brazil’s national development bank BNDES are better positioned. The pain is concentrated among over-leveraged operators who expanded aggressively during the 2020-2023 commodity upcycle and now face a punishing combination of low prices, high rates, and weather setbacks.

Broader Economic Implications

Agribusiness accounts for roughly 25% of Brazil’s gross domestic product, making the sector’s financial health a macroeconomic concern. A wave of judicial recoveries can tighten credit conditions for the entire farm belt, as banks and input suppliers become more cautious about extending new financing. That credit contraction can depress planting decisions, reduce input purchases, and ripple through rural communities.

The Brazilian government has historically intervened during agricultural debt crises, offering restructuring programs and subsidized credit lines. No major relief package has been announced for the current cycle, but political pressure is likely to build if filings continue at the current pace. Foreign investors should monitor Brasília for policy signals that could alter the trajectory of creditor recoveries.

For now, the data tells a clear story: Brazil’s farm sector is under severe financial strain, and the courts are becoming the venue where much of that stress is being resolved. The 33% jump in first-quarter filings is a warning sign that the worst may still lie ahead.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is judicial recovery in Brazil?

Judicial recovery (recuperação judicial) is a court-supervised process similar to Chapter 11 bankruptcy in the United States. It allows financially distressed companies to freeze debt collections, negotiate with creditors, and present a restructuring plan to avoid liquidation.

Why are Brazilian farmers filing for judicial recovery now?

A combination of low global grain prices, high domestic interest rates (Selic), elevated input costs for fertilizers and seeds, and adverse weather – particularly drought in the South – has squeezed margins and triggered a liquidity crisis for leveraged producers.

How does this affect foreign investors in Brazilian agribusiness?

Foreign creditors, including banks, commodity traders, and bondholders, face delayed debt collection, potential haircuts on principal, and extended maturities. Equity investors in Brazilian agribusiness companies may see write-downs as counterparty credit quality deteriorates.

World.title: BNDES Fleet Renewal: US$3.9 Billion for Trucks and Buses
World.content:
Brazil · Business

Key Facts —Total Approved BNDES approved R$20 billion (~US$3.9 billion) on July 29, 2026, representing about 95% of the program’s roughly R$21 billion (~US$4.1 billion) budget. —Eligible Vehicles Financing covers new, nationally manufactured trucks, tractor-trucks, buses, minibuses, and road implements. Semi-new trucks are allowed only for autonomous drivers and cooperative members. —Interest Rate The credit line offers subsidized and facilitated credit terms. Specific rate figures reported by some outlets are not officially confirmed by the bank. —Application Deadline New financing proposals must be submitted by August 28, 2026. —Beneficiary Breakdown Of the roughly R$20 billion, about R$19.1 billion (~US$3.75 billion) went to fleet-owning companies across about 17,200 operations, and about R$900 million (~US$176 million) to autonomous truckers across about 2,100 operations.

Brazil’s national development bank has committed nearly R$20 billion (~US$3.9 billion) to the BNDES fleet renewal initiative, a massive credit line designed to replace tens of thousands of ageing trucks and buses with modern, less-polluting models. The program, which some outlets refer to as “Move Brasil 2,” had a total budget of roughly R$21 billion (~US$4.1 billion) and will stop accepting new proposals on August 28, 2026.

BNDES Fleet Renewal: US$3.9 Billion for Trucks and Buses. (Photo internet reproduction)

How the BNDES Fleet Renewal Credit Line Works

The BNDES fleet-renewal credit line finances the purchase of new heavy vehicles and road implements. It also incorporates a specific sub-program called the BNDES Fleet Renewal Program (Programa BNDES Renovação de Frota), structured with R$6 billion (~US$1.18 billion) in federal funds authorized by Provisional Measure No. 1,328/2025, plus an additional R$4 billion (~US$784 million) from BNDES itself.

Financing limits reach up to R$50 million (~US$9.8 million) per client. Standard repayment terms extend to 60 months with a grace period of up to 6 months. However, autonomous truck drivers receive special treatment, with payment terms of up to 10 years (120 installments) and a 12-month grace period.

The program requires a direct environmental trade-off. To access the best conditions, owners must hand over an old vehicle for dismantling. The Fleet Renewal Program specifically targets trucks with more than 20 years of use for scrapping.

Who Qualifies for the Financing

The program casts a wide net across the transport sector. Eligible beneficiaries include autonomous cargo carriers, individuals associated with cooperatives, individual entrepreneurs, and legal entities operating in road or urban cargo and passenger transport.

The rules on vehicle eligibility are strict. New trucks and tractor-trucks must be nationally manufactured and accredited in the BNDES’s Credentialed Financial Institutions (CFI) system. Semi-new trucks and tractor-trucks are permitted only for autonomous transporters and cooperative members. The program also finances buses, minibuses, and road implements in its expanded phase, broadening the impact beyond cargo to urban passenger transit.

The Industrial Angle: A Boost for Local Manufacturing

The ‘national manufacturing’ requirement explicitly channels credit toward factories installed in Brazil. While BNDES did not publish an official list of beneficiary companies, the rule directly favors major manufacturers with local production lines, which media reports suggest include Mercedes-Benz, Volkswagen Caminhões e Ônibus, Scania, Volvo, and bus bodybuilder Marcopolo.

For foreign investors, this policy signals sustained demand for heavy-vehicle components and assembly operations located within Brazil. The government designed the credit expansion to sustain industrial activity after the first phase of the program was rapidly exhausted. By tying cheap credit to domestic production, the state creates a captive demand cycle for locally made capital goods.

Why the Fleet Needs Renewal

Brazil’s heavy-vehicle fleet suffers from advanced age, which increases logistics costs, fuel consumption, and accident risks. The program specifically targets the replacement of vehicles older than 20 years. These legacy trucks and buses operate with obsolete diesel technology, emitting significantly higher levels of pollutants than modern models.

The government’s stated goals include reducing environmental impact, improving road safety, and lowering Brazil’s structural logistics costs. By scrapping old vehicles, the program aims to modernize the commercial transport backbone of Latin America‘s largest economy. The credit line also covers road implements, allowing for a complete overhaul of the transport equipment chain.

Timeline and Execution

The window for action is narrow. BNDES set a deadline of August 28, 2026, for submitting new operations. The rapid exhaustion of the previous phase prompted the government to double the credit volume and improve conditions in April 2026.

The nearly full commitment of the roughly R$21 billion envelope suggests strong latent demand from transport companies and autonomous drivers. For foreign investors in logistics, auto parts, or commercial vehicle manufacturing, the program represents a short-term fiscal impulse that will refresh a significant portion of the circulating fleet over the next year.

What It Means for Foreign Investors

The BNDES fleet renewal program is a direct intervention in Brazil’s capital goods market. It lowers the acquisition cost for transport operators, potentially boosting freight capacity and efficiency. Investors in Brazilian logistics operators or road infrastructure concessions may see improved fleet productivity and lower maintenance downtime among contracted carriers.

The program also reinforces Brazil’s industrial policy of using state banks to drive environmental upgrades. Foreign manufacturers without local production, however, are effectively locked out of the financing benefits. The policy rewards companies that have invested in Brazilian factories, creating a protective moat around local assembly operations during the renewal cycle.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the interest rate for the BNDES fleet renewal program?

The credit line offers subsidized and facilitated credit terms. The specific BNDES Fleet Renewal Program calculates the final rate as the sum of the Financial Cost, the BNDES Rate, and the Financial Agent Rate. Autonomous truck drivers receive more favorable conditions, including longer payment terms of up to 10 years.

Can foreigners or foreign companies apply for this BNDES credit?

The program is open to legal entities in Brazil’s road transport sector. A foreign-owned company with a locally registered Brazilian subsidiary operating in cargo or passenger transport could potentially qualify, provided it meets all eligibility rules. However, the purchased vehicles must be nationally manufactured and accredited in the BNDES system.

What happens to the old trucks under this renewal program?

To access special financing conditions, owners must deliver their old vehicle for dismantling. The BNDES Fleet Renewal Program specifically targets trucks with more than 20 years of use. This scrapping requirement ensures the oldest, most polluting vehicles are permanently removed from circulation rather than resold into the secondary market.

World.title: Costa Rica Bill Would Bar Uber Drivers From Airport Pickups
World.content:
Land at Juan Santamaría, open your ride app, and under a bill moving through Costa Rica’s Congress there would be no legal ride waiting for you. Lawmakers filed 282 changes to that bill. A legislative committee finished working through them on Tuesday and approved nine of them.

The bill now goes back to the full Assembly for a first vote. Legislators can still try to revive changes the committee threw out, so what sits in the text today is not necessarily what gets voted on. One approved change shuts platform drivers out of airports, ports, docks and international maritime terminals. They could not pick you up or drop you off at any of them unless whoever runs the place gives express permission.

The reason is that those terminals operate under concessions, and at airports the orange taxis hold that concession — there are roughly 100 of them. So if the provision survives, an orange taxi would be your legal option at Juan Santamaría. There is one possible way around it. Uber said in June that it is testing putting orange airport taxis inside its own app. If that works, you could still book an airport ride through the app. It would just arrive as an orange taxi.

The pricing part of the bill is the piece most often described wrong, so it is worth being exact. The bill does not set your fare. It sets a floor on what the driver has to earn per kilometer. You would still pay one of two ways: the app quotes you the whole trip up front, or you and the driver agree a price before you set off.

Nothing in the text caps or fixes what you end up paying. The Public Works and Transport Ministry would work out the driver’s minimum using fuel costs, repairs, typical mileage, a minimum profit per trip, insurance and Caja contributions, then update the number twice a year, in February and August.

Whether that pushes your fare up is a prediction, not a fact. The Chamber of Commerce argues the floor amounts to price control and would make trips cost more, and that locking apps out of airports and ports cuts competition and leaves travelers fewer options. It counts around 35,000 people who make their main living through platforms, has separately cited close to 40,000 people earning some income that way, and puts users at roughly two million.

Aprimotec, an association representing platform drivers, asked lawmakers this month to stop the bill, saying it would turn a private service into a taxi service and damage the income of 35,000 families. Uber has said nothing publicly about the version the committee just approved.

Taxi drivers want the bill passed, and their argument is straightforward. The apps have run for eleven years with no rules while taxis carry costs the apps do not. Taxi groups say concessions have fallen from 13,500 to about 9,000. The squeeze is current: more than 2,000 taxis came off the road in July when their concession deadlines passed, and the taxi drivers’ union has asked for six more months so more of them can get their paperwork in order. The transport ministry says the text came out of talks involving taxi drivers, the platforms themselves and the national transport chamber.

For anyone driving, the bill trades a grey zone for a checklist. Right now the work is not clearly legal, and fines start at ₡122,597 (about $270) and can end with your plates pulled or your car impounded. Under the new rules you would need a license you have held for at least a year, an approved course, registration as a taxpayer, registration with the Caja as an independent worker where it applies, a criminal record certificate filed every year, insurance, no unpaid traffic fines, and an identification sticker on your windshield.

In the law’s first year you would pay ₡25,000 (about $55). Your car would need to pass inspection annually, keep the marchamo current, stay under an age limit set later, and carry both mandatory insurance and a liability policy. Seven seats is the maximum. You could drive someone else’s car with the registered owner’s permission.

Sharing a ride with a stranger would end. Combining separate passengers’ requests into one trip becomes one of the most serious offenses in the bill, alongside waiting at bus stops for passengers, cutting in front of buses and cruising the streets looking for riders.

As a passenger you would get some things in writing. You would have the right to know the price, the driver and the car before you get in, to pay in cash or electronically, and to get a receipt at the end. Anyone under 15 would have to travel with an adult, and riders aged 15 to 17 would come with extra rules set later.

The companies would have obligations of their own. Each would have to register a legal entity in Costa Rica, pay its taxes, collect and hand over sales tax, and report its drivers, cars and trip numbers every three months. Each would need a system for handling complaints and for dealing with harassment and discrimination. Permits would last ten years and could be renewed. A company caught running without one would get a month to fix it, and possibly a second month if the delay was not its fault.

Cutting off a platform’s payments would require a judge. Fines would run from one to ten base salaries, the reference figure Costa Rican law uses to scale penalties. In the worst cases a platform could be shut out entirely, or a driver blocked from signing up again for one to five years. The fees and fines would go into a Mobility Fund for roads, transport upgrades and enforcement.

Taxis get changes too. Inspection moves to once a year, temporary permits become possible where service is short, and a concession holder can name who takes over the concession if they die. None of this is settled because lawmakers can still reopen rejected changes on the floor, both the airport ban and the per-kilometer floor could look different by the time anyone votes. Eleven years after the apps arrived, Costa Rica still has not decided what they legally are.

World.title: Costa Rica Wins Its First Surfing Gold Medal in Regional Games History
World.content:
Costa Rican surfer Rachel Agüero Cabezas won the women’s shortboard title at the Central American and Caribbean Games in the Dominican Republic tpday, delivering Costa Rica its first gold medal in surfing in the history of the regional competition.

The 20-year-old beat Barbados’ Chelsea Tuach 10.50 points to 7.33 in the final at Playa Encuentro in Cabarete, on the northern coast of Puerto Plata province. Agüero’s score came from two waves graded 5.83 and 4.67, while Tuach posted a 5.00 and a 2.33. According to the National Olympic Committee, Agüero took control of the heat from the opening minutes and never surrendered the lead. Tuach needed a wave scored at 5.51 or better to overturn the result and never found one.

Agüero reached the final by eliminating the surfer most observers had installed as the favorite. In the fourth round she defeated Nicaragua’s Candelaria Resano, an Olympian and world championship medalist, by 12.57 points to 11.33. She had opened the competition on the first day of the event with 11.16 points, built on waves of 7.33 and 3.83, to win her heat ahead of Puerto Rico’s Havanna Cabrero and Colombia’s Margarita Conde. That 7.33 stood as the highest-scoring women’s wave of the opening day.

The result caps a season that has established Agüero as the leading woman in Costa Rican competitive surfing. She arrived in the Dominican Republic as the two-time national Open champion, having sealed her second consecutive title only weeks earlier at the closing round of the Banco LAFISE national circuit at Playa Hermosa de Jacó, the beach where she lives and trains.

In March she won the Denga Santa Teresa Pro at Playa Carmen. She has also been competing on World Surf League regional events, the tier where surfers accumulate the results and ranking points that open the door to the sport’s professional circuits. Costa Rica had never won a surfing gold medal at these Games before Wednesday. The country’s only previous podium finishes in the sport came at San Salvador 2023, when Lía Díaz and Anthony Flores each took bronze in longboard.

Sam Reidy added another on Tuesday, beating the Dominican Republic’s Gian Marco Oliva 14.50 to 11.60 in the men’s shortboard bronze heat, a result the Costa Rican Surf Federation described as the first shortboard medal at the Games. Flores finished fourth in the men’s longboard event this year after losing his bronze heat to Mexico’s Heriberto Torres.

The surfing competition ran from July 25 until today at Playa Encuentro, a break that has become one of the Caribbean’s most reliable competitive venues, and drew 71 surfers from 12 countries across shortboard, longboard and stand-up paddle surf. Agüero’s medal was Costa Rica’s third gold of Santo Domingo 2026. The first two came in taekwondo, through Jaycee Bassett and Neshy Lindo.

This edition of the Games is the 25th and marks a century since the first was held in Mexico City in 1926. Organizers programmed 40 sports, more than the Los Angeles 2028 Olympic schedule, and more than 6,200 athletes from 37 countries and territories are competing over 16 days.

Costa Rican surfing has been producing this kind of result with increasing regularity. Díaz became the first surfer from Costa Rica or anywhere in Central America to qualify for the World Surf League’s Longboard Tour, a circuit that opened its season at Huntington Beach in California this month.

Leilani McGonagle won a place on the 2026-27 Challenger Series, the qualifying tier immediately below the elite Championship Tour. Bodyboarder Dulce Agüero reached a podium at Pipeline in Hawaii in March. The national federation has said its planning is now oriented around the qualifying events for the 2028 Olympics, where surfing will again be on the program.

For Agüero, the initial reward is a regional title at 20 and a clear line of sight to the next stage. The Pan American Games in Lima in 2027 come first, and the Olympic qualifying calendar follows behind it.

World.title: Costa Rica Warns of Poor Air Quality as Saharan Dust Arrives
World.content:
A new push of Saharan dust is expected to spread across Costa Rica this week, bringing hazy skies, reduced visibility and poorer air quality, with Thursday and Friday forecast to be the most difficult days. The dust will affect nearly all of Costa Rica, although higher concentrations are expected in Alajuela, western parts of the Central Valley and some areas of Cartago.

Residents may notice a pale or milky appearance in the sky known as calima, caused by fine particles suspended in the atmosphere. Visibility over mountains and other distant landmarks could also become noticeably worse. The conditions are expected to become more apparent beginning Wednesday before reaching their strongest point on Thursday, July 30, and Friday, July 31. Air quality should begin improving Saturday as the dust moves north toward other parts of Central America and Mexico.

People with asthma, allergies and other respiratory conditions face the greatest risk. Children and older adults should also reduce the amount of time they spend outdoors during the highest concentrations. The warning extends beyond people with existing health problems. Residents in generally good health are being advised to avoid long periods of strenuous outdoor activity on Thursday and Friday, including extended runs, cycling or outdoor exercise lasting several hours.

Fine particles carried within the dust can enter the respiratory system and cause irritation. Possible symptoms include coughing, itchy eyes or throat, headaches, chest discomfort, breathing difficulty and worsening asthma or allergy attacks. People who must remain outdoors should limit their exposure and consider wearing a well-fitting mask, particularly if they have respiratory problems. Anyone who develops discomfort while exercising should stop the activity and move indoors.

The Saharan dust originated over North Africa and traveled thousands of kilometers across the Atlantic Ocean and Caribbean Sea before reaching Central America. These events are common during the middle of the year, when strong trade winds carry dry air and mineral particles westward.

The approaching dust will combine with stronger winds, locally raised soil particles, pollen and smoke still present from regional burning. Together, those elements can increase the amount of material suspended in the air even when the Saharan particles are not clearly visible. Lower rainfall will make the situation more noticeable. Rain normally helps remove dust and other particles from the atmosphere, but Costa Rica is expecting a significant reduction in precipitation over the next several days.

The dry air associated with Saharan dust can also limit the development of rain clouds, allowing particles to remain suspended longer. The episode is not expected to produce dangerously polluted conditions across the country. However, prolonged exposure could cause problems for sensitive people and make outdoor activity uncomfortable even for otherwise healthy residents.

You may also encounter hazier views from mountain overlooks, volcanoes and higher-elevation destinations. Flights are not currently expected to face major disruptions, although distant visibility could be reduced. Conditions are forecast to improve considerably over the weekend as the main concentration of dust moves away from Costa Rica.

World.title: Costa Rica Expels Second-Division Club for 10 Years Over Match-Fixing
World.content:
The Costa Rican Football Federation has thrown a second-division club out of the sport for ten years after its investigators concluded the team took part in manipulating four matches during the 2025 season, in what is now the fifth match-fixing case in Costa Rican football to end in sanctions.

The Disciplinary Commission of the Federación Costarricense de Fútbol found that Municipal Garabito Fútbol Club SAD, which competed in the Liga de Ascenso under the name San Carlos FC, breached Article 66 of the federation’s Disciplinary Code. The resolution bars the club from any football-related activity for a decade. The federation’s legal department has since notified every affiliated league — the first division, the Liga de Ascenso, the amateur Linafa structure, futsal, beach football and women’s football — that the prohibition applies to the legal entity regardless of category or format.

The case rests on a report by the federation’s Integrity Office, led by Carlos Ricardo Benavides, which examined four Liga de Ascenso fixtures from the 2024-2025 season. All four ended in lopsided defeats. San Carlos FC lost 8-2 to Quepos Cambute on January 19, 2025, fell 5-1 to Cofutpa on February 9, lost 6-2 away to Municipal Grecia on March 1, and lost 5-2 to Jicaral on March 9. According to the resolution, the investigation found a sustained pattern of irregularities in sports betting linked to matches the club played, together with atypical movement in betting markets.

Much of that evidence came from outside Costa Rica. Sportradar, the sports data firm that assists FIFA with integrity investigations, issued alerts on several of the club’s fixtures after analysing both the state of betting markets before kickoff and the swings recorded while games were in progress. In the Quepos Cambute match, San Carlos FC was leading 1-0 at the 27th minute when heavy money began moving on a San Carlos defeat; the game finished 8-2 to Quepos Cambute.

Sportradar filed a report flagging irregular movement five days later, on January 24. Investigators also drew on reports from the bookmakers Betway, VBet and 9 Olybet and from the International Betting Integrity Association. The Integrity Office concluded that the relationship between the market swings and what happened on the pitch pointed to a high probability of deliberate intervention by the club.

The commission’s finding, as set out in the resolution, is that Municipal Garabito Fútbol Club SAD, known as San Carlos FC, played an active part in the conduct. The franchise had been based in the Pacific canton of Garabito before its owners moved the operation north; the club then competed as San Carlos FC in the Northern Zone. It was relegated from the Liga de Ascenso at the end of the 2024-2025 season and did not subsequently compete in Linafa. The club has no connection to AD San Carlos of the first division, nor to Inter San Carlos, which recently won the Liga de Ascenso title.

Three players who turned out for the club were sanctioned in a separate resolution that became final on June 25 of this year. That file concerned an approach made in April 2025 to players at Deportivo Upala, who were offered money to lose a Liga de Ascenso fixture against San Carlos FC.

The attempt failed because the Upala players reported it. Hansell Arauz Ovares, a retired forward who won four national titles with Deportivo Saprissa between 2014 and 2016, and Henry Cooper Bennett, a former Limón FC striker, were each banned for 15 years. Goalkeeper Fabián Rodríguez Esquivel received 15 years in the same file and a further 20 years in a separate case in which the Integrity Office concluded he had approached a Guadalupe FC player about fixing a first-division match, bringing his total ban to 35 years. All three bans cover any football-related role, whether as a player, coaching staff or club official.

The club expulsion is the second of its kind in Costa Rica. Puerto Golfito FC was excluded for ten years in 2024 on similar grounds. In 2025, three Municipal Turrialba officials — Enrique Valencia, Ernesto de la Torre and Rolando Pereira — were suspended for five years over an alleged manipulation attempt. Each of the cases sanctioned so far has originated in the lower tiers of the Costa Rican game, where budgets are thin, wages are low and matches still attract enough betting volume abroad to make manipulation worth someone’s while.

In notifying every affiliated league of the expulsion, the federation asked each to apply its integrity protocols and strengthen preventive measures. The Integrity Office has indicated that further resolutions are pending.

World.title: Trump’s Granddaughter Puts Guanacaste Beach Town in Front of 1.5 Million Viewers
World.content:
A travel vlog posted last week by Kai Trump, the eldest granddaughter of U.S. President Donald Trump, has put a small stretch of Guanacaste coastline in front of one of the largest young American audiences any Costa Rican destination has reached this year.

The 19-year-old published the video to her YouTube channel on July 25, where it went out to more than 1.5 million subscribers. She framed the trip as a send-off with high school friends before the group scatters to university, with Trump herself starting at the University of Miami this fall.

The footage moves through the familiar sequence of a Guanacaste beach holiday — mornings at the hotel pool, a climb to a ridgeline lookout, boogie boarding in the surf, ice cream, long outdoor dinners, card games, and a sunset she describes as spectacular. At one point she tells the camera she never wants to leave and would move to Costa Rica.

According to records from the Dirección General de Migración y Extranjería, Trump was here from June 11 to June 14 and stayed at a hotel in Playa Las Catalinas, in the area of Santa Cruz, Guanacaste. That places the visit roughly six weeks before the video reached the public, a gap that is standard practice for creators who edit and stage travel content for release when it will draw the most attention.

Las Catalinas is an unusual setting for this kind of exposure. Founded in 2006 on a previously undeveloped stretch of Pacific coast, the planned town covers about 485 hectares (1,200 acres) and was laid out on car-free, fully walkable principles, with plazas arranged around Playa Danta and a network of trails climbing into the dry forest behind it.

It sits roughly an hour by road from Daniel Oduber Quirós International Airport in Liberia, which is what allows a four-day trip of this kind to work at all. The development has spent close to two decades positioning itself toward exactly the high-spending, design-conscious North American traveler the vlog’s audience will grow into.

The video did not travel cleanly. Within days of release, U.S. and British outlets seized on the contrast between the trip and domestic economic sentiment, citing polling that found the overwhelming majority of Americans surveyed believe Costa Rica is in an affordability crisis. Commenters on the video and on aggregated coverage split between praise for the destination and criticism of the timing. Trump has faced similar reaction before, including over a grocery-shopping video posted in March, and has said publicly that the criticism does not affect her.

None of that argument is about Costa Rica, and the destination itself came through the coverage largely untouched. Costa Rica has become a recurring stop for the family — Trump’s aunt, Ivanka Trump, spent Passover and Easter week here in 2025 with her husband and children, drawing a similar mix of enthusiasm and criticism at the time. Trump has said on her own channels that Costa Rica ranks among her favorite places to travel, and she has a long-standing friendship with a Costa Rican classmate that predates the trip.

What the episode illustrates is how little control a destination has over the terms on which it gets seen. Guanacaste’s tourism spends heavily to reach American travelers in their twenties and thirties, a demographic that increasingly makes destination decisions from short-form video rather than from advertising. A four-day trip in June, edited and released in late July by someone with a national profile, delivered that reach in a single upload — bundled together with a political argument Costa Rica had no part in and no ability to steer.

World.title: Ride-app protest could slow your drive across the Valle Central this morning
World.content:
If you have a flight out of Juan Santamaría today, a shuttle booked to the airport, or a drive between Cartago and San José, leave earlier than you planned. Ride-app drivers have called a protest for 9 a.m. today, and the roads they say they will use are the ones that carry nearly everyone.

Organizers say the convoy will roll along Ruta 1 in Alajuela, through Ochomogo, past Sabanilla and onto Circunvalación, finishing at Casa Presidencial in Zapote. Those details come from the drivers themselves. As of first light Wednesday, the Policía de Tránsito had not published an advisory confirming the route, so treat that list as the plan rather than the result. Plans like this one shift, shrink or start late.

What the drivers have called is a tortuguismo, a go-slow. Nobody blocks anything. The convoy simply travels in a pack at a crawl, and every vehicle behind it travels at the same speed. That distinction is the whole story for you. A closure gets you a detour, an officer waving you around, and a police post you can see from a distance. A go-slow gets you none of that. There is no sign, no announcement, and no way to tell you are in it until you already are. Once you are boxed in on a divided highway, your only real option is to wait.

Ruta 1 is the reason this matters to travelers. It is the corridor between San José and Juan Santamaría, so anything that slows it slows every airport transfer, every hotel shuttle and every rental car heading for a return desk. Ochomogo sits on the climb between Cartago and San José and is the pinch point for that whole side of the valley. Circunvalación is the ring road that absorbs traffic coming off Ruta 27 and feeds it around the capital toward Zapote. Between them, those three points decide whether the Valle Central moves.

If you are flying out this morning and have not left yet, go now. Whatever cushion you would normally give yourself, add an hour on top of it. That sounds excessive on a normal Wednesday, and on a normal Wednesday it would be. The problem with a go-slow is that the delay is not proportional to the protest.

A few dozen vehicles moving at 20 kilometers per hour (about 12 miles per hour) for half an hour can leave a line that takes two hours to drain, because the road behind them keeps filling at normal speed while the front of it empties at a crawl. You do not lose the time the protest lasts. You lose the time it takes the backlog to clear.

Check in online before you leave, and if you have a bag to drop, know your airline’s cutoff rather than guessing at it. If you are running late, call the airline from the road rather than waiting until you reach the counter. Missing a bag cutoff by ten minutes is a different problem than missing a flight, and airlines can sometimes do something about the first if they hear from you early.

If you are already on Ruta 1 and traffic ahead of you dies, stay in the lane you are in. Weaving between lanes to get past a convoy does not work, and on that stretch it puts you alongside heavy trucks that cannot stop quickly. Do not try to overtake the group. If you have not yet committed to the highway, Ruta 3, the old road through Heredia and Alajuela, runs roughly parallel and gives you a way to reach the airport without joining the line. It is slower on a good day and it will be crowded today, but a slow road that is moving beats a fast road that is not.

Coming from Cartago, the alternative to Florencio del Castillo is the old road, and this week that carries a complication of its own. The Romería is already underway. Tránsito started its operation on July 25 with about 150 officers on that corridor and reinforces it between July 31 and August 2, and pilgrims are walking the shoulder in numbers. The old road is an option this morning, but drive it expecting people on foot rather than a clear run.

If you are not traveling and have nothing that cannot move, the simplest answer is to not drive between roughly 9 a.m. and midday. Reschedule the Zapote appointment. Take the errand in the afternoon. Every vehicle that stays home is one that is not in the line in front of somebody trying to catch a plane.

Behind all of this is a bill that has been moving through the Legislative Assembly for years. Expediente 23.736 would regulate transport offered through platforms such as Uber and DiDi, requiring drivers to register with the CCSS and Hacienda, pay an annual permit, and meet insurance and background requirements. The Comisión de Gobierno y Administración finished working through 282 mociones de fondo on Tuesday and approved nine of them, sending the revised text back to the plenary. That vote is what put drivers on the road this morning.

The drivers want two things added before it passes. They want a ceiling on the commission platforms take from each fare, and they want guaranteed benefits and due process when a company deactivates an account. Drivers made both demands at the Assembly earlier this month, saying they had not been heard during the drafting.

Aprimotec, an association representing platform drivers, asked the Assembly and the Executive on July 20 to stop the bill’s advance altogether, arguing the text was written around the traditional taxi sector and would push drivers out of the work rather than formalize it. The taxi sector sees it differently. Canatrans, Fenacotaxi, the Foro Nacional de Taxistas and other transport groups have publicly backed the bill, framing it as legal certainty and fair competition.

Neither side is likely to settle it this morning. What will be settled by lunchtime is whether you made your flight.

World.title: ‘BAD FREAK’ CHARGED ON STEAMY WEDNESDAY; ‘WAR RIOR’ ON THE RUN – WHO WON THE FIGHT?
World.content:
‘BAD FREAK’ CHARGED ON STEAMY WEDNESDAY; ‘WAR RIOR’ ON THE RUN – WHO WON THE FIGHT?

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A viral Facebook fight between two Belize City women known on social media as “Bad Freak” and “War Rior” has resulted in a disorderly conduct charge, with one woman fined and the other still being sought by police.

Twenty-two-year-old Britney Nichole Daly, also known as “Bad Freak,” appeared in Court #3 at the Belize City Magistrates’ Court on Wednesday, July 29, where she pleaded guilty to disorderly conduct.

The charge arose from a public fight on Freedom Street on Tuesday, July 28, involving Daly and Shala Smith, also known as “War Rior.” Video of the altercation quickly circulated on social media.

Police reportedly arrived after the fight had ended and those involved had already dispersed. Authorities later used footage from the Police Fusion Centre’s surveillance cameras to identify the women, leading to Daly’s detention.

Daly, a musician who resides at #22 Freedom Street, was fined $150 plus $5 in court costs. She has until September 30, 2026, to pay the total, or she will face one month in prison.

Outside the courthouse, Daly was asked what prompted the fight.

“To prove a point,” she replied before entering a waiting taxi.

Police say Smith remains at large and is being sought for the same charge of disorderly conduct.

World.title: Man charged and fined $1,000 for molesting wild jaguar cub
World.content:
Man charged and fined $1,000 for molesting wild jaguar cub

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): The case of the wild jaguar cub handled in the Mountain Pine Ridge Forest Reserve has reached its legal conclusion. The Belize Forest Department has announced that Ruben Stoll was charged under the Wildlife Protection Act in connection with the incident, and has paid a fine of BZ$1,000, approximately US$500.

According to the department’s official statement issued from Belmopan on July 29, 2026, Stoll was charged under the Wildlife Protection Act, Chapter 220 of the Laws of Belize, in connection with the incident involving the handling and molestation of a wild jaguar cub within the reserve.

Following the incident, the department stated, Stoll voluntarily returned to Belize and surrendered himself to the authorities, indicating he had been outside the country. He was subsequently charged and paid the fine.

The department paired the announcement with an unambiguous message to the public. Wildlife, it stressed, is not to be treated as pets, photo props, or tourist attractions, and approaching, touching, handling, or otherwise disturbing wild animals can place both people and wildlife at serious risk.

The legal foundation is broad by design. The jaguar is one of Belize’s protected species, and the Wildlife Protection Act defines “to hunt” as “to kill, take, or molest by any method and includes attempting to kill, take, or molest by any method any species of wildlife,” prohibiting the hunting of protected wildlife, obviously immature wildlife, and any female accompanied by its young. A cub, in other words, is covered several times over.

“No one is above the laws of Belize,” the department declared, reminding Belizeans and visitors alike that while the country welcomes the world to enjoy its extraordinary biodiversity, everyone bears responsibility to respect its wildlife, protected areas, and laws.

The resolution will nonetheless leave some Belizeans weighing the arithmetic: a thousand dollars for the molestation of a protected jaguar cub, the national animal’s most vulnerable form, is a figure the public conversation may judge against the offence. The penalty applied is the penalty the law provides, and any change to it belongs to lawmakers.

The department’s closing guidance is the piece worth carrying forward, for every trail, reserve, and encounter: observe wildlife from a safe distance. Admire it. Photograph it. But never touch it, harass it, or interfere with it.

World.title: Wingz Police battle B-Town Savage Storm in Friday’s Big 6K Match
World.content:
Wingz Police battle B-Town Savage Storm in Friday’s Big 6K Match

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Belmopan, clear your Friday. July 31 brings the Big 6K Match to the FFB Stadium, and when the final whistle blows, the night is only getting started.

The football comes in doubles. The 6K Qualifier kicks things off at 7:30 p.m. with a north versus west clash, Progresso FC Amateur out of the north taking on Benque Power from the western border. Then the main event at 9:30 p.m.: Wingz Police, backed by Wingz Belmopan, against B-Town Savage Storm in the Big 6K Match, sanctioned under the Football Federation of Belize and presented by Play Chune Marketing.

And when the stadium empties, the city lights up. Three clubs, three afta parties, one Friday night. La Cabana runs with Cloud 9, Dalla, Movements and Absoh. MJ’s Dragon brings Eclipse, Fyah Statah and Freezy. Glow Lounge stacks DJ Sambo and DJ Smallz, Wakky, Cinimax and DJ Rhyno.

Whatever your vibe, there is a dance floor with your name on it, and the hardest decision of the night will not be made at the stadium.

Friday, July 31. FFB Stadium, Belmopan. Come for the ball, stay for everything after.

World.title: Minister of Economic Transformation and delegation meet Belizean students in Taiwan
World.content:
Minister of Economic Transformation and delegation meet Belizean students in Taiwan

By Zoila Palma: Today, Osmond Martinez, Minister of State in the Ministry of Economic Transformation, and his delegation met with Belizean students in Taiwan.

The students shared their experiences and perspectives on their studies, culture, and life in Taiwan.

Minister Martinez emphasized that studying in Taiwan contributes to Belize’s human capital development by exposing students to advanced training and real-world innovation in areas where the country needs deeper expertise, particularly information technology, international relations, public health, and border security.

Minister Martinez and his delegation are visiting Taiwan from July 27 to 31, 2026.

World.title: Institute for Social and Cultural Research discuss safeguarding living traditions of Deer Dance
World.content:
Institute for Social and Cultural Research discuss safeguarding living traditions of Deer Dance

By Zoila Palma: On July 24, 2026, the Institute for Social and Cultural Research (ISCR-NICH) and cultural advocates from the communities of Armenia, Maya Mopan, and Valley of Peace met to discuss the ongoing efforts to safeguard the living traditions of the Deer Dance.

Led by ISCR Director Rolando Cocom, the engagement provided an opportunity for community practitioners to share their knowledge, reaffirm the importance of honouring cultural traditions and community protocols, and identify meaningful pathways for continued collaboration in safeguarding this cherished heritage.

Looking ahead, ISCR will extend consultations to Deer Dance practitioners from communities in southern Belize. Through continued dialogue and mutual respect, we aim to strengthen partnerships with community practitioners, ensuring that safeguarding efforts remain community-led, respecting traditions, and sustainable for future generations.

ISCR extended appreciation to Francis Fonseca, Minister of Culture; Albert Vaughan, NICH President; and the Ministry of Indigenous Affairs for their continued commitment and encouragement in safeguarding and promoting the enduring traditions of our Belizean people.

World.title: New cohort of 23 Peace Corps volunteers begins service in Belize
World.content:
New cohort of 23 Peace Corps volunteers begins service in Belize

By Zoila Palma: A new cohort of 23 Peace Corps volunteers has officially begun their service in Belize following an oath ceremony led by U.S. Chargé d’Affaires Rhonda Slusher.

The ceremony was attended by Dr. Nadine Rogers, members of the Peace Corps community and government representatives, formally welcoming the volunteers into the Peace Corps’ more than six-decade partnership with Belize.

The volunteers will serve in the Youth Development and Primary Education sectors, supporting locally led initiatives aimed at strengthening youth development and education.

Their assignments will include work with the Youth Empowered by Sports (YES) project, as well as literacy programs and other classroom-based initiatives, while living and working alongside Belizean communities.

As the Peace Corps marks 65 years of global service, the new volunteers will continue a longstanding legacy of partnership, cultural exchange and community-driven development.

World.title: Protected Areas Conservation trust convenes conservation forum
World.content:
Protected Areas Conservation trust convenes conservation forum

By Zoila Palma: The Protected Areas Conservation Trust (PACT) recently convened conservation partners for its “Connect. Reflect. Advance.” forum—a collaborative event designed to strengthen partnerships, celebrate achievements, and chart the future of conservation investment under the Conservation Investment Strategy 2.0.

Hosted in Belize City on July 23 and in Dangriga Town on July 24, the two days of sessions brought together protected area co-managers to exchange experiences, address shared challenges, and maximize the impact of conservation initiatives across Belize.

The “Connect. Reflect. Advance.” forum represented PACT’s commitment to fostering collaboration, transparency, and continuous learning among its partners. By creating space for open dialogue and collective problem-solving, the forum enhanced the effectiveness of ongoing investments while reinforcing a shared commitment to protecting Belize’s rich natural heritage.

PACT says that as it continues rolling out its Conservation Investment Strategy 2.0, the insights and commitments generated during these sessions will help shape future funding streams and strengthen partnerships that deliver meaningful environmental, social, and economic benefits for Belize.

World.title: International News: Fauci invokes 5th amendment during heated Senate Hearing on COVID-19 response
World.content:
International News: Fauci invokes 5th amendment during heated Senate Hearing on COVID-19 response

By Zoila Palma: Today, Dr. Anthony Fauci invoked the Fifth Amendment and declined to answer questions from senators during a Republican-led Senate committee hearing examining his handling of the COVID-19 pandemic.

Fauci was subpoenaed by Sen. Rand Paul of Kentucky, who has spent years accusing the retired infectious disease expert of misleading Congress and the public—allegations Fauci has rejected, ABC reports.

During the hearing, Fauci repeatedly responded to questions by saying, “On the advice of counsel, I respectfully decline to answer based upon my rights under the Fifth Amendment.” The constitutional protection allows witnesses to decline to provide testimony that could potentially incriminate them and does not, by itself, amount to an admission of guilt.

Paul pressed Fauci on issues including federal funding for research in China, virus mutations and the origins of COVID-19, arguing that Fauci had helped fund dangerous research and later misled the public. Fauci, however, said he believed the hearing was intended to elicit statements that could support Paul’s repeated calls for his prosecution.

The hearing also highlighted the deep partisan divide over the pandemic and its origins.

The confrontation came as Fauci’s decision to remain silent limited direct exchanges with Paul but gave the senator greater opportunity to present his accusations without detailed responses from the witness.
