Dutch airline KLM booked a higher-than-expected profit in the first half of the year, despite the rise in fuel prices caused by ongoing conflicts in the Middle East.

The company reported revenue of €6.9 bn in the six months to June, an 8% increase compared to the same period last year.

The airline benefited from a decrease in flights from competitors like Qatar Airways and Emirates because of the unrest in the region.

“The measures we are implementing are having a positive impact on our results,” CEO Marjan Rintel said in a statement.

Those measures included passing on higher fuel prices to customers, particularly on long-haul flights.

Yesterday, the Air France-KLM airline group announced they had put in an offer for a stake in Portugal’s TAP airline. Lisbon said last year that it was seeking a major international airline to buy most of the 49.9 percent stake that it planned to sell.

German airline Lufthansa also submitted a bid.

World.title: Man who strangled partner jailed after new forensic method used
World.content:
A man has been convicted of attempting to kill his partner in the first case to use new techniques to detect signs of strangulation in domestic violence.

The 33-year-old man from Rozenburg grabbed the woman by the neck as an argument turned violent last November. Police were alerted by neighbours and pulled the man away from his victim, who later said she was “turning blue”.

She was examined by a medical specialist using a new procedure developed in Rotterdam to gather forensic evidence faster in suspected cases of strangulation.

The doctor said the attack could have been fatal if it was prolonged, a detail that allowed prosecutors to argue that the attack should be classed as attempted manslaughter.

The procedure was introduced last December to try to detect strangulation, which is seen as an early warning sign of femicide, in domestic abuse investigations before the victim’s injuries heal and the evidence disappears.

200 referrals

The medical agency FARR, based in Rotterdam, anticipated receiving 200 inquiries a year, but was called on 150 times in the first three months. In 92% of cases doctors concluded the injuries could have been caused by strangulation. Nine in 10 victims were female and 78% of inquiries were related to domestic violence.

“It’s a huge number,” the agency’s managing director Geranda Zeelenberg told NOS. “Previously we hardly ever saw these people. They were probably always there, but the research we’ve begun has increased awareness of these cases.”

The man from Rozenburg was sentenced to 360 days in prison for attempted manslaughter, including 169 days suspended, and a community service order of 150 hours, in line with the prosecution’s demands.

His lawyer told the court he had no recollection of the events on the night of the attack because he had been taking alcohol and amphetamines, but argued that he had attacked her to try to force her to have sex rather than attempting to kill her.

World.title: Middle East conflict adds to pressure to fill Dutch gas reserves
World.content:
The Netherlands is lagging behind its European partners in filling its gas reserves for the winter, just as a key supplier in the Middle East has announced further restrictions on supplies caused by the conflict between the US and Iran.

QatarEnergy extended “force majeure” restrictions on its LNG cargoes until the end of September, affecting a total of 24 cargoes to European customers.

The company signed a contract to supply up to 3.5 million tonnes of liquified gas to the Netherlands per annum, which came into force this year, but the invocation of force majeure has put this commitment in jeopardy.

The Netherlands’ gas reserves are currently at 36.6% capacity, well below the EU average of 56%.

Following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, which triggered a spike in prices, the EU set a target of reaching 90% capacity by November 1. Since then European nations have had to find alternatives to Russian gas.

The Netherlands achieved this level for the first three years, but in 2025 it peaked at just 74% and at the start of April this year the four Dutch storage facilities were at less than 5% capacity.

Energy minister Stientje van Veldhoven said last month she was “confident” that the gas reserves would be filled for the winter, but admitted that the government needed to be “vigilant”.

Demand for gas has also increased during the summer as more consumer and businesses install air conditioning, putting more pressure on energy.

The Dutch government also has agreements to buy gas from Norway and the United States, or could resort to the open market.

The wholesale price of gas on the TTF market, operated by Gasunie, has risen by 50% since mid-June as a result of ongoing attacks by Iran and the US on facilities in the Middle East and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz.

World.title: Sitting targets: thieves make off with 88 museum cafe chairs

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Thieves walked off with all of the chairs from the Bonnefanten Museum café in Maastricht in the early hours of Monday.

Café manager Freek Joosten told local news network L1 that camera footage showed the perpetrators making several trips carrying stacks of chairs at around 4am.

The designer seats are valued at more than €21,000.

The chairs were tied down with iron cables and the grounds are monitored by multiple cameras. The museum has reported the theft to the police.

The museum, which sits on Avenue Céramique in the Limburg capital, specialises in visual arts.

The terrace was recently renovated and the chairs were from designer Fermob Luxembourg. The thieves also took a waste container.

Visitors are still welcome in the café. Joosten has temporarily reallocated the chairs from his catering business to use on the terrace.

Police have asked anyone who saw anything unusual in the vicinity on the night of July 26 to 27, or who may have camera footage, to contact them.

World.title: Water authorities to discuss further drought restrictions
World.content:
Talks are being held in The Hague on Thursday on whether extra measures are needed to conserve drinking water and protect rivers and canals during the ongoing drought.

Water boards, providers of drinking water and the highways agency Rijkswaterstaat are among the agencies attending the discussions at the infrastructure ministry, AD.nl reported.

The Netherlands is currently at level two on a three-stage scale of water shortages, which authorises officials in the ministry to hold crisis talks. An actual crisis is level three.

A spokesman for infrastructure minister Vincent Karremans would not be drawn on the possible outcomes of the meeting, but water boards could agree to bring in further restrictions on river traffic or close sluices.

Key inland routes such as the Twentekanaal, which links three towns in the east of Overijssel, and Deventer’s harbour introduced restrictions this week after the IJssel river dropped to historic low levels.

“By limiting sluice openings we can retain as much fresh water a possible, but these measures have an impact on river traffic and the economy,” the spokesman explained.

Water regulators could introduce one-way traffic on sections of river where the navigable area has narrowed to prevent ships becoming stuck while overtaking, but that will slow down delivery times or force freight to be transported by road.

The flow in the Rhine is down to 650,000 litres per second at Lobith, the point where the river enters the Netherlands – one-third of the normal level for July. Before this year the slowest rate recorded was 782,000 litres per second in the drought year of 1976.

The height of the river is expected to drop to 6.35 metres by the weekend, which would be 15cm below the previous record low.

The Scheldestromen water board in Zeeland issued a ban on Thursday on drawing surface water from ditches, creeks and other waterways to prevent water levels dropping further. The authority warned that the restriction was likely to be in place for a lengthy period of time.

World.title: Extra supervision for KLM’s maintenance arm over safety concerns
World.content:
Dutch flag carrier KLM’s maintenance division has been put under s etricter supervision because of concerns about its workplace safety culture.

The environment and transport inspectorate (ILT) confirmed to the Volkskrant that the special measures had been put in place at KLM Engineering & Maintenance since May and would last for the rest of the year.

The company handles more than 3,000 aircraft and components a year on behalf of major airlines such as British Airways, Lufthansa and Emirates, as well as KLM and Transavia. It recorded a turnover of €2.4 billion last year, 18% of KLM’s total activity.

The ILT would give details of what issues had prompted the move, citing confidentiality, but stressed there were no implications for aircraft safety.

A spokesman told the Volkskrant that KLM’s security management was at the “minimal level of maturity and the supervision would focus on “compliance and administrative findings that can lead to operational security risks”.

World.title: Deventer closes harbour indefinitely due to low river levels
World.content:
Deventer is closing its harbour to ships from this weekend after the summer drought caused the water level in the river IJssel to drop to exceptionally low levels.

The municipal council said on its website that the sluice gates would close to prevent “damage to water barriers, problems for ships and risks for houseboats”.

The rules state that the sluice gates must be closed if the level of the river outside the harbour falls below 45cm above Normaal Amsterdams Peil (NAP), the baseline measure roughly equivalent to sea level.

That level is expected to be reached on Saturday. Ships will be allowed to enter the harbour until Thursday, but will have to leave by Friday evening.

The last time Deventer’s harbour was closed due to low water levels was in 2018, when it was able to reopen after two weeks.

The Twentekanaal, which runs between Almelo, Hengelo and Enschede, has been closed since last Saturday because the water level is too low. The regional liaison group Twente Board has written to infrastructure minister Vincent Karremans asking for financial support for affected businesses.

Koninklijke Binnenvaart Nederland (KBN), the collective body for inland waterway operators, said the closure would cost the local economy between €125,000 and €500,000 a day. The canal will reopen once the water level rises to 9.10 metres above NAP.

World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Support for Ukraine joining the European Union has fallen sharply in Poland, with opposition reaching a record high of 40%, a survey carried out by the Polish state research agency CBOS shows. The figures show that 50% of Poles still support Ukraine’s EU membership, but that is a significant decline from 74% in October 2023, when the question was last asked, and from a record 90% in March 2022, shortly after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The shift comes as public sentiment towards Ukrainians in general in Poland has deteriorated in recent years. The latest CBOS poll shows that, among those who support Ukraine’s EU accession, most favour a gradual process, with 41% of all respondents saying Ukraine should join the EU but “without undue haste”. “Only 9% of respondents currently support Ukraine’s earliest possible EU membership, which is the lowest figure in the history of these surveys,” CBOS reported. Meanwhile, opposition to Ukraine’s EU membership has increased by 23 percentage points since October 2023, reaching its highest level in the history of CBOS surveys. People with right-wing political beliefs are most likely to be opposed to Ukraine’s accession (53%), while the age group with the highest percentage of people opposed is those aged 18-24 (58%). The survey also found that a majority of Poles expect the war in Ukraine to end with territorial concessions from Kyiv – 55% of respondents said they believed Ukraine would lose some territory, a view that has remained dominant since December 2024. Compared with the previous survey, however, pessimism has eased. The proportion of respondents who expect Ukraine to lose part of its territory fell by 8 percentage points, while the number expecting Russia to take control of the entire country declined from 8% to 6%. On Western support for Ukraine, 39% of respondents said the military, financial and humanitarian assistance provided by countries in the West was sufficient. Meanwhile, 27% said aid was excessive, while 22% said it was insufficient. Russia has published purported archival documents relating to massacres of Poles by Ukrainians in WWII. Kyiv had warned that Russia was planning to release the files in order to stir tensions, while Polish media note that the material contains nothing new https://t.co/CI0cfAlDle — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 6, 2026 Ukrainians are Poland’s largest foreign national group, with almost 1.6 million living in the country, but recent polls have shown growing hostility towards them, fuelled in part by anti-Ukrainian rhetoric from far-right parties and a tougher stance towards Kyiv from some opposition politicians. In its annual survey of attitudes towards national and ethnic groups, CBOS found earlier this year that the proportion of Poles who said they disliked Ukrainians increased by five percentage points this year, the largest rise recorded among all groups surveyed, reaching 43%. Tensions between the two countries have also been heightened by disputes over historical issues and a series of recent incidents targeting Ukrainians in Poland. The number of reported hate crimes against Ukrainians in Poland is up 30% so far this year, police data show. The figures come following recent high-profile cases of verbal and physical attacks against Ukrainians, who are Poland's largest immigrant group https://t.co/pcTsJddDz7 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 17, 2026 The number of reported hate crimes against Ukrainians rose by 30% in the first half of 2026 compared with the same period a year earlier, according to newly reported police data. Last weekend, three men were filmed violently attacking a Ukrainian woman and her partner outside a shop in Wrocław, apparently because of her accent. Two of the assailants have since been detained by police, while their victims required treatment in hospital. In response, Prime Minister Donald Tusk called for Poles to “wage war on violence”, saying that the perpetrators of such acts “have become emboldened precisely because they now have political role models, political patrons, and political support”. A newly sworn-in judge of Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK) has said he will refuse to sit on the court until four other judges appointed by parliament earlier this year, but blocked by the president, are allowed to take their seats. It is the latest development in a months-long dispute between the opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki and the government, which considers the TK to be improperly staffed and therefore illegitimate. Although Nawrocki swore in Sławomir Patyra, who was appointed by the ruling majority in parliament in June, as a TK judge on Tuesday, he continues to refuse to swear in four other judges appointed by parliament earlier this year. Po złożeniu przysięgi Patyra ogłosił, że zamierza odmówić orzekania. To gest solidarności z czwórką sędziów, od których prezydent nie chce przyjąć przysięgi https://t.co/jdbKusQ3H9 — OKO.press (@oko_press) July 28, 2026 Shortly after his swearing-in ceremony at the presidential palace on Tuesday, Patyra arrived at the TK headquarters in Warsaw, where he was accompanied by four other judges appointed by parliament this year, including two whom Nawrocki has refused to swear in. There, he announced that his decision not to sit on the court was a matter of loyalty to the constitution and his belief in judicial ethos. “I cannot imagine taking an oath today to uphold the constitution, only to start breaking that constitution tomorrow,” he said. Patyra told journalists that he would “submit a declaration of refusal to adjudicate” due to his solidarity with judges who are “unlawfully deprived of the chance to participate in the work of the tribunal”. He added that, along with the other judges chosen this year, he is “fully mobilised to restore the Constitutional Tribunal to its proper, constitutional, systemic form”. Under Polish law, when a vacancy emerges among the 15 positions on the TK, the lower house of parliament, the Sejm, chooses who should fill it. However, to take office, the judge must swear an oath before the president. In April, after the Sejm had chosen six candidates to fill vacancies on the court, Nawrocki took the unprecedented step of inviting only two of them to be sworn in. He argued there were doubts over the legality of how all six had been chosen, but decided to accept two to ensure the TK had the necessary quorum to function. Those two have been able to take up their seats on the court, but the other four remain in limbo. Although they arranged their own private swearing-in ceremony without the presence of Nawrocki, TK’s chief justice Bogdan Święczkowski has refused to accept them. In May, the European Court of Human Rights ordered that the quartet be allowed to take up their positions. But the TK – where judges appointed under the former Law and Justice (PiS) government retain a majority – issued its own ruling endorsing Nawrocki’s right not to swear in the new judges. The European Court of Human Rights has ordered Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK) to accept four judges whom opposition-aligned President Nawrocki refused to swear in. The decision was welcomed by the government but rejected by the TK itself https://t.co/9NxInPdYk9 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 6, 2026 On 11 June, the Sejm then chose another judge, Patyra, to fill a newly opened vacancy on the court. In his case, the legal doubts Nawrocki had expressed regarding the previous appointments, which in some instances were made more than a year after the vacancies had arisen, did not seem to apply. Yet for weeks the president refused to confirm whether he would swear him in. That prompted Patyra to write to Nawrocki in early July and then again later in the month, asking the president to indicate a date on which he could take his oath. After repeated requests, Nawrocki finally decided last week to invite Patyra to the presidential palace. The president’s chief of staff, Zbigniew Bogucki, noted that “there were some doubts” but “the president dispelled them” and added that Patyra was chosen “in accordance with all procedures”. Nowo wybrany przez Sejm Rzeczypospolitej Polskiej uchwałą z dnia 11 czerwca 2026 r. sędzia Trybunału Konstytucyjnego Sławomir Patyra złożył wobec Prezydenta RP ślubowanie. pic.twitter.com/VLMRAIg1Yj — Kancelaria Prezydenta RP (@prezydentpl) July 28, 2026 The TK has been at the heart of the rule-of-law crisis that has developed in Poland over the last decade. In 2015, former PiS-aligned President Andrzej Duda refused to swear in three judges legally chosen by the Sejm. Shortly afterwards, PiS won parliamentary elections and nominated three replacements for those judges, who were sworn in by Duda. Those three judges and their successors have been deemed illegitimate in a succession of rulings by Polish and European courts. Due to their continued presence on the court, the current government, which replaced PiS in 2023, rejects the TK’s legitimacy and refuses to recognise its rulings. Under both Święczkowski, a former member of the PiS government, and his predecessor Julia Przyłębska, a close personal associate of PiS leader Jarosław Kaczyński, the TK has been widely seen as issuing rulings aligned with the political interests of PiS. World.title: Former Polish PM Morawiecki forms parliamentary caucus  rival to PiS, deepening opposition split
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Former Polish Prime Minister Mateusz Morawiecki says that 40 MPs and one senator aligned with him will form their own parliamentary group, deepening a split in the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) after a dispute over party direction and loyalty declarations. The move marks the most serious internal challenge in years to PiS, which ruled Poland from 2015 to 2023, and follows months of tensions between Morawiecki’s more moderate faction and party conservatives who have pushed the group in a hard-right direction. Once formally established, Morawiecki’s caucus would become the third-largest bloc in the Sejm, Poland’s lower house of parliament. Powstanie klub parlamentarny „Rozwój Plus”. Morawiecki zdecydował#PAPInformacjehttps://t.co/IftRdgpIPw — Polska Agencja Prasowa/Polish Press Agency (PAP) (@PAPinformacje) July 29, 2026 One of Morawiecki’s allies, Marcin Horała, told reporters that the creation of the caucus did not mean they were leaving PiS, but “simply setting up a parliamentary group so that we can get on with our work”. He noted, however, that PiS’s parliamentary group “has stopped treating us as its members”. Morawiecki, meanwhile, said that his group remained ready to cooperate with PiS as a “second lung” of the party’s broader political camp, but suggested that the group was moving in a different direction. He said that parts of PiS’s messaging were increasingly influenced by “dissidents and schemers” as well as hardline factions, including Sovereign Poland (Suwerenna Polska), a nationalist group that was previously a junior coalition partner of PiS and often clashed with Morawiecki when he was prime minister. Reacting to Morawiecki’s announcement, party chairman Jarosław Kaczyński said the former prime minister had carried out a planned split of the party despite his efforts to reach a deal. “Until the end I made efforts to reach an agreement, unfortunately Mateusz Morawiecki clearly had his own political plan in mind, carried out on the basis of a split in PiS,” Kaczyński wrote on X. The announcement follows a dispute that began after Morawiecki launched his Development Plus (Rozwój Plus) association in April. The former prime minister insisted the association was intended to complement PiS with a pro-development agenda rather than rival it. However, critics within PiS viewed it as an attempt by Morawiecki to build an alternative power base that could eventually evolve into a separate party ahead of the 2027 parliamentary election. Seeking to end the standoff, the party ordered PiS lawmakers to resign from all outside political associations by last Thursday, or face “consequences” including “the loss of membership in PiS”. On Friday, Kaczyński said that “around 30 MPs” had failed to comply and had therefore effectively resigned from the party, adding that Tuesday’s meeting of the party’s political committee would simply confirm this fact. Poland's right-wing opposition PiS party is set to split after a more moderate faction of over 30 MPs loyal to deputy leader @MorawieckiM refused to sign a loyalty pledge demanded by leader @OficjalnyJK, who says that means they have effectively resigned https://t.co/TuqYpGI5ak — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 24, 2026 On Tuesday, the party announced that instead, the committee had referred the cases of 44 members, who either failed to submit the required declarations or submitted them on the wrong form, to the party’s disciplinary officer for individual review, delaying a final decision. “From a formal and legal perspective, Mr Mateusz Morawiecki has not yet been removed from the list of members,” PiS spokesman Rafał Bochenek said on Tuesday. PiS disciplinary officer Karol Karski told the Polish Press Agency (PAP) he would examine each case individually. “I am open to speaking with each of them so they can present their positions,” Karski said. “At this point, I can initiate proceedings against the individual in question, refer the case to a peer disciplinary tribunal with a motion for punishment – this could include a temporary suspension or expulsion from PiS.” PiS has for the last two decades been the dominant force on the Polish right, including periods leading governments in 2005-2007 and 2015-2023. However, since losing power at elections in 2023, when the party won 35% of the vote, the party has seen its average support in polls fall to around 23-24%, the lowest level in 14 years. Support for PiS has fallen to its lowest in 14 years, as the party grapples with internal division, the rise of far-right challengers, living in President Nawrocki's shadow, and the unpopularity in Poland of PiS ally Donald Trump, writes @danieltilles1 https://t.co/QRScBpEQQG — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 2, 2026 Meanwhile, it has been challenged by the rise of the far right, where two parties, Confederation (Konfederacja) and Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP), now together poll at a similar combined level of support to PiS. In response, Kaczyński in March named a hardline figure, Przemysław Czarnek, as PiS’s candidate for prime minister in next year’s elections. Czarnek was seen as someone who could appeal to far-right voters, while also potentially working with the far right if a coalition was needed after the elections. However, there has been no rise in support for PiS since Czarnek was named, prompting growing concern from more moderate figures within the party, led by Morawiecki. The national-conservative opposition PiS party has named its candidate to be prime minister if it wins next year’s parliamentary elections. Przemysław Czarnek is a hardline conservative who played a prominent role in PiS's campaign against "LGBT ideology" https://t.co/sSJLON00hW — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 7, 2026 They argue that PiS has wrongly disowned many of the successes of its time in office before 2023, and they fear that its rightward shift damages its chances of winning over more centrist voters. Adam Szłapka, the spokesman of the current more liberal government, said Braun was “the ultimate playmaker in this whole game”, who had helped push far-right rhetoric into the political mainstream. “The worst thing about this whole situation is that Poland’s largest opposition party has, in effect, started to adopt Grzegorz Braun’s agenda from A to Z,” Szłapka told broadcaster TVN24. Ostatecznym rozgrywającym w całej tej rozgrywce nie jest ani prezes Jarosław Kaczyński, ani Mateusz Morawiecki, tylko Grzegorz Braun – ocenił w #JedenNaJeden w TVN24 rzecznik rządu Adam Szłapka. W rozmowie z @AgataAdamek komentował sytuację w PiS. World.title: Polish court finds regulation allowing foreign same-sex marriage registration unconstitutional
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK) has ruled that a new regulation allowing the registration of foreign same-sex marriage certificates in Poland was partly unconstitutional, saying it went beyond technical administrative changes and conflicted with the constitution’s definition of marriage. The regulation, introduced by the digital affairs ministry after rulings by the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) and Poland’s Supreme Administrative Court (NSA), was due to take effect on 23 August. The government, which considers the court to be improperly constituted, says it will not implement the ruling. The government has issued a regulation allowing foreign same-sex marriages to be entered in the civil registry The decision comes in response to an EU court order and marks a major change in a country that does not allow same-sex unions under domestic law https://t.co/2an5mGtnHl — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 22, 2026 Polish law does not allow same-sex couples to marry or enter into civil unions, and a bill that would have granted such limited rights to unmarried couples was recently vetoed by the opposition-backed president. Until this year, same-sex couples who married abroad were also unable to register their marriage certificates in Poland. After the CJEU ruled that Poland must recognise such marriages, the digital affairs ministry changed civil status forms. Instead of separate fields for “man” and “woman”, the new templates use “man/woman”, allowing registry offices to record both opposite-sex and same-sex marriages. Lawmakers from the national-conservative opposition Law and Justice (PiS) party, however, challenged the regulation, arguing that the digital affairs minister had exceeded his powers because the changes were not merely technical but affected the legal definition of marriage. The tribunal, which is widely seen as being under PiS’s influence, agreed. The tribunal said the new forms allowed relationships that do not match the constitution’s definition of marriage as a union between a man and a woman to be recorded as marriages. It said regulations can only implement existing laws and cannot change matters reserved for the constitution or parliament. The tribunal also said that registering a foreign marriage certificate cannot produce legal effects that conflict with the basic principles of Polish law. It added that changing the constitutional definition of marriage would require amendments to the constitution and related laws. Some legal experts argue that, while the constitution states that a “marriage, being a union of a man and a woman… shall be placed under the protection and care of the Republic of Poland,” that phrasing does not rule out other legally recognised unions receiving state protection. Poland has begun recognising foreign same-sex marriages. But the legal consequences for such couples remain unclear, especially as Polish law does not allow any form of same-sex union We asked five experts for their view on what this will mean in practice https://t.co/h2KHmW8sMI — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 19, 2026 Shortly after the ruling, government members said they would not comply with the tribunal’s decision and that the regulation would enter into force as planned. “The illegal Constitutional Tribunal is once again attempting to obstruct a state that is enforcing the law in force and the rulings of European courts,” digital affairs minister Krzysztof Gawkowski said. “The transcription of foreign same-sex marriage certificates is and will remain legal,” he said, adding that 184 same-sex couples had so far had their foreign marriage certificates transcribed. Katarzyna Kotula, the government official responsible for equality issues, said the TK ruling on the issue of transcriptions “has no legal force whatsoever”. Nielegalny Trybunał Konstytucyjny po raz kolejny próbuje zatrzymać państwo, które wykonuje obowiązujące prawo i wyroki europejskich sądów. Transkrypcja zagranicznych aktów małżeństw jednopłciowych jest i będzie legalna. Rozporządzenie, które przyjęliśmy porządkuje dokumenty i… — Krzysztof Gawkowski (@KGawkowski) July 28, 2026 The TK has been at the heart of the rule-of-law crisis that has developed in Poland over the last decade. In 2015, former PiS-aligned President Andrzej Duda refused to swear in three judges legally chosen by the Sejm. Shortly afterwards, PiS won parliamentary elections and nominated three replacements for those judges, who were sworn in by Duda. Those three judges and their successors have been deemed illegitimate in a succession of rulings by Polish and European courts. Due to their continued presence on the court, the current government, which replaced PiS in 2023, rejects the TK’s legitimacy and refuses to recognise its rulings. Fifteen months since the change of government, Poland's rule-of-law crisis continues – indeed, many Poles think the situation has got worse.@J_Jaraczewski explains the roots of the crisis, what its impact has been, and how it might be resolved https://t.co/7KOCURV3dU — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 17, 2025 Under both Święczkowski, a former member of the PiS government, and his predecessor Julia Przyłębska, a close personal associate of PiS leader Jarosław Kaczyński, the TK has been widely seen as issuing rulings aligned with the political interests of PiS. For a long time, the government refused to appoint new judges to the Constitutional Tribunal as the terms of the previous judges expired, with some vacancies remaining unfilled for over a year. In recent months, the government has resumed appointing new judges, but President Karol Nawrocki, an ally of PiS, is refusing to administer the oath of office to some of them. World.title: Residents oppose move to add Polish village to list of protected monuments
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. A decision to designate a village as a protected monument has sparked fierce opposition from residents, who have vowed to “fight until the end” against measures they say will limit their ability to renovate and build on their properties. The village in question, Ostaszów in southwestern Poland’s Lower Silesia province, was established in 1936 by Nazi Germany as an agricultural settlement of around 42 farms. At the time, the region still belonged to Germany. The Lower Silesian Provincial Conservator of Monuments argues Ostaszów has “unique, homogeneous historical architecture” requiring state protection, but local officials say that the way the decision was made, despite opposition from residents, shows “the voice of local communities has no significance”. After World War Two, most of Lower Silesia, including the village, became part of Poland. The village’s architecture has remained largely unchanged, with its residential buildings connected to barns, forming unique cohesive farmstead units. Around 250 people live there. Earlier this year, the residents were told proceedings had begun to add the village to the register of protected monuments, reports the Gazeta Wyborcza daily. The provincial conservator said on Friday it had reached a decision. “The unique, above-standard historical, scientific and artistic value of Ostaszów as a monument cannot be questioned,” it wrote in a statement. It noted that a study by a team working under the culture ministry had found that the village was the only preserved settlement of its kind in Lower Silesia. Residents and local officials said they planned to appeal against the decision, arguing it would create additional bureaucracy and interfere with property owners’ ability to decide on building and renovation work. “We have a years-long legal battle ahead of us, but we won’t give up. We will fight until the end. We believe that decisions about the 42 homes in Ostaszów should be made by their residents, not by harmful officials,” residents wrote in a statement quoted by the Polish Press Agency (PAP). “In a cardboard state, the voice of local communities has no significance – only orders and bans count. Our future is to be decided by a heartless official from [the Lower Silesian capital of] Wrocław who does not even have time to meet with the victims of his decisions,” said the village head, Sylwia Mazur. Wieś Ostaszów wpisana do rejestru zabytków. Mieszkańcy będą się odwoływaćhttps://t.co/ZxmH2lbHnb pic.twitter.com/cPdL73PXIH — Dzieje.pl (@dziejepl) July 26, 2026 The conservator noted, however, that until the appeals process is concluded, construction works cannot proceed. It added that it planned to cooperate with locals to “develop principles of renovation and investment procedures in accordance with the regulations on the protection of monuments”. It also urged residents not to spread “scandalous narratives” about the decision leading to an “open-air museum, the impossibility of renovation, and the blocking of investments”. It said other villages in Lower Silesia were subject to similar protections without hindering their development. Gazeta Wyborcza cited some residents saying that the launch of proceedings in January had already forced them to pause work on their properties. Others complained that the decision will increase renovation costs due to strict conservation requirements. The Opole Provincial Conservator of Monuments said that, as of 2021, some 86 villages across Poland had been added to the register of monuments because of their historic layouts. World.title: Poland enters race to host EU-backed AI gigafactory
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Poland has joined the European Union’s plan to build artificial intelligence (AI) gigafactories with a view to hosting one of the bloc’s new computing centres. Deputy digital affairs minister Dariusz Standerski said Poland had completed a key legal step by joining the joint procurement process. The move enables Poland to bid for one of seven AI gigafactory projects planned under the EU programme, potentially attracting investment of more than 10 billion zloty (€2.3 billion) while giving businesses, researchers and public institutions access to advanced AI computing capacity. “On behalf of the Republic of Poland, I have signed the Joint Procurement Agreement, which means that Poland joins the AI gigafactory initiative,” Standerski told daily Rzeczpospolita. Under the proposed model, AI gigafactories will be designed, financed, built and operated by private consortia selected through a European tender organised by the European High Performance Computing Joint Undertaking (EuroHPC JU). In the first procurement round, EuroHPC JU plans to select seven projects comprising four medium-scale facilities and three large-scale sites. Poland is bidding for a medium-scale project, which would initially provide computing capacity equivalent to at least 25,000 AI accelerators before expanding to at least 75,000. The EU and its member states will support the projects by committing to purchase computing services during the initial years of operation, providing demand certainty for investors. “Poland and the EU will each buy 17% of the power, and the remaining two thirds will be made commercially available by a private consortium; Poland will commit to purchasing its own pool for five years,” Standerski said. Standerski also told the newspaper that companies’ interest in the project is “enormous”. “This means that, from the very first day the gigafactory is operational, part of its computing capacity will already have been sold,” he added. Poland’s government will spend 1.9 billion zloty (€437 million) equipping the majority of schools with so-called AI labs before the start of the next school year. The money will fund laptops, AI software and interactive displays, among other equipment https://t.co/outNQIGCv0 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 19, 2026 Standerski said the government would not designate a site for the facility, with the final location to be determined by the winning consortium through the European procurement process. He said the government had previously identified 10 locations across Poland capable of hosting. Last week, the deputy minister also said Poland was preparing to sign an agreement with the Czech government, under which cooperation would involve mutual purchases of computing capacity between the two countries. He also said Lithuania had committed to a one-sided arrangement to buy computing power from a Polish AI gigafactory. Częstochowa will become the first city in Poland to use the Polish Large Language Model to support the use of AI in providing municipal services. It will help write letters, analyse inquiries from residents, and summarise long documents https://t.co/SLrmVg9VBz — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 11, 2025 Earlier this month, Poland’s government approved a resolution enabling the country to participate in the European AI Gigafactory programme, committing more than 400 million zloty towards what the government says would be the largest computing centre in the country’s history. The government also pledged to purchase AI services worth €100 million between 2028 and 2033, with a matching contribution from the European Union. According to the government’s timetable, the European procurement process is expected to begin later this year. World.title: Poland asks US to extradite former minister Ziobro over criminal charges
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland has formally asked the United States to detain and extradite former justice minister Zbigniew Ziobro, who is wanted on multiple criminal charges. Ziobro, a senior figure in the former national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government, is accused of offences including leading an organised criminal group and abuse of office. Having previously fled Poland to Hungary, where Viktor Orbán’s government, an ally of PiS, granted him asylum, Ziobro arrived in the United States in May following a change of government in Budapest. Wniosek o ekstradycję podejrzanego Zbigniewa Ziobro: ⬇️https://t.co/YC7T3RrIEc — Prokuratura (@PK_GOV_PL) July 27, 2026 Ziobro served as justice minister in the PiS government from 2015 to 2023. Last year, prosecutors announced that they wanted to charge him with 26 crimes, including leading a criminal group and approving the unlawful purchase of Pegasus spyware. In October, parliament approved the lifting of Ziobro’s immunity from prosecution. By then, however, he had already travelled to Hungary, and in December he was granted political asylum by the Hungarian government. In February this year, Warsaw’s district court approved a request from prosecutors to place Ziobro in pretrial detention. That decision was needed in order for the authorities to issue domestic and European arrest warrants against the suspect. However, Ziobro’s lawyers appealed against the decision. While that appeal was waiting to be heard, Orbán lost power in Hungary and, as his successor Péter Magyar was being sworn in, Ziobro left the country and flew to the United States. In July, a Warsaw court rejected Ziobro’s appeal, opening the way for Poland to seek the politician’s extradition from the US. Ziobro has no valid travel documents after Poland cancelled his passports and Budapest revoked his refugee status. The extradition request covers 19 of the 26 offences listed in the indictment, the prosecutors said. The documents submitted include the final order for Ziobro’s detention, the indictment, a wanted notice and evidence supporting the case. The request will now be sent through diplomatic channels to the US Department of Justice, where it will be assessed to determine whether it meets the formal requirements of the Polish-US extradition treaty, prosecutor Anna Adamiak said. If the request satisfies those requirements, it will be referred to a US federal court, where a judge will decide on the legal admissibility of Ziobro’s extradition to Poland. A court has upheld a request by prosecutors to bring former justice minister Zbigniew Ziobro, who is wanted on 26 criminal charges, into detention. The decision paves the way for Poland to request Ziobro's extradition from the US, where he fled in May https://t.co/vIPRjvgQnA — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 2, 2026 Asked how long the extradition process could take, Adamiak said previous cases suggested proceedings could last anywhere from a few months to several years, depending on their nature and complexity. Adamiak noted, however, that the extradition proceedings would not determine Ziobro’s guilt. “Its role is merely to assess whether the surrender of that person in extradition proceedings is legally permissible in light of treaty regulations and domestic law,” she told reporters, quoted by online news service Wirtualna Polska. “However, the decision on surrender is, of course, a decision made by the state, so other circumstances may also play a role,” she added. PiS, Poland’s largest opposition party, enjoys close ties with US President Donald Trump’s administration. Poland's conservative opposition enthusiastically welcomed Trump's return to the White House, but it is becoming increasingly difficult for them to maintain a tough anti-Russian line while also showing allegiance to the US president, writes @danieltilles1 https://t.co/4PW6H9nMEF — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 7, 2025 Asked at a news conference about the likelihood of Ziobro’s extradition and when it might take place, Poland’s Prime Minister Donald Tusk said the question should be directed at “the other Donald”, reported the Polish Press Agency (PAP). “We will, in accordance with the law, seek all available means to ensure that these politicians, against whom such serious charges have been brought, appear before a Polish court sooner or later,” he added. “We are waiting for positive signals from Washington. Will they come? I don’t know.” Ziobro has long denied all accusations, saying the case against him is an act of “political revenge” by Tusk’s government. Commenting on the extradition request on the conservative television channel Republika, Ziobro said he was pleased that the case would be heard “in the United States, on American soil, and before an American court”. He claimed that the proceedings would show that the Polish government “regularly breaks the law, ignores procedures, rejects democratic principles, has taken control of the prosecutor’s office unlawfully, and is trying to destroy the opposition”. World.title: Revolut Opens Private Market Funds to Czech Investors
World.content:
Revolut is expanding its investment services in the Czech Republic, giving retail customers access to funds focused on private equity, private credit and infrastructure.

The new products will become available in the Revolut app from July 31. The fintech has signed distribution agreements with four major asset managers — Apollo, Ares, Hamilton Lane and Partners Group — which collectively manage more than $2.8 trillion in assets.

The move gives Czech retail investors access to parts of the private markets that have traditionally been aimed largely at institutional investors.



Private market investments have often required substantial minimum commitments, frequently above €100,000, or around CZK 2.5 million. Revolut’s new offering is designed to lower that barrier and allow customers to add private assets to portfolios that may already include stocks, bonds and exchange-traded funds.

Investments will be available directly through the Revolut app.

The funds will be offered through the European Long-Term Investment Fund framework, known as ELTIF 2.0.

How ELTIF 2.0 works

The structure is intended to provide investors with greater flexibility than traditional private equity funds, where capital can remain committed for several years and withdrawals may not be possible during that period.

The products offered through Revolut use an “evergreen” structure. This allows investors to put money into funds with existing portfolios rather than waiting for a traditional investment cycle to begin.

ELTIF 2.0 also provides scheduled liquidity windows during which investors can request the redemption of their holdings, subject to the conditions of the individual fund.

That does not mean the investments are as liquid as publicly traded shares. Private market assets remain difficult to sell quickly, and investors should expect to hold their money for the long term.

Revolut already offers Czech customers access to a range of traditional investments, including US and European stocks, ETFs, bonds and commodities. The addition of private market funds expands the investment options available through the same app.

World.title: From Old Town to Main Station: Tourist Charged €150 for Short Taxi Ride
World.content:
A tourist has reported an alleged taxi scam in Prague, claiming that a journey from Old Town Square to Prague Main Railway Station ended with an unexpectedly high fare and a disputed payment.

The incident reportedly took place on July 25 at around 16:15. According to the complaint, the driver charged CZK 980 for the ride, an amount the passenger said was far higher than the expected price for such a short distance.

The tourist claims that the driver refused to accept payment by card and requested cash instead.



“I paid him 100 Euros for the fare. He just took the note, swapped it and lied to me saying what I gave was 100 in Czech currency, and demanded me to pay the remaining 50 euro taxi fare,” the tourist said in his complaint.

“So I paid the initial 100 euro that was swapped, plus the 50 euro taxi fare.”

According to the passenger, the total amount paid for the ride was therefore €150 (over 3,600 CZK). He said he was rushing to catch a train to Bratislava and was unable to resolve the dispute at the scene.

The tourist also claimed that no receipt was provided after the payment. According to his account, the driver said an invoice would be sent by email, but it was never received.

The case has been reported to the relevant authorities, while details of the incident have also been shared online to raise awareness among other visitors.

Travellers are also encouraged to use established taxi applications or services recommended by hotels, restaurants, and official tourist information centres. Paying by card and confirming the expected price in advance can help avoid disputes.

World.title: Babiš Warns Czechia Could Become Net EU Payer by 2029 as Contributions Surge
World.content:
The Czech prime minister also said Brussels is likely to permit a larger budget deficit as Prague seeks funding for hospitals, highways, and other domestic investment.

Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babiš has expressed alarm over the country’s rapidly increasing payments to the European Union, warning that the Czech Republic could become a net contributor to the bloc as early as 2029.

Following talks with Finance Minister Alena Schillerová, Babiš said Czech payments into the EU budget had risen by 22 billion crowns (€911 million) this year alone.

“I was shocked by how much we are paying into the European Union,” he said, as cited by Echo24. “If in one year we are told that we will pay 22 billion more, that is a lot.”



Officials currently expect the Czech Republic to become a net contributor to the EU budget for the first time in its history in either 2029 or 2030.

Babiš was also asked about next year’s state budget deficit. When asked whether it would exceed this year’s planned shortfall of 310 billion crowns (€12.8 billion), he replied, “Don’t test me. I don’t know what the deficit will be.”

Schillerová said a reliable estimate would only be possible after the Finance Ministry publishes its updated economic forecast next month.

The government has informed the European Commission that it expects next year’s structural deficit to reach as much as 2.9 percent of GDP, compared with 2.4 percent this year. According to Schillerová, Brussels has provisionally accepted the higher ceiling.

“We have to invest in hospitals, highways and bypasses,” he said, justifying the overspend but maintaining that the deficit should remain significantly below 400 billion crowns (€16.6 billion).

Planned spending includes psychiatric hospitals, surgical facilities, oncology centers, highways and city bypasses. The government also intends to maintain defense expenditure at 2 percent of GDP.

World.title: Hundreds of Czech Castles and Chateaus to Offer Free Entry on Two Special Days
World.content:
Visitors will be able to explore more than 100 state-managed castles, chateaus, monasteries, and other historic landmarks across Czechia free of charge on August 30 and September 27.

The initiative follows a spring pilot program that granted free admission to selected state museums and galleries. According to the Ministry, strong public interest in that campaign encouraged officials to extend the concept to historic monuments managed by the National Heritage Institute (NPÚ).

The free admission will apply to the standard sightseeing route at each participating site, along with selected additional visitor circuits where available.



Tours will operate under normal conditions, meaning visitor numbers will remain limited and capacity restrictions will continue to apply.

The National Heritage Institute is expected to publish a complete list of participating sites, opening hours, reservation requirements, and visitor information on its website in the coming days.

The latest initiative builds on an earlier trial introduced this spring.

Between April and June, visitors were granted free entry on selected Sundays to five of the country’s largest state museums: the National Museum in Prague, the Moravian Museum in Brno, the Silesian Museum in Opava, the National Technical Museum in Prague, and the Technical Museum in Brno.

According to the Ministry of Culture, attendance at those museums nearly doubled during the pilot period, with the Silesian Museum recording the largest increase in visitor numbers. Selected state galleries also participated in the program earlier this year while officials assessed the financial impact of waiving admission fees.

The ministry has said one of its long-term objectives is to help restore visitor numbers at cultural institutions to levels seen before the COVID-19 pandemic.

World.title: On this Day, in 1419: the First Defenestration of Prague
World.content:
Six hundred years ago, an angry crowd stormed Prague’s New Town Hall and threw several royal councillors from its windows.

The attack, known as the First Defenestration of Prague, took place on July 30, 1419, and is widely regarded as the event that ignited the Hussite Wars—a conflict that transformed medieval Bohemia and left a lasting mark on Czech history.

Yet the violence that unfolded that summer day had been years in the making.

Its roots lay in the teachings of Jan Hus, a Czech theologian, university lecturer, and religious reformer who became one of the most influential figures of the late Middle Ages. Hus openly criticized corruption within the Catholic Church, particularly the sale of indulgences and the growing power of the church hierarchy. Rather than viewing the Church as an institution led by the pope and bishops, he argued that the true Church was the community of faithful believers.

Summoned before the Council of Constance in 1415 to defend his beliefs, Hus was arrested despite receiving a promise of safe conduct. After refusing to renounce his teachings, he was convicted of heresy and burned at the stake.



His execution outraged many across Bohemia. While members of the nobility saw it as the unjust killing of one of the kingdom’s own, Hus’s followers spread his ideas far beyond Prague through a network of priests and former university students. The capital, home to Charles University and the Bethlehem Chapel where Hus had preached, became the center of a rapidly growing reform movement.

Bohemia’s political circumstances also allowed the movement to flourish. Neither King Wenceslas IV nor the Archbishop of Prague took decisive action to suppress it, allowing religious tensions to deepen over the following years.

By the summer of 1419, the situation had reached a breaking point.

On July 30, radical Hussite preacher Jan Želivský led a religious procession through Prague after delivering an impassioned sermon. Although the march may have appeared spontaneous, historians believe the confrontation had been carefully prepared. Some participants reportedly arrived carrying concealed weapons, expecting violence.

The procession made its way to Prague’s New Town Hall, demanding the release of Hussite supporters imprisoned there. When the councillors refused, the crowd forced its way inside.

The assault was led by Jan Žižka, a military commander who would later become one of medieval Europe’s greatest generals. Several councillors were seized and thrown from the building’s windows. Although the fall itself was not fatal for everyone, those who survived were beaten to death by the waiting crowd below.

For medieval society, the act carried a powerful symbolic meaning. Publicly casting powerful officials from an elevated position represented the dramatic downfall of those who had abused their authority.

The defenestration did not, by itself, begin the Hussite Wars, but it made peaceful reconciliation increasingly unlikely. Just weeks later, King Wenceslas IV died, leaving the throne to his brother Sigismund, whom many Bohemians blamed for failing to protect Jan Hus at Constance. Relations between the Hussites and the crown rapidly collapsed, and in 1420 the first crusade against Bohemia was launched.

The wars that followed lasted more than a decade. They devastated much of the kingdom but also produced extraordinary military victories under Jan Žižka and established the Hussites as one of medieval Europe’s most formidable fighting forces.

The First Defenestration of Prague remains one of the defining moments in Czech history—a single act of violence that turned years of religious unrest into a revolution whose legacy can still be seen throughout the country today.

World.title: Czech Company Enters Fortune Global 500 for the First Time
World.content:
A Czech company has entered the Fortune Global 500 ranking for the first time in history.

Energy and industrial group EP Group (EPG), controlled by Czech businessman Daniel Křetínský, placed 179th in the latest edition of the prestigious list of the world’s largest companies by revenue.

The ranking, published annually by the U.S. business magazine Fortune, evaluates companies based on their total sales. EP Group reported revenues of $75.387 billion, equivalent to around CZK 1.6 trillion.

To put the figure into perspective, the Czech state budget expects total revenues of CZK 2.118 trillion this year.



EP Group’s portfolio includes stakes in major companies across Europe, including British postal operator Royal Mail, Slovak energy producer Slovenské elektrárne, German retail chain Metro and French energy giant TotalEnergies.

With its debut in the ranking, EP Group has also placed Prague among the headquarters of the world’s largest corporations. The Czech capital is now one of 242 cities worldwide where at least one Fortune Global 500 company is based.

Only 14 other countries in the Fortune Global 500 ranking have a single representative, including Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Poland, Austria and Thailand.

EP Group is also among a very small number of newcomers. Only 13 companies worldwide entered the top 500 this year for the first time, while another 11 returned after previously dropping out of the ranking.

The company’s rise reflects the growing importance of energy, infrastructure and industrial businesses in the global economy.

US companies dominate the ranking

American companies continue to lead the Fortune Global 500, with 141 firms making the list — the highest number since the global financial crisis in 2008.

World.title: Inside IAM Prague: How a Travelling Exhibition Laid the Foundation for One of the City’s Top-Rated Museums
World.content:
Just off Old Town Square, past the cafes and the crowds waiting for the Astronomical Clock, sits a museum that started almost by accident.

Today, IAM Prague has welcomed well over 1 million visitors from around the world and has held TripAdvisor’s Travelers’ Choice Award for five straight years.

From Shopping Malls to Old Town Square

The museum wasn’t originally supposed to be a… museum. Co-founder Jakub Bechyně and his partner Patrik Proško had been running a traveling illusion exhibit that moved between shopping malls, renting space for a month at a time before packing up and relocating. It worked, but it wasn’t permanent.

Then, in 2017, the owner of a building on Old Town Square approached them with an idea: turn part of it into a museum. The catch was the timeline. They wanted it open in two months.

Rather than build something from scratch, the team pulled from what they already had on the shelf, opening with one floor and sixteen exhibits in 2018. The collection has grown to more than 60 pieces since.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Illusion Art Museum Prague (@iamprague)

The museum moved to its current location in 2022 after the original building was sold. The new space, ideally located between Old Town Square and Wenceslas Square, needed walls removed and floors rebuilt to accommodate the art. The costs were substantial, but it turned out to be a good problem to have as the location dramatically increased the exhibition’s visibility to passersby on one of Prague’s busiest tourist thoroughfares.

Choosing Technique Over Fame

IAM Prague doesn’t chase famous names. It chases techniques. The team looks for a specific kind of illusion craft, one with real artistic quality, a genuine optical trick, and ideally a story behind it worth telling.

That approach led them to reverse-perspective specialist Patrick Hughes, and to artists whose work they discovered secondhand and eventually acquired outright rather than simply displaying on loan. In several cases, the museum ended up owning the pieces after renting them for years and deciding they belonged permanently in the collection.

About 80 percent of the exhibition has changed since opening. Early pieces built quickly to fill the space have gradually been replaced as the museum brought in stronger, more polished work from local and international artists.

The exhibition’s evolution continues, with four new pieces from international artists like Jonty Hurwitz and Andrej Boleslavsky, ranging from traditional mirror anamorphoses to digital art, recently unveiled in June.

History Hidden in Plain Sight

Much of what makes IAM Prague distinct is how it uses illusion as a delivery method for history. A glass-art piece featuring four endangered animals turns out to double as an environmental message.

A defenestration scene lets visitors reenact one of Prague’s most repeated historical events, tied to the 1618 uprising that helped trigger the Thirty Years’ War. Even the museum’s own opening date, a century after Czechoslovak independence in 1918, was picked on purpose.

One exhibit nods to Karel Čapek, the Czech writer who coined the word “robot,” a term that entered global use even though it comes from a Slavic word for forced labor.

Another traces the story of Tomáš Baťa, the industrialist who pioneered mass shoe manufacturing and built factories across multiple continents, including a Pakistani city that still carries his name today.

AI’s Impact on Art & Travel

Though much has been made on artificial intelligence’s impact on the world of art, the team’s biggest current concern isn’t AI-generated art replacing the exhibition’s themselves. It’s the shift in how travelers plan their trips.

For years, visibility depended on traditional guidebooks, online travel agencies, physical advertising, and street presence. Increasingly, travelers are relying on AI chat tools to create itineraries, shifting the importance of more “traditional” visibility mechanisms, which is forcing venues like Illusion Art Museum Prague to adapt.

Despite the changing landscape, the plan going forward leans further into digital and kinetic art, including new motion-based installations recently brought in from Berlin by artists like Florian Goerlitz.

For a museum that started as a temporary mall exhibit, the goal has stayed consistent since day one: make people stop, look twice, and leave with a story they didn’t expect to learn.

World.title: Nearly One in Five Prague Farmers’ Market Vendors Fail Veterinary Inspections
World.content:
Nearly one in five vendors inspected at Prague’s farmers’ markets during the first half of 2026 were found to have breached food safety or labeling regulations, according to the State Veterinary Administration (SVS).

Between January and June, veterinary inspectors checked 53 vendors across Prague and identified violations in 10 cases, representing almost 19 percent of all inspections.

Nationwide, inspectors carried out 165 inspections, with irregularities detected in 27 cases, or roughly 16 percent.

Officials said the most common problems in Prague involved improper storage temperatures for food of animal origin, incorrect or incomplete product labeling, and inadequate protection of food from contamination during sale.

Inspectors also highlighted several cases they considered particularly serious. In one instance, a vendor was found producing meat products without the legally required authorization while packaging them with the identification mark of a production facility that no longer exists. Authorities said such practices can mislead consumers about where products originate.



The SVS warned that food safety risks increase during the summer months, especially at outdoor markets where high temperatures make it more difficult to maintain proper cooling conditions.

Across the Czech Republic, labeling violations were the most frequently recorded offense this year, accounting for 26 cases. Problems related to hygiene and production practices—including incorrect storage temperatures and insufficient protection against contamination—followed with 22 cases.

Inspectors also documented 18 violations involving improper handling of food products and 12 cases where the origin of goods was unclear or could not be verified.

The SVS noted that a single inspection may uncover multiple breaches. While inspectors found violations in 27 inspections nationwide, the total number of individual offenses reached 82.

Inspection results remained largely unchanged compared with the same period last year. During the first six months of 2025, inspectors also carried out 165 inspections, finding violations in 16 percent of them. The main difference was that hygiene-related shortcomings topped the list last year, while labeling issues have become the most common problem in 2026.

Looking at the full year, the SVS carried out 380 market inspections across the Czech Republic in 2025, compared with 372 inspections in 2024. The proportion of inspections uncovering violations rose slightly from 17 percent to 18 percent.

World.title: Historic heat, drought: Paks NPP may be switched off, Hungary’s power supply could be pushed into crisis, industry may grind to a halt
World.content:
Because of the Danube’s exceptionally low water level, the Paks nuclear power plant could be taken completely offline on Thursday or Friday, Péter Magyar, the prime minister, said at a press conference in Budapest on Thursday. The government is also reviewing its rotational crisis plan, which could mean shutting down parts of Hungarian industry if there is not enough electricity. Romania has already shut down its nuclear plant, and it remains uncertain whether it will be able to buy power.

Too little water in the Danube — Paks must be shut down

Magyar said that, for now, the energy supply remains secure for both households and businesses, and the same is true of drinking water for 99.9 per cent of the country. He added, however, that because the Danube has fallen to a record low, reactor blocks must be taken offline continuously, in what amounts to a planned shutdown. “It appears, at present, that the complete shutdown of the Paks plant could happen as early as today, but perhaps more likely tomorrow,” he said. That would be an unprecedented measure since the start of operation in 1982.

That would mean a loss of 2,000 megawatts of capacity, a substantial share of domestic consumption, though one that could be covered by imports. Import capacity stands at 3,600 to 3,800 megawatts.

The prime minister also said that the Danube Steam Power Plant had broken down in the meantime, causing a further 400 megawatts to be lost. There is a chance it could be restarted later in the day, but if an old component does not work, production could be interrupted for weeks. In that case, further steps would certainly be required.

Earlier, it was decided to cut the output of the second block of the Paks Nuclear Power Plant by half, according to MTI.

Romania has already shut down its nuclear plant

Although Paks is still operating for the time being, Romania has already shut down its sole nuclear plant at Cernavodă. The Danube’s flow at the border point of Baziaş has fallen to 1,500 cubic metres per second. By contrast, the long-term average in July is 4,700 cubic metres per second, and in August 3,900 cubic metres per second.

There is not enough water in the River Danube, so hotel boats must remain halted. Photo: depositphotos.com

Experts say that by 3 August Romania could face an energy deficit of 500 megawatts during evening peak hours, rising to more than 1,000 megawatts between 4 and 9 August, which will also have to be covered by imports. It is doubtful, however, where it will be able to buy power, as every neighbouring country is grappling with similar problems.

Hungarian industry could also be halted within days

Péter Magyar said that after his joint press conference with Bavarian premier Markus Söder, he would review the rotational crisis plan with Bálint Ruff, the minister heading the Prime Minister’s Office, and István Kapitány, the minister for economy and energy. This is a possible industrial shutdown plan that would be triggered if the Hungarian grid cannot meet demand or if enough electricity cannot be fed in. They will also visit Százhalombatta, the MOL refinery, and Paks.

Péter Magyar and Markus Söder. Photo: MTI

Water handed out at stations in heat alert

The MÁV group is preparing for the third-level heat alert by handing out water and setting up misting gates, while drinking fountains are operating at several rail and bus stations so that anyone can refill their bottle or flask, the company said on Thursday, according to MTI. Dávid Vitézy, the minister for transport and investment, also asked Magyar Közút and motorway operators on Facebook to be ready to distribute drinking water to motorists if traffic backs up.

Free bottled water is also being handed out at Budapest-Kelenföld and Budapest-Népliget coach stations, as well as at the bus stations in county seats with heavier traffic, between 10 AM and 5 PM, MTI reported.

If you missed: Hungarian agriculture, as we know it, is nearing the end – but researchers already have a plan

Third-level heat alert in force since midnight

The third-level heat alert came into force from 00:00 on Thursday and will remain in place until 24:00 on Tuesday, as ordered by the national chief medical officer. According to HungaroMet’s warning, average temperatures in Győr-Moson-Sopron, Komárom-Esztergom, Veszprém, Fejér, Bács-Kiskun and Csongrád-Csanád counties will exceed 27C on Thursday, while elsewhere — apart from Nógrád, Heves, Borsod-Abaúj-Zemplén and Szabolcs-Szatmár-Bereg counties — the average temperature is expected to be above 25C. Average temperatures above 27C are also expected in Vas, Tolna and Pest counties on Thursday, HungaroMet said.

Sustained high temperatures over several days reduce physical and mental performance, increase fatigue and the risk of accidents, and worsen the course of cardiovascular, respiratory and kidney diseases. The most serious consequence of heat stress is heatstroke, a life-threatening condition; if someone feels unwell, they should be taken immediately to a cool place, cooling should begin at once, and an ambulance should be called if necessary, MTI reported.

World.title: Hungarians in America: National Museum’s new exhibition explores their fate – video
World.content:
The Hungarian National Museum’s new temporary exhibition dubbed The American Dream explores the fate of Hungarians who emigrated to the United States, also paying tribute to the 250th anniversary of the US’s independence.

New, exciting National Museum exhibition to be open for months

The exhibition explores how hundreds of thousands of Hungarians sought happiness on the other side of the ocean in the past 250 years, the state secretary for public collections and heritage protection told the opening of the exhibition on Wednesday. Zsolt Sári added that the exhibition’s three galleries tell the story of the dream of freedom, prosperity and success.

“There are few anniversaries in world history that are both a national celebration and a universal historical milestone,” the museum’s director general said. The 250th anniversary of the United States’ independence is such an occasion, Gábor Zsigmond added.

American dream never belonged to a single nation

Caroline Savage, charge d’affaires ad interim at the US Embassy in Budapest, said that this exhibition was a fitting way to commemorate the 250th anniversary of the US and to celebrate the remarkable shared history of Hungary and the US.

She added that the American Dream had never belonged exclusively to a single nation; it had been shaped by millions of people who brought their talents, determination and heritage with them to the US. She added that countless businesses founded by Hungarians have advanced science and medicine, created works of art and helped shape every aspect of American society.

If you missed – Video: Century-old Ford Model T takes centre stage at Hungarian National Museum

Visitors will be able to see memorabilia that belonged to 19th century statesman Lajos Kossuth, a cigarette case that belonged to renowned actress Katalin Karády, a rifle used by zoologist and museum founder János Xantus during the American Civil War, and Hungarian former professional basketball player Kornél Dávid’s jersey that he wore while playing for the Chicago Bulls. In addition, the exhibition running through 1 November explores the lives of ordinary Hungarians who found a new home in the US.

PM Magyar and Transport Minister Vitézy open Budapest Transportation Museum

World.title: Hungarian agriculture, as we know it, is nearing the end – but researchers already have a plan
World.content:
We have already seen AI-generated visualisations of what Szeged might look like with a dried-up Tisza and a desertified landscape. The picture is not quite so bleak, but the fact remains that our lakes and rivers are facing record-low water levels, while vast swathes of the country are turning to desert. Hungary’s 19th-century water-management system, and the agricultural model built upon it, now require urgent and thorough overhaul. Hungarian agriculture as it is known today may disappear — but what comes next? A new study by Hungarian researchers offers some clues.

Wheat, maize and sunflower in the Great Plain desert?

There are many reasons for the drying of the Great Plain, above all ourselves: the descendants of those who, in the mid-19th century, decided that every last patch of land must be brought under cultivation. There was even an idea to drain Lake Balaton and farm that too. To this was added the torment of Hungary’s reduced status after Trianon, when successive governments sought to secure stable foreign currency earnings through the export of arable crops, chiefly cereals. The situation did not change under communism either: the fertile Hungarian soil was thus required to produce wheat, maize and sunflower rather than fruit and vegetables. That era, however, may now be drawing to a close.

Summer harvest in Hungary: lowering yields. Photo: Facebook/István Nagy

We too have reported in numerous articles on the desertification of the Great Plain. The essence of these reports can perhaps be summed up as follows: without intervention, vast areas may become unfit for human habitation, and certainly for agriculture. The reasons are climate change, drought, low rainfall, and the lack of irrigation and water retention. The artificial water system of the Carpathian Basin — and within it Hungary — has, since the days of Széchenyi and Vasvári, been geared towards draining away as quickly as possible the precipitation arriving here as runoff or melting snow, and sending it beyond the country’s borders.

New 10,000 km² European sand desert forming in Hungary: Over 620,000 lives at risk

Shocking difference. Photo: Facebook/Időkép

The soil-water table has paid the price. During extreme droughts, groundwater has sunk so low that it now lies beneath the root zone of plants. In other words, there may be arable land available, but if accessible water disappears from the soil, crops cannot survive.

What could replace it?

According to researchers, the answer lies in water retention and a wholesale rethinking of land use. In areas where cultivation is kept alive only by EU subsidies, arable farming should be abandoned and priority given instead to retaining water. One new study suggests that, in practice, this would mean flooding 1.5 million hectares of arable land — almost a third of the country’s total cultivated area.

The effect would be twofold: groundwater levels would rise, the root zone would once again reach the water table, and maize yields could increase by 20 to 28 per cent, while today’s droughts effectively wipe out everything in their path.

On poorer land, too, it may make more sense to switch back to the once-familiar practice of pasture-based farming, or to higher-value vegetable and fruit production. Naturally, this would need to be done using the most advanced drip-irrigation technology and other water-saving methods. That, too, may be in farmers’ interests: the study argues that on many marginal sites, conventional arable farming can now be sustained only with subsidies, while loss-making farming makes little sense either for farmers or for the Hungarian economy.

Bombs emerge from the Danube: record-low water levels expose suspected WWII explosives near Budapest

Change is coming

The key to change is therefore not irrigation alone. Water must be retained, farming adapted to the landscape, and intensive production concentrated where the conditions genuinely allow it.

The study, published in the journal Geography and Sustainability, was carried out by 15 Hungarian researchers and was supplemented in the article by Zsolt Pinke, a researcher at the Institute of Soil Sciences of the HUN-REN Centre for Agricultural Research, as reported by Válasz Online.

Perhaps the study’s most important message is this: the question is not whether Hungarian agriculture will change, but whether we adapt deliberately to a drying Great Plain — or wait until drought forces the issue.
