World.title: Third-degree heat alert from today in Hungary – what it means
World.content:
A third-degree heat alert has come into force, ordered by the chief medical officer from 12 midnight on Thursday until midnight on Tuesday. According to HungaroMet’s Thursday morning bulletin, the average temperature in a further three counties may exceed 27C.

Third-degree heat alert in Hungary again

HungaroMet’s warning shows that on Thursday the average temperature will climb above 27C in Győr-Moson-Sopron, Komárom-Esztergom, Veszprém, Fejér, Bács-Kiskun and Csongrád-Csanád counties, while elsewhere — except in Nógrád, Heves, Borsod-Abaúj-Zemplén and Szabolcs-Szatmár-Bereg — it is expected to top 25C, the Hungarian news agency wrote.

On Thursday, the average temperature will also exceed 27C in Vas, Tolna and Pest counties, HungaroMet said.

On Friday, the average is forecast to rise above 29C in Komárom-Esztergom, Fejér and Bács-Kiskun counties. In Nógrád, Borsod-Abaúj-Zemplén and Szabolcs-Szatmár-Bereg counties it will be above 25C, and elsewhere above 27C.

Hot weather remains

Prolonged high temperatures reduce both physical and mental performance, increase fatigue and the risk of accidents, and have an adverse effect on the course of cardiovascular, respiratory and kidney diseases. World.title: Toxic metal levels found in wells near Semcorp plant in Hungary, Greenpeace calls for investigation
World.content:
Tests carried out on private wells near the Chinese-owned Semcorp battery separator film plant in Debrecen have found manganese concentrations far above Hungary’s drinking water limit, with two wells exceeding the legal threshold by more than ten times. Environmental organisations say the findings warrant further investigation, although they stress that the source of the contamination has not yet been identified.

The results were announced by Greenpeace Hungary and the Mothers for the Environment of Mikepércs Association, which commissioned laboratory tests following growing public concern after an industrial accident at the Semcorp factory earlier this year.

Tests followed February industrial accident

According to 444.hu, the investigation was launched after a February incident at the Semcorp plant raised fears that pollutants could have reached local groundwater. While the latest laboratory analyses did not detect the substances previously linked to the factory accident, all three tested private wells contained manganese concentrations significantly above the drinking water limit.

According to the organisations, the measured concentrations were 790, 520 and 240 micrograms per litre, compared with Hungary’s drinking water limit of 50 micrograms per litre. The sampled wells are used by local residents for everyday purposes, including drinking, cooking, watering livestock and irrigating gardens.

Cause of high manganese levels remains unknown

Despite the elevated readings, Greenpeace and the local environmental group emphasised that the current data do not prove the Semcorp plant is responsible.

They noted that the Debrecen area’s geological conditions mean the elevated manganese could also have a natural geological origin. However, they said the results justify additional hydrogeological and environmental investigations to determine the source of the contamination.

The organisations plan to submit the laboratory findings to the relevant authorities and formally request an official investigation. They are also calling for broader testing of substances associated with battery manufacturing technologies.

If you missed it: Hungary orders complete shutdown of Chinese battery supplier’s Debrecen factory

Semcorp has faced growing scrutiny

The Chinese battery materials manufacturer has come under increasing pressure in recent months. Following the February industrial incident, environmental groups reported finding chemicals associated with the factory’s production processes in nearby wastewater samples, prompting an official investigation.

In late June, environmental authorities suspended operations at the Debrecen facility after groundwater samples reportedly revealed pollution exceeding regulatory limits. Official data later showed aluminium concentrations in groundwater more than 13,000 times above the applicable limit.

Soon afterwards, Debrecen Mayor László Papp publicly described the pollution as “simply unacceptable” and urged authorities to consider revoking the company’s environmental permit if necessary. On 1 July, he went further, calling on Semcorp to leave the city altogether.

The factory was subsequently ordered to halt all operations with immediate effect after fire safety inspectors identified serious violations that endangered people and property. Authorities also imposed a HUF 3 million fire safety fine, while police launched an environmental damage investigation.

Semcorp said at the time that it accepted the authorities’ decisions and had begun an internal investigation under senior management supervision.

World.title: Swimming banned at popular free Balaton beach after water quality concerns
World.content:
Authorities have imposed a temporary swimming ban at Helikon Beach in Keszthely after routine water quality testing found the latest sample did not meet the required standards.

The announcement was made on Wednesday by the Municipality of Keszthely, following a decision by the Public Health Department of the Zala County Government Office. Officials said the temporary restriction was introduced to protect public health after the most recent water sample produced an “unsatisfactory result” during regular monitoring.

Other Keszthely beaches remain safe

The municipality stressed that the issue is limited to Helikon Beach. The city’s other two beaches, Keszthely City Beach and Libás Beach, continue to have excellent water quality, and swimming there remains completely safe.

New water quality tests will be carried out at Helikon Beach in the coming days. The beach will reopen as soon as health authorities confirm that the water once again complies with safety standards.

One of Lake Balaton’s newest free beaches

The temporary closure comes just a few months after Helikon Beach became one of the most notable free-access beaches on Lake Balaton.

Since 1 May, visitors have been able to use the municipally owned beach free of charge after the town removed the fences that had previously enclosed the paid beach. The symbolic dismantling of the barriers was carried out jointly by the mayor and local volunteers.

The current restriction is temporary, and local authorities have thanked visitors for their patience and understanding while waiting for the follow-up laboratory results.

World.title: Hungarian fake Jesus arrested in Italy after fleeing prison sentence for fraud
World.content:
A 73-year-old Hungarian man known in the media as the “Zala county fake Jesus” has been arrested in Italy after fleeing Hungary to avoid serving a prison sentence for defrauding his followers of HUF millions.

The man was detained by Italian police in Macerata on 7 July, a spokesperson for the Zala County Police Headquarters confirmed. Hungarian and Italian authorities have since begun extradition proceedings, although no date has yet been set for fake Jesus’ return to Hungary. His status on the Hungarian police’s wanted persons database has also been updated to “captured”.

Fake Jesus sentenced to four and a half years in prison

The man was the subject of a nationwide arrest warrant after failing to report to prison to begin serving a four-and-a-half-year sentence. According to the Zalaegerszeg Regional Court, he could not be located at his registered address, prompting the court to issue a warrant for his arrest.

He had originally been sentenced in October 2024 to six years’ imprisonment for 23 counts of fraud and one count of disorderly conduct. The court also ordered him to pay a HUF 300,000 fine and nearly HUF 19 million, plus interest, in compensation to his victims. On appeal, the sentence was reduced to four years and six months in November 2025, taking into account his advanced age and previous clean criminal record.

Followers allegedly manipulated for decades

According to the courts, the man claiming to be Jesus’ reincarnation spent decades presenting himself as a spiritual healer, energy therapist and saviour of souls. He organised group sessions and private consultations in several Hungarian cities, including Zalaegerszeg, Nagykanizsa, Pécs, Budapest and Böhönye.

During these gatherings, he reportedly preached about unconditional love, God, the Saviour, modesty, self-sacrifice and rejecting material wealth, while claiming he had little understanding of financial matters.

Investigators found that he portrayed himself as the reincarnation of Jesus, gradually gaining the trust of people seeking healing or spiritual guidance. Prosecutors said he created emotional dependence among his followers and increasingly influenced their personal relationships, career choices and financial decisions.

Millions collected for charitable causes apparently funded luxury lifestyle

The court found that the man persuaded followers to donate money for what he described as charitable or noble causes, including buying homes, supporting people in need and funding children’s camps. Instead, prosecutors said the money was spent financing his own luxurious lifestyle.

The victims were defrauded of nearly HUF 20 million (EUR 55,200) in total. Some followers reportedly continued to believe in his spiritual mission throughout the investigation, while others questioned his activities but felt unable to break free from his influence. According to the court, he warned followers that anyone who “betrayed” him would become seriously ill.

Throughout the legal proceedings, the man denied criminal wrongdoing. While acknowledging that he was not Jesus, he maintained that he nevertheless possessed exceptional spiritual knowledge.

World.title: Hungarian parliamentary committee backs lifting Tisza MP’s immunity over drink-driving case
World.content:
Hungary’s parliamentary Immunity Committee has recommended lifting the parliamentary immunity of Tisza Party MP Lőrinc Varga in connection with a drink-driving offence committed in 2024, before he became a member of parliament.

Committee chair Edit Sasi-Nagy, also a Tisza Party MP, told the Hungarian News Agency (MTI) after Wednesday’s meeting that the proposal will be submitted to Parliament for a vote next Monday.

According to Sasi-Nagy, the offence took place in 2024, when Varga was neither an MP nor a parliamentary candidate. However, because the court proceedings were still ongoing when he was elected to Parliament, the case was suspended, and the court requested that his parliamentary immunity be lifted so the trial could continue.

Committee unanimously supports lifting immunity

Sasi-Nagy explained that the committee follows a long-established practice: in public prosecution cases, it generally recommends suspending parliamentary immunity, while in private prosecution cases, it recommends maintaining it.

On that basis, the committee unanimously voted to recommend lifting Varga’s immunity. Varga, one of the youngest MPs in the Tisza Party parliamentary group, publicly addressed the incident in May.

In a social media post, he acknowledged responsibility, writing that during a routine police check following a gathering with friends, alcohol had been detected in his system the following morning.

“I made a mistake, and I fully accept responsibility,” he said at the time.

Magyar, Toroczkai and Takács retain immunity in defamation cases

The committee also considered several private prosecution cases involving other MPs. It unanimously recommended maintaining the parliamentary immunity of Prime Minister Péter Magyar in a defamation case initiated by a politician.

Similarly, the committee proposed maintaining the immunity of László Toroczkai, leader of the Mi Hazánk (Our Homeland) party, in four separate court proceedings relating to the same alleged act involving defamation and insult.

The committee also unanimously recommended preserving the immunity of Fidesz MP Péter Takács, who is likewise facing private defamation and insult proceedings.

Committee: immunity protects political work, not criminal offences

Summing up the decisions, Sasi-Nagy said the private prosecution cases illustrate the original purpose of parliamentary immunity: ensuring that elected representatives can carry out their political duties without being hindered by private legal disputes.

By contrast, she noted that public prosecution cases—such as Varga’s alleged drink-driving offence—are generally treated differently, which is why the committee recommended allowing the criminal proceedings to continue.

World.title: Colliers: Romania land market slows in H1, developers position for 2027-2028
World.content:
Romania's land market remained active in the first half of 2026 despite a slowdown in completed transactions, as developers continued acquiring sites for projects expected to reach the market in 2027-2028, according to a new report by real estate consultancy Colliers. Retail remained the strongest-performing segment, while residential land continued to attract investor interest despite a period of market adjustment.

Colliers said numerous land transactions are currently under negotiation or at the pre-contract stage, but relatively few large deals were finalized in the first six months of the year amid uncertainty over energy costs, construction budgets, and the domestic political environment.

“The land market is going through a period of repositioning; it is by no means at a standstill. We are seeing a significant number of discussions, negotiations, and transactions in progress, even though fewer large deals were completed in the first half of the year," said Sînziana Oprea, director of Land Agency at Colliers Romania.

She added that retail remains the most active segment, while residential land continues to attract interest, including from new market entrants, although buyers are negotiating more cautiously and putting greater pressure on pricing, payment terms, and permitting certainty.

According to the report, demand for retail land remains robust across Romania, supported by the continued expansion of discount, food, and DIY retailers, particularly in smaller cities. Residential land also continues to attract interest, including from international investors, with some major developers increasingly looking beyond Bucharest to regional cities.

The industrial land segment, however, remains subdued, as many investors already have sufficient land reserves and are waiting for better opportunities before making new acquisitions. Colliers noted growing interest instead in specialist projects such as student housing, medical facilities, and educational developments.

The consultancy also said infrastructure continues to shape investment decisions, with the Bucharest A0 ring road generating stronger investor interest than planned subway extensions.

At the same time, the number of land plots offered for sale has increased, partly because institutional and international investors are considering exits amid political uncertainty.

“Supply is more substantial than in the past, and this is changing the balance of negotiations. […] Buyers are responding very cautiously: they are more selective, negotiate more carefully, and are in a stronger position than during the years when the market was dominated by sellers," Oprea said.

Colliers expects selective price increases of 5-10% for prime plots with strong development potential and advanced permitting, while sites with weaker planning documentation or limited access could come under downward price pressure.

Looking ahead, the consultancy said the current pace of acquisitions suggests developers are preparing for the next real estate cycle rather than responding to immediate market conditions.

“For developers, land acquired today is not a bet on the current market, but a way of positioning themselves for the market of 2027-2028. […] Those making decisions during this period are already looking towards the next growth cycle,” Sînziana Oprea said.

World.title: Developer Urban Spaces seeks EUR 1.3 mln for Bucharest build-to-rent project via Growceanu
World.content:
Romanian residential developer Urban Spaces announced the launch of its first public fundraising campaign, seeking EUR 1.3 million for the build-to-rent component of its Urban Spaces Aviației project in Bucharest. The campaign is being conducted through Growceanu, a regulated Romanian investment platform for private companies.

The funding round, open until September 30, represents 20% of the capital of the Urban Spaces BTR company and is open to both individual and corporate investors.

Urban Spaces BTR is part of the mixed-use Urban Spaces Aviației development, the company's largest project to date, with an estimated value of EUR 150 million. The overall project will comprise more than 400 apartments, alongside office, retail, and leisure spaces.

The build-to-rent component includes 32 apartments and 13 underground parking spaces, which are planned to be professionally managed and rented on short-, medium- and long-term leases. Thanks to flexible layouts, the apartments can be configured as up to 40 accommodation units, the company said.

Around 70% of the invested capital is expected to be returned after the development phase, with the remaining investment generating income through the operation of the rental units.

“For the first time, we are opening up the opportunity for investors to join us in developing an Urban Spaces project through a regulated investment platform," said Gavril Zaharia, CEO and co-founder of Urban Spaces.

The campaign also marks Growceanu's first real estate offering, expanding the platform beyond its traditional focus on technology companies.

World.title: Romanian major bank BRD posts 2.5% increase in net profit in H1 2026
World.content:
BRD (BVB: BRD), one of the major banks present in Romania, reported a net profit of RON 784 million in the first half of the year, up 2.5%, according to the report submitted to the Bucharest Stock Exchange.

In H1 2026, BRD Group’s net banking income reached RON 2,206 million, up +1.8% year-on-year. Net interest income, which accounts for 70% of net banking income, totaled RON 1,548 million in H1 2026, up +1.4% year-on-year.

Net fee and commission income amounted to RON 452 million, compared with RON 453 million in H1 2025, remaining broadly stable compared with the previous year. Increased customer activity and the solid contribution of custody, brokerage, asset management and off-balance-sheet commitment activities were offset by the decrease in fee income from services, amid the process of cleaning inactive accounts.

Other banking income reached RON 206 million, up +9% year-on-year, mainly reflecting higher income related to associated entities, as well as the recognition of an exceptional (“one-off”) income.

In the context of persistent double-digit inflation and the doubling of the turnover tax, operating expenses decreased by 0.5% year-on-year in H1 2026, supported by cost discipline and the absence of contributions to the Deposit Guarantee Fund and the Resolution Fund (FGDB and FR) in 2026. Personnel expenses decreased by 8.3% year-on-year, reflecting the optimization of the Group’s workforce activity and operating model.

Excluding the turnover tax and the cumulative contributions to guarantee funds related to 2025, the other categories of operating expenses increased by +3.1% year-on-year, mainly as a result of higher IT&C expenses, generated by the depreciation of previous investments and the continuation of infrastructure and digitalization projects.

The turnover tax for the January-June 2026 period doubled compared with H1 2025, reaching RON 139 million (equivalent to 4% of gross revenues), compared with RON 66 million in the same period of the previous year.

In this context, BRD Group’s gross operating profit increased by +4.2% year-on-year, to RON 1,112 million in H1 2026.

The cost/income ratio improved to 49.6%, compared with 50.7% in H1 2025. Excluding the impact of the turnover tax and other contributions related to 2025, the cost/income ratio would have stood at 43.3% in H1 2026, compared with 45.4% in H1 2025, representing an improvement of 214 basis points.

BRD's non-performing loan ratio at the bank level reached 2.7% at the end of June 2026, below the banking system average of 2.9% recorded at the end of May 2026, while the coverage ratio for non-performing loans remained at a comfortable level of 65.6%. Net cost of risk recorded a limited increase compared with the same period of the previous year, with a net allocation of provisions of RON 147 million, compared with RON 142 million in H1 2025, amid the combined effect of portfolio developments and the revision of macroeconomic outlooks.

BRD Group recorded a net profit of RON 784 million in H1 2026, up 2.5% compared with the level of RON 764 million recorded in H1 2025. Excluding the impact of the turnover tax, return on equity (ROE) stood at 17%, compared with 17.3% one year earlier.

BRD’s capital adequacy ratio, at the individual level, stood at 22% at the end of June 2026, stable compared with the end of June 2025 (excluding the impact of temporary regulatory treatments, “quick fix”).

Net outstanding loans, including leasing financing, reached RON 58.3 billion, up +11.6% year-on-year (of which financial leasing receivables increased by +1.6% year-on-year). Growth was recorded both in the corporate segment and in retail, despite persistent macroeconomic difficulties. Corporate lending was the main driver of portfolio expansion (+16.5% year-on-year), supported by strong commercial activity in the large corporate segment. Retail loans also made a solid contribution, with net loan balances increasing by +8.0%, supported by resilient demand for housing loans.

In the first half of 2026, BRD continued to expand its sustainable financing activity, with cumulative production of EUR 2.63 billion since 2021, of which EUR 304 million was granted in H1 2026. At the same time, the bank assumed important roles in structuring sustainable financing, both independently and together with Societe Generale.

The total deposit base reached RON 73.7 billion, up +4.1% year-on-year, amid higher inflows from individual customers. Retail deposits, a stable and diversified source of financing, increased by +7.4% year-on-year, due to attracting a higher volume from individual customers. Corporate deposits recorded a decrease of -1.1% year-on-year, mainly reflecting balance sheet adjustments to liquidity conditions, market conditions, and the fluctuating financing needs of large companies.

World.title: KFC opens Drive Thru restaurant near Romania’s Bran after EUR 1 mln investment
World.content:
Sphera Franchise Group, the operator of the KFC brand in Romania, opened the chain's first Drive Thru restaurant in the Bran area following an investment of approximately EUR 1 million. Located in Bran Plaza in Tohanu Nou, Brașov County, the new outlet is Sphera's sixth KFC opening this year.

The restaurant covers around 350 square metres and offers indoor and outdoor seating, as well as Drive Thru, takeaway, Click & Collect and dine-in services. It is equipped with self-order kiosks and digital menu boards.

With the new opening, KFC now operates four restaurants in Brașov County and 113 permanent locations in Romania.

The new restaurant has created 30 jobs, ranging from kitchen and cashier positions to restaurant management roles.

Sphera Franchise Group is Romania's largest food service group, operating the KFC, Pizza Hut, and Taco Bell brands in Romania, as well as KFC in Moldova and parts of Italy. The Bucharest Stock Exchange-listed company operates more than 180 restaurants across Romania, Moldova, and Italy and employs around 5,000 people.

World.title: Romanian healthcare sector strike enters third day, PM condemns “disinformation”
World.content:
The strike in the Romanian healthcare sector entered its third day on Thursday, July 30, and union representatives warned that street protests will follow if the government does not offer them additional guarantees that the planned Wage Law will not cut any income in the system. Government representatives, on the other hand, said that the protest was politically manipulated and assured that no income will decrease, as per the text of the law.

Staff at two hospitals in Bucharest, the “Bagdasar-Arseni” Emergency Clinical Hospital and the “Floreasca” Emergency Clinical Hospital, argued for Digi24 that the reduction of bonuses will affect employees’ monthly incomes.

The head of the ICU Department at the “Floreasca” Hospital, Radu Țincu, explained that the difference between salary and actual income received is essential for staff working in particularly difficult conditions. According to him, part of the income in the ICU and Emergency Department comes from the bonus for difficult working conditions. If that bonus is reduced, healthcare workers’ income will decrease even if the actual salary does not decrease.

Currently, only emergencies are being handled in medical units, while patients scheduled for consultations, investigations, or non-urgent interventions are forced to wait until normal activity resumes.

Meanwhile, interim prime minister Ilie Bolojan stated during an interview on Wednesday, July 29, that the healthcare strike is based on “disinformation and lies.” He accused Alexandru Rogobete, the former Social Democrat (PSD) health minister, of “behaving irresponsibly” during the strike while doing nothing to prevent it while in office.

“One of the lies is related to the fact that incomes, if the Wage Law were adopted, would decrease not only in healthcare but also in other fields. There is an explicit provision in the law stating that if there is someone - and there are approximately 20-30% of those in the budgetary sector - who has a higher level of pay than they should have, their salaries will not decrease,” Bolojan said. Instead, he argued that the Wage Law would gradually equalize diverging income levels over time.

The interim PM, who also leads the center-right National Liberal Party (PNL), said that former coalition partners in the Social Democratic Party have created expectations regarding salaries in the public sector that cannot be met due to Romania’s financial constraints.

“We can increase the wage fund in Romania only as much as the Romanian economy can afford. Otherwise, we return to where we started,” the official said, referring to the public deficit issue, which ballooned in 2024 during the former PSD-led government of Marcel Ciolacu.

In reply, the former health minister claimed to be the author of true reforms in the Romanian public healthcare system. "Reducing the incomes of healthcare workers does not constitute reform," Alexandru Rogobete said.

World.title: Romania’s men’s sabre team wins bronze medal at 2026 Senior World Fencing Championships
World.content:
Romania’s men’s sabre team won bronze at the World Championships in Hong Kong after beating Hungary 45 to 39. Before that, Romania lost against South Korea in the semifinals (44-45).

Comprising Vlad Covaliu, Radu Nițu, Răzvan Ursachi and George Dragomir, Romania’s sabre team defeated Italy in the quarter-finals, with a score of 45-36. Previously, Romania’s team had defeated Great Britain (45-17) and Venezuela (45-30).

The Romanian sabre fencers lost by a decisive touch in the semifinal against South Korea, after being led 35-26 at one point. In the second-to-last bout, however, fencer Vlad Covaliu won 12-5, recovering points for Romania.

In the final bout, Radu Nițu entered at 38-40. The score was tied at 44, but Oh Sanguk scored the final touch.

From the stands, Mihai Covaliu, Olympic champion and former coach of the Romanian team that won the world title, constantly encouraged the young sabre fencers, according to the Romanian Fencing Federation.

The Hong Kong World Championships 2026 brought together over 1400 athletes from 113 nations, all competing for the top spots. Romania already had a bronze medal, through Radu Nițu in men’s sabre.

World.title: Beko upgrades Romania logistics hub with EUR 1.3 mln investment
World.content:
Beko Romania invested approximately EUR 1.3 million to modernize its spare parts logistics hub in Căteasca, Argeș County, doubling its storage capacity and expanding its role within the company's regional after-sales operations. The facility serves 22 markets in Central and Eastern Europe and also ships spare parts to destinations including the United States, China, Morocco, Israel, and South Africa.

The investment included the expansion of the hub's logistics infrastructure, the implementation of a digital warehouse management system E-WMS, the installation of an automated conveyor system, new picking equipment, and upgrades to its Wi-Fi and security infrastructure.

According to the company, the Căteasca hub manages more than 35,000 stock-keeping units, or SKUs, and over 550,000 spare parts. It also supplies Beko's central warehouse in Italy, which serves Western European markets.

The upgraded facility has enabled the introduction of direct-to-consumer (B2C) deliveries and reduced delivery times to 3-4 days for Eastern European markets, from 7-10 days previously. Delivery times for service teams in Romania have been shortened to around 24 hours.

Beko said more than 90% of deliveries are now completed within seven days, while over 70% arrive within two days. Spare parts availability has increased by more than 15%, exceeding 90%, according to the company.

World.title: Western Romania: Art Encounters Foundation eyes further international collaborations with revamped HQ opening
World.content:
The new Art Encounters Foundation center, set to open in September with the exhibition Picasso en visite, will allow the Timișoara-based institution to expand its international collaborations while continuing to support the new generation of artists and curators.

The center, dedicated to contemporary art, education and public engagement, is housed in the building previously known as Casa ISHO.

It will be the first dedicated contemporary art venue in Timișoara built to international museum standards for climate control, security and the conservation of artworks, Art Encounters said. These facilities make it possible to host exhibitions in partnership with leading international museums and collections, opening a new stage in the foundation's exhibition program.

The exhibition Picasso en visite is organized in a partnership with the Musée Picasso in Antibes.

Alongside the exhibition galleries, the center includes an art library and bookshop designed as spaces for research and dialogue, open to artists, students and the wider public. Its education facilities will host year-round activities including workshops for children and schools, family programs, student workshops, adult courses, lectures, book launches and other events dedicated to learning and public engagement.

The ground floor will also house Focus Art Encounters, the foundation's new platform for experimental artistic and curatorial practices. It will present exhibitions, performances, site-specific interventions and interdisciplinary projects developed with artists, curators and researchers from Romania and abroad. Particular attention will be given to emerging artists and collaborations across art, architecture, design, film, literature and new technologies, the foundation explained.

"The opening of the new Art Encounters space allows us to design the foundation's program as an ecosystem in which exhibitions, research, education and experiment reinforce one another. Alongside expanding our international collaborations, we will continue to support a new generation of artists and curators, while the Focus program will provide a dedicated platform for experimental practices and interdisciplinary dialogue. We want Art Encounters to become an active institution where visitors return not only for a single exhibition, but for an ongoing program of encounters with contemporary art," Diana Marincu, the artistic director of the Art Encounters Foundation, said.

The transformation of the headquarters has been designed by Attila KIM Architects. The development and implementation of the ground-floor interior design have been carried out in collaboration with Andreea Andresoiu. Beyond upgrading the building to international museum standards, the project included the installation of a lift and the reconfiguration of visiting routes, and making the venue fully accessible to visitors with disabilities.

"With its new headquarters, the Art Encounters Foundation is contributing to the development of Timișoara's cultural infrastructure by creating a space dedicated to contemporary art, education, and bringing people together. We envision it as a year-round destination, with a continuous program of exhibitions, educational activities and events for audiences of all ages. At the same time, the new venue provides the conditions needed to collaborate with international museums and cultural institutions, strengthening Timișoara's place on the European contemporary art map," Ovidiu Șandor, the founder and president of the Art Encounters Foundation, said.

The building housing the Art Encounters Foundation's permanent headquarters has been made available by the foundation's founder and his family. The transformation and fit-out of the new venue, representing an investment of several hundred thousand euros, has been financed through private funding and contributions from partner companies.

"For years we have built a community around contemporary art and helped establish Timișoara on Romania's and Europe's cultural map through exhibitions, biennials and large-scale projects. Today we are building its home as well: a place where people come for outstanding exhibitions, cultural education, to browse a book in the Art Encounters library, enjoy a conversation over coffee, or simply spend time in an open and welcoming environment," Georgia Bacinschi, director of the Art Encounters Foundation, said.

World.title: Kosovo Detains Two on War Crime Allegations Amid Mass Grave Excavation
World.content:
The alleged mass grave location in Kalluder, near Zubin Potok. Photo: BIRN

Pristina Basic Court ordered 30 days’ detention to two Serbs suspected of war crimes during the 1999 war in Kosovo.

The suspects, M.J. and M.B., were arrested on Monday in a police operation. The prosecution says the case is related to the ongoing excavation of a suspected mass grave near Zubin Potok in northern Kosovo.

The works, which started on Monday, are being conducted on the request of the Special Prosecution and by order of the Court of Pristina for exhumation, autopsy and identification of mortal remains.

“The court assessed that the imposition of pre-trial detention in this criminal case is an adequate measure, as there is a real risk that if the defendants are released, they may flee with the aim of hiding and escaping criminal responsibility; also, taking into account that the defendants are also citizens of Serbia, there is a real risk that they will easily flee,” the court said on Wednesday.

On Wednesday, Prime Minister Albin Kurti echoed suspicions that the grave might hold the remains of 23 Albanian civilians from Mitrovica who were taken by Serbian forces on April 19, 1999 and never found since.

“Our immediate suspicion when we learned that mortal remains were found was that it was the group of 23 intellectuals in Mitrovica who were kidnapped and forcibly disappeared. We cannot confirm that it is them, but this was our immediate suspicion. However, we must wait for our institutions to tell us what it is about,” Kurti said.

“But it seems that we have a mass grave in the village of Kalluder, Zubin Potok, in the north, which was an area that had not been examined before,” he added.

Kushtrim Gara, from the Kosovo government’s commission on missing persons, said the location has been in the focus of relevant institutions for a long time but did not give more details due to the sensitivity of the case.

“We are waiting for the completion of all examinations and the exhumation process, and any information that can be shared will initially be shared with the families of the missing persons, because the victims are at the centre of this process,” Gara said.

On July 28, the Serbian government’s Office for Kosovo criticised the arrests and accused the Kosovo authorities of putting local Serbs under undue pressure.

“These unfounded actions add to the unrest in Serbian communities and create a sense of insecurity and fear among the Serbian people, which is the goal of the regime in Pristina, which has no political legitimacy and is trying to build its position by oppressing the Serbian people,” the office said.

A report published on Wednesday by Kosovo’s Institute of Crimes Committed During the War concluded that 1,578 persons are still missing from the 1999 Kosovo war.

World.title: Former Turkish PM Davutoglu Quits Politics After Failing to Unite Conservatives
World.content:
Former Turkish Prime Minister Ahmet Davutoglu announced on Wednesday that he is leaving politics and is dissolving his failing Future Party.

“We have decided to withdraw from party politics and bring the Future Party’s political activities to an end, in order to avoid becoming part of the polluted political climate,” Davutoglu said in a statement.

The party currently has four seats in parliament. The party was established in 2019 with high hopes and entered parliament in 2023 thanks to a political alliance with the main opposition Republican People’s Party, CHP.

However, it failed to become a popular choice among conservative and Islamist voters, who are seen as the bastion of President Recep Tayyip Erdogan’s ruling Justice and Development Party, AKP.

According to Davutoglu, his party tried to gather conservative forces together but did not succeed.

“From the outset, we sought to unite this new group internally first and then, if possible, merge it with the other conservative parties into a single party. Where that was not possible, we aimed to build a close, organic alliance. However, those efforts were ultimately unsuccessful,” he said.

Davutoglu was an architect of an AKP foreign policy that has seen Turkey extend its influence across the former Ottoman lands of the Balkans and the Middle East.

Known as the policy of “zero problems with neighbours”, Davutoglu developed the strategy while working as a professor of international relations at institutions including the prestigious Malaysian Islamic University.

In 2003, he was appointed an ambassador by then Prime Minister Abdullah Gul before going on to become chief foreign policy advisor to Gul’s successor, Erdogan, and then foreign minister in 2009.

The neighbourhood policy was outlined in his 2001 book, Strategic Depth, which advocated greater Turkish engagement and influence in the region, focusing on the Balkans, the Caucasus, the Middle East and Central Asia.

His star rose when he was appointed prime minister in 2014, when Erdogan moved into the presidency. But a number of disagreements between the two and Davutoglu’s efforts to play a more visible role in domestic and foreign policy led to his resignation in 2016, under pressure from Erdogan. He finally resigned from the AKP in 2019.

Davutoglu saw the Balkans as a “natural and historical hinterland” for Turkish foreign policy given the strong bonds forged through centuries of Ottoman domination.

His promotion of Turkish ‘soft power’ saw the growth of government-backed bodies such as the Turkish aid agency, TIKA, the Yunus Emre cultural institutes, Turkish universities in the Balkans, media outlets and the Turkish Religious Authority, Diyanet.

Davutoglu founded the Future Party mainly with former AKP figures in a bid to challenge the President. According to recent opinion polls, however, the party had lost support.

The four Future Party MPs are expected to join the AKP or remain independent in parliament.

Despite his fading career in politics, Davutoglu still sounded a proud note. “This is not a decision of surrender. It is a decision to draw a moral line. This is not an abandonment of politics; it is a call for everyone to rethink politics.” Davutoglu wrote.

World.title: Hungary Enters Post-Print Age as Political Dailies Disappear
World.content:
End of an era

Urban believes that printed political newspapers could survive for another decade or so in larger European countries, but in smaller markets they are fast becoming an unsustainable business. Printing and distribution costs simply cannot compete with the economics of online publishing.

“Hungary is once again a pioneer, partly because the Orban government captured much of the media market,” Urban says. “It took control of most publishing houses and kept them afloat through state advertising and politically motivated advertising contracts.”

But as their content became more ideological and one-sided, readers deserted them. Most established media brands have now lost their credibility to such an extent that they can no longer sustain themselves on the competitive market or rely on subscriptions.

Nepszava’s story is somewhat different. Although it has been a consistent critic of the Orban government, it also relied – for the most part – on government advertising for the past four years. When Orban’s government lost power in the April 12 election, those revenues evaporated overnight.

“The journalists at Nepszava clearly produced critical reporting on the government,” Urban admits. “But, unfortunately, the company behind the newspaper was not financially independent from the state.”

Now struggling to survive as an online-only publication, Nepszava is finding that competition in the digital market is fierce. “We are in a lose-lose situation,” admits Nepszava’s Horvath. “Without a print edition, we have lost our subscribers. We don’t have s either. So, at the moment, we have no revenue at all.”

Both Nepszava and Magyar Nemzet have fallen well behind their competitors in the online news market. During the Orban years, many of Hungary’s independent media outlets reinvented themselves as online platforms and managed to develop sustainable business models while maintaining editorial independence. Many operate behind paywalls and most receive some EU grant funding, while traditional advertising has only slowly returned – if at all.

Magyar Hang, for example, a critical weekly newspaper, was forced to find a printing house in Slovakia when its business was turned away by a printing and distribution sector consolidated in the hands of Orban allies, but this helped the paper maintain its independence.

“Being online became a kind of guarantee of independence, while most of the print media was captured,” Urban points out.

The consequence is that many of the media outlets that were close to Orban’s government now find themselves on the brink following the April election. Regional newspapers, once an important source of information (disinformation, critics would argue) outside of Budapest and pillars of local communities, are also being converted into weeklies by August 1. Some pro-government outlets such as the tabloid Bors have already been closed, while others are making major layoffs. The weekly Mandiner, which also has a strong online presence, has reportedly laid off more than half its staff.

Some wonder how historians will evaluate this period in Hungary 50 or 100 years from now if no printed archives remain. In theory, the information will survive online, but all it takes is for someone to flick a switch for an archive to become inaccessible.

“It is a legitimate concern that online news could simply disappear if the servers are shut down,” Urban warns. “That would mean that stories, investigations and entire archives of media content could become inaccessible.”

Still, she believes there is no way back for print dailies. Weekly publications, offering more in-depth reporting, interviews and features, may still have a future, but online media is simply unbeatable when it comes to breaking news.

“This is another trend where Hungary is, sadly, once again a trendsetter,” Urban says. “But sooner or later, the rest of Europe will follow.”

World.title: Romania’s Farmers Feel the Heat as River Danube Dries Up
World.content:
The Danube is a vital European transport route for goods such as cereals, construction materials and fuel products, including exports from Ukraine.

In 2023, freight transport on the navigable stretch of the Danube between Germany and the Black Sea reached 55.2 million tonnes, according to the Central Commission for the Navigation of the Rhine. The summer season is one of the busiest periods of the year, including for Ukrainian grain exports.

In southern Romania, much of the agricultural production transported along the Danube is shipped to the Black Sea port of Constanta.

But with the current restrictions, many farmers cannot sell their crops according to existing contracts. Daniel Nica, a farmer from Macesul de Jos, has 20,000 tonnes of wheat, barley and rapeseed stored in his silos, awaiting transport on the Danube.

“When we harvest the maize, we won’t have enough storage space,” he explained.

Like many farmers in the area, he usually sells to traders using the small port of Bechet. His company farms around 10,000 hectares of land in Dolj County, of which 2,500 hectares of maize are irrigated. Since early July, the irrigation canals supplied with water pumped from the Danube have dried out completely.

For Romanian farmers, such restrictions have become increasingly common in recent years. Coupled with repeated droughts, the lack of water availability is putting pressure on agriculture in Romania, one of the European Union’s largest agricultural producers and exporters of cereals.

This year, Romanian farmers have reported better rainfall than during previous summers, when some farmers reported total crop losses. But concerns remain over the longer term, especially for smaller producers.

Mugurel Ionut Stancu drives us through endless fields of sunflowers and maize, alongside a completely dried-up irrigation canal.

“Maize is currently at the stage when it needs the most water, as the kernels are filling. Without sufficient water supply, this will inevitably lead to lower yields and reduced quality,” he said.

Stancu joined the family farming business inspired by his grandfather, who had been cultivating land in the Valea Stanciului area, around 30 kilometres north of the Danube. Here too, farmers rely on water pumped from the river. Stancu’s family now farms 300 hectares, 58 of which have been irrigated since 2021.

“The need for irrigation emerged because droughts were persisting year after year, and spring crops, particularly maize and sunflower, were simply no longer profitable,” he recalled.

But lack of water availability could mean that this investment will take far longer than expected to pay off.

To increase the flow of water into the irrigation canals, authorities are dredging parts of the Danube to raise the water levels near pumping stations. Along the river, similar operations are being carried out to widen navigation channels for commercial barges.

“We began dredging works as early as April. The operations were divided into three sections, and a total of 270,000 cubic metres of sediments were dredged,” outlined Adrian Maizel from the Lower Danube River Administration.

But some experts fear these measures will not solve the problem in the long term.

“Dredging could lead to even lower groundwater levels,” warned Camelia Ionescu, who heads the water and climate project for WWF Romania, a nature protection campaign organisation.

Communist policies also to blame

World.title: Media Changes in Montenegro Intensify Alarm About Foreign Influence
World.content:
As Montenegro enters the final stage of its European Union accession process, concerns over harmful foreign influence are returning to the centre of public debate.

Experts are warning that media ownership changes, disinformation campaigns and political interference could all test the country’s democratic resilience ahead of elections expected in 2027.

The debate has intensified after a series of ownership changes and planned acquisitions involving some of Montenegro’s most influential media outlets, raising questions over the future of media pluralism and editorial independence in a country seeking to complete its EU path.

Both the European Commission and European Parliament have warned Montenegro about foreign interference, hybrid threats and information manipulation.

World.title: Two Greek Firefighters Die Battling Wildfire on Crete
World.content:
Two firefighters have died while battling a forest fire in the Krya Vrisi area of ​​Rethymno, on the island of Crete, the Greek Fire Service announced on Wednesday. State television reported that one was a seasonal firefighter and the other was a five-year veteran. They were reportedly trapped in their vehicle in the flames.

The Fire Service expressed its condolences to the families and loved ones of the deceased in a statement issued on Wednesday: “They fell heroically in the line of duty to protect the lives and property of citizens and the natural environment.”

The fire in Rethymno started in a forest area due to strong winds. Currently, 110 firefighters are operating on the front in six groups on the ground, with 27 vehicles, four helicopters as well as water tankers.

Strong winds are blowing in the area. Emergency messages have been sent to nearby residents to evacuate their homes. The villages of Krya Vrysi, Saktouria and Melampes have already been evacuated.

The Rethymno Arson Investigation Unit is investigating the causes of the fire.

Wildfires have also broken out in Messinia and Laconia in the Peloponnese and on the island of Mytilene, in the North Aegean.

A fire broke out on Tuesday on the island of Paros, in the Cyclades, which was brought under control – but a battle is still being fought to prevent a resurgence.

World.title: Counting the Dead: Kosovo Compiles List of 13,190 War Victims
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Shqip Bos/Hrv/Srp

Twenty-seven years after hostilities ended, Kosovo will publish on Wednesday the first official list of victims of the 1998-99 war – dead and missing.

Based on physical files stretching hundreds of metres and more than 22 terabytes in digital form, the list compiled by the state Institute of Crimes Committed During the War in Kosovo, ICCW, runs to 13,190 names, but remains ‘preliminary’.

“For each victim, at least eight different sources of information were used before being included in this preliminary list, and I believe each case underwent thorough verification,” said Atdhe Hetemi, director of the institute.

“This is a preliminary institutional list and remains open to additions and revisions based on new documents and evidence.”

World.title: Why Serbia’s Most Successful Football Club and Party Appear Unchallengeable
World.content:
Ludogorets Razgrad surrendered their title to Levski Sofia last season in the Bulgarian league, ending their streak of 14 consecutive league titles. The ripple effect of that reached Belgrade – the nine-time consecutive champions of the Serbian SuperLiga, Red Star Belgrade, now possess the longest winning streak in European football, dating back to the 2013-14 season.

The domestic winning streak enjoyed by Red Star (or Crvena Zvezda, as they’re known at home) is surpassed only by that of the Serbian Progressive Party, SNS, whose election victories began in 2012. The SNS has “scored” six successful election wins since then. Meanwhile, Red Star will be looking to continue their victories in the new Serbian SuperLiga season, which just got underway this month.

Football and politics are often the two biggest topics in many European nations and Serbia is no different. What is starkly different to other European nations, however, is how connected and similar Serbia’s football and politics are.

Usually, when looking at sporting success, such as Red Star’s title victories, fans would refer to this as a dynasty – the type of dynasty that deserves praise for every aspect of the club, from the top to the bottom.

World.title: How Can Sweden Have Cheaper Petrol Than Croatia With No Domestic Production?
World.content:
July the 30th, 2026 – Sweden produces almost no domestic oil, yet drivers there usually have access to much cheaper petrol than Croatia. How is that possible? The answer is more complex than you might realise.

The answer to the question posed above is that fuel prices are not simply determined by whether a country has oil reserves. Slobodan Mufic explained for Index that the final price at the pump depends on a combination of factors, including taxes, government decisions, competition between fuel companies, transport costs and market conditions.

Sweden imports the oil that it needs, but it has an incredibly highly developed energy market and strong purchasing power. The country has also introduced policies that influence the cost structure of fuels and energy, meaning the absence of domestic oil production does not automatically lead to higher prices. Croatia, meanwhile, also relies heavily on imported oil, but fuel prices are shaped by different economic conditions. The Croatian government has repeatedly intervened in the fuel market by setting maximum retail prices and adjusting measures such as excise duties to protect consumers from price increases.

Another important factor is the difference in wages. A litre of petrol may cost a similar amount across Europe, but what matters for citizens is how much of their income goes towards filling up their cars.

The comparison between Sweden and Croatia shows that having domestic oil production is not the only factor that determines fuel prices. Countries without their own oil can still have cheaper petrol if their tax systems, markets and economic conditions create lower costs for drivers. So while Croatia and Sweden both depend on imported energy, the price drivers behind the pump are much more complicated than simply asking: “Who has oil?”

World.title: Croatia’s Greatest Strength is Outstanding English Skills Says Global Study
World.content:
July the 30th, 2026 – Croatia’s greatest strength is the outstanding English skills of its population, according to a recently commissioned global outsourcing study.

Croatia’s strongest competitive advantage on the global outsourcing market is its exceptional command of the English language, according to the 2026 Global Talent Index for Outsourcing published by the U.S. consulting company Ataraxis. Katarina Kusec reports for Poslovni that the study assessed 193 UN-recognised countries using five key criteria: labour costs, English proficiency, talent availability, digital infrastructure and political stability.

The report highlights Croatia as one of the emerging success stories in Europe’s outsourcing industry, which is worth hundreds of billions of dollars annually and is no longer dominated solely by traditional outsourcing hubs such as India and the Philippines. Eastern European countries are becoming increasingly competitive, with Croatia standing out as a “hidden gem” in the European market.

croatia’s english skills see it receive 100 out of 100

According to the study, Croatia is one of only two countries in Eastern Europe, alongside Romania, to achieve a perfect score of 100 out of 100 for English proficiency. This places Croatia alongside native English-speaking countries such as the United Kingdom, the United States and South Africa, giving it a significant advantage when competing for international business.

The report notes that strong English skills are only part of Croatia’s appeal. The country also scored 90 out of 100 for digital infrastructure and 84 out of 100 for labour costs, creating a balanced profile that is attractive to companies looking to outsource high-value work. Croatia is home to almost 70,000 technology professionals, providing a solid foundation for further growth in the sector.

500 new croatian ict companies are established yearly

The country’s technology industry is also expanding rapidly. According to HUP-ICT, around 500 new ICT companies are established in Croatia every year, making it one of the most dynamic parts of the national economy.

Croatia’s digital infrastructure also compares favourably with the rest of Europe. The country has 82.7% coverage of very high-capacity broadband networks, 77.9% fibre-to-the-premises coverage, and 97.8% 5G network coverage, placing it above the European average in several key categories. These factors strengthen Croatia’s position as an attractive destination for international companies seeking outsourcing partners.

The Ataraxis report concludes that Croatia’s combination of excellent English proficiency, competitive labour costs, strong digital infrastructure and a growing technology sector gives it a unique opportunity to attract more international outsourcing projects and strengthen its position in the global digital economy.

World.title: Taxi Fares Vary Across Croatia as New Rules Aim for Price Transparency
World.content:
July the 30th, 2026 – Taxi fares vary wildly across Croatia as new rules aim to further increase price transparency and end the practice of ripping off customers.

Poslovni reports that the cost of taking a taxi in Croatia differs significantly depending on the city, with some destinations charging more than double the starting fare of others. According to data from the international cost-of-living platform Numbeo, Pula is among the most expensive Croatian cities when it comes to the average price per kilometre, while Osijek remains the cheapest.

the highest starting fare isn’t in dubrovnik…

The data show that the highest starting fare is found in Rijeka and Šibenik, where the average base price is 5 euros. In Dubrovnik and Opatija, the average starting fare is 4 euros, while it is 3.32 euros in Split. Zagreb and Osijek actually have the lowest average starting fare at just 2 euros.

When it comes to the cost per kilometre, Pula, Dubrovnik and Zadar top the list at an average of 2 euros per kilometre. Split follows at 1.60 euros, while Rijeka, Opatija and Šibenik average 1.30 euros per kilometre. In the City of Zagreb, the average is 1.25 euros, and Osijek has the lowest average price at just 1 euro per kilometre.

The figures are based on user-submitted data collected by Numbeo and represent average prices. Actual fares may vary depending on the taxi company, time of day, traffic conditions and any additional charges applied during the journey.

the road transport act seeks to increase transparency

Meanwhile, the Croatian Parliament has adopted amendments to the Road Transport Act aimed at making taxi pricing more transparent. Under the new rules, passengers must be shown the maximum fare and the planned route before the journey begins. The legislation also allows a future regulation to set maximum permitted prices for the starting fare, price per kilometre and waiting time.

The changes are intended to improve consumer protection and reduce the risk of unexpectedly high taxi bills, particularly during the busy summer tourist season, while bringing greater transparency and consistency to Croatia’s taxi market.

World.title: Croatian Hospitality Revenue Rises 12%, Accommodation Up 15%
World.content:
July the 30th, 2026 – Croatian hospitality revenue has risen by 12% along the Adriatic coastline and on the islands, with accommodation also up by 15% in the peak summer season.

As Jadranka Dozan reports for Poslovni, regardless of of growing debate about tourist spending and concerns over the strength of this year’s season, the latest fiscalisation data show that businesses across Croatia’s Adriatic coast are recording solid growth in revenue during the busiest part of the summer.

In the first 26 days of July, restaurants, cafés and other hospitality businesses in the seven Adriatic counties recorded over 568 million euros in turnover. That represents an increase of 11.7%, or around 60 million euros more than during the same period last year. The growth was accompanied by an 8.7% increase in the number of receipts issued, indicating both higher visitor spending and increased business activity.

The strongest hospitality revenues were recorded in Split-Dalmatia County, where businesses generated 162.5 million euros, followed by Istria with 100.8 million euros. Both counties posted year-on-year turnover growth of more than 14%, while also recording increases in the number of receipts. The smallest annual increase among the Adriatic counties was in Zadar County, where turnover rose by just under 6%. Meanwhile, Lika-Senj County recorded the highest percentage growth, with fiscalised turnover rising by 23% alongside a 14% increase in receipts.

Accommodation providers also reported strong results. Businesses offering accommodation generated around 582 million euros in fiscalised turnover during the same period, representing an increase of approximately 15% compared with the 506 million euros recorded one calendar year earlier. They issued more than four million receipts and invoices, up 5.7% year-on-year.

Among accommodation providers, Istria remained Croatia’s leading region, with 228 million euros in turnover, an increase of 12.7% compared with last year, achieved with 3.5% more receipts. Split-Dalmatia County followed with more than 107 million euros, recording a 17% increase in turnover and 5% more receipts. Only Dubrovnik-Neretva and Šibenik-Knin counties recorded accommodation turnover growth below double digits, although both still posted increases of close to 10%.

The latest figures come after a slower June prompted concerns about the tourist season. Tourism and Sports Minister Tonči Glavina recently said that Croatia could be satisfied with the current results, noting that the key indicators during the peak part of the season show traffic at roughly the same level as last year. The fiscalisation data now suggest that, despite ongoing discussions about prices and tourist spending, businesses along the Adriatic are continuing to generate healthy revenue growth during the height of the summer season.

World.title: Dinamo Secure European Autumn for Ninth Consecutive Year
World.content:
Dinamo Zagreb have booked their place in the third qualifying round of the Champions League following a dramatic victory over Thun, with their next opponents now confirmed. The result also guarantees the Zagreb club a ninth successive European autumn, with at least a place in the Conference League already secured.

Dinamo to face Kauno Žalgiris

Dinamo will face Lithuanian champions Kauno Žalgiris in the third qualifying round after Željko Sopić’s side edged out Faroe Islands champions KÍ Klaksvík across two legs. The first leg ended goalless, before Žalgiris claimed a 1-0 victory in the return fixture thanks to a goal in the 85th minute from former Hajduk player Leon Kreković. The first leg against Dinamo takes place on August 4th at Maksimir, with the return fixture scheduled for August 11th in Lithuania.

The comeback against Thun

Dinamo’s passage to the third round came via one of the more dramatic evenings in recent European memory. Thun raced into a 2-0 lead inside 22 minutes through Brighton Labeau and Marco Burki, and Dinamo looked helpless in the early stages. Everything changed in the 67th minute when Burki was shown a red card following a VAR intervention, and the Zagreb side took full advantage. Dion Drena Beljo leveled matters in the 74th minute before Lukas Kačavenda made it 2-2 in the 78th. The tie was forced into extra time, where Moris Valinčić produced a moment of brilliance in the 112th minute to seal a memorable 3-2 victory.

Should Dinamo overcome Žalgiris, they advance to the Champions League play-off round and secure at minimum a place in the Europa League group stage. Elimination at this stage would send them into the Europa League play-off instead. Either way, Dinamo’s European autumn is already guaranteed; even in the event of further exits, a place in the Conference League group stage awaits.

World.title: Croatian Inspectors Step Up Crackdown on Illegal Holiday Rentals
World.content:
July the 29th, 2026 – Croatian inspectors have begun stepping up their crackdown on illegal holiday rentals up and down the coastline in particular, with plenty of fines already issued.

As Poslovni reports, Croatia’s State Inspectorate has intensified its inspections of holiday accommodation advertised on platforms such as Booking.com and Airbnb, targeting property owners who rent to tourists without meeting the country’s latest, strict legal requirements. The inspections form part of a broader effort to combat the shadow economy in the tourism sector and ensure fair competition among registered accommodation providers.

thousands of euros seized, thousands fined…

According to the State Inspectorate, inspectors have already uncovered numerous cases of illegal short-term rentals during this year’s tourist season. As a result, authorities have confiscated 343,000 euros in income believed to have been earned through unlawful renting, while fines imposed have exceeded 81,000 euros.

The inspections focus on identifying individuals advertising tourist accommodation without the required registration or operating in breach of Croatian tourism regulations. Authorities are checking online listings as well as conducting on-site inspections to verify whether accommodation providers comply with the law.

inspections will continue throughout summer

When inspectors discover illegal activity, they can issue fines, prohibit further renting and confiscate the financial gains obtained through unlawful operations. Officials say these measures are intended to discourage unregistered rentals and protect hosts who operate legally and meet all regulatory obligations. The State Inspectorate said inspections will continue throughout the peak summer tourist season, with online booking platforms remaining one of the primary tools used to identify suspected illegal accommodation.

Officials stress that the goal is not only to punish offenders but also to ensure equal market conditions, protect consumers and improve the overall quality and transparency of Croatia’s tourism sector. As demand for private accommodation continues to grow, authorities say stronger enforcement is necessary to prevent unfair competition and safeguard public revenue.

World.title: Airbnb Loses Its Advantage Over Booking.com for Croatian Hosts
World.content:
July the 29th, 2026 – Airbnb no longer has any advantages or particular benefits over Booking.com for Croatian hosts after the company announced significant changes recently.

As Ana Roksandic reports for Poslovni, Croatian private accommodation hosts are facing a significant changes after Airbnb announced a new commission model that many say removes one of its biggest advantages over Booking.com. Under that company’s new system, Airbnb will no longer charge guests a separate service fee. Instead, hosts will pay a 15.5% commission, replacing the previous model in which hosts paid around 3% while guests covered most of the platform’s fee.

According to Vedran Tomić, president of the Save Small Family Renters Association (SMOi), the change has been met with negative reactions from Croatian hosts. He said Airbnb’s biggest advantage had been its lower direct cost for hosts, but that will now disappear. He also pointed out that Croatian hosts must pay VAT on the commission, meaning they will now pay VAT on the full 15.5% fee instead of just the previous 3% commission.

one last summer of airbnb advantage for croatian hosts…

The new commission structure will apply as of the 13th of October. Airbnb says the change responds to feedback from hosts who found the previous pricing model confusing because guests saw an additional service fee added to the advertised accommodation price. Under the new model, guests will simply see the final price, while the commission is deducted from the host’s payout.

The changes come as Croatia’s short-term rental market is already evolving. Data from analytics platform AirDNA shows that the number of active listings has fallen in the country’s largest cities. In Split, active listings dropped from around 10,300 in June 2025 to 8,906 in June 2026, a decline of 13.5%. Zagreb recorded an even steeper fall of 25%, with analysts linking the decline to more property owners switching to long-term rentals. The market is increasingly favouring larger and more professional operators, while less profitable listings are leaving the sector.

Tomić believes the commission change is unlikely to reduce demand from travellers, but it could weaken Airbnb’s position in Croatia because it no longer offers hosts a financial advantage over Booking.com. He estimates that Booking.com controls around 70% of the Croatian market, while Airbnb accounts for roughly 20%, with the remaining 10% shared by other booking platforms.

accommodation competitiveness isn’t even the biggest issue for croatian tourism

Damir Krešić, director of Croatia’s Institute for Tourism, said higher commissions are not good news for the sector, but argued that accommodation is not the biggest competitiveness issue facing Croatian tourism. In his view, greater concerns are the rising costs of food, drinks and transport services, where Croatia has become less competitive.

Krešić also encouraged private hosts not to rely on a single booking platform. He said global platforms have given small Croatian hosts access to guests worldwide, but becoming too dependent on one intermediary weakens their bargaining position. Instead, he recommends that hosts advertise across two or three platforms to diversify their bookings and reduce risk.

World.title: Luka Modrić Visits Unfinished Villa Construction Site in Istria
World.content:
July the 29th, 2026 – Croatian footballing legend Luka Modrić has paid a visit to an unfinished villa construction site in Istria before heading off on a yacht. Could he be thinking of buying it?

As Poslovni reports, a jet black limousine with tinted rear windows stopped at a construction site in Istria a few days ago, shortly before midday. Luka Modrić, 40, captain of the Croatian national football team, got out at the parking area in front of an unfinished villa that still requires final stonework for a Mediterranean appearance.

He was accompanied by experts who went around the site with him explaining different things and pointing out important construction details. The group then entered the private property and remained inside for about half an hour. According to one of the site’s neighbours who contacted the media about the group, Luka Modrić appeared interested in the property as a possible investment, though that is not confirmed.

The same day he was later seen boarding a yacht that he rents each summer for roughly a week or ten days of family holiday along the Adriatic coastline. Media reports state that, after earlier investments in central Dalmatia and the far south of Croatia, members of the Modrić family have shown interest in property in Istria. Vanja Modrić is said to have expressed interest on several occasions in locations around Rovinj, but no purchases have so far been officially completed.

the football legend has acquired multiple properties in both croatia and spain

Over the course of his career Modrić has acquired several residential properties in Croatia and Spain.

In the elite Zadar suburb of Kožino, near where he grew up, the family owns a villa with an outdoor pool, children’s playground, garden, sea view, wine cellar, ten-car garage, gym, an eighteen-seat cinema, children’s playroom and massage room. It is used as a family base during the summer break in the football season. In October 2024 a storm damaged the access road; the damage was later repaired. The property had earlier attracted attention over reports of beach concreting in front of the estate; Modrić stated that the area in question is public land, not a private beach.

In Zagreb, the family owns a 286-square-metre villa on Pantovčak, purchased back in 2017 from former footballer Zvonimir Boban. Land-registry records show Modrić transferred ownership to his wife Vanja shortly afterwards. Before that purchase the family had lived in apartments in Ravnice and Babonićeva Street. Modrić also owns a 220-square-metre penthouse with a 29-square-metre loggia in a newly built building on Tkalčićeva Street in the city centre; media estimates placed its value at around 1.4 million euros.

Over in the Spanish capital of Madrid, where Luka Modrić spent many years playing for Real Madrid, the family owns a villa in the La Moraleja district, acquired in 2019 on a 10,000-square-metre plot. Spanish media describe it as having nine bedrooms and nine bathrooms, with the main living areas, kitchen and sitting room on the ground floor and guest rooms upstairs, plus an outdoor pool, garden and recreation space. According to media reports, part of the portfolio is formally registered in Vanja Modrić’s name.

World.title: Turkish Airlines: Entry into Russian airspace was a one‑off weather-related decision
World.content:
Turkish Airlines, whose July 12 flight from Tallinn to Istanbul briefly entered Kaliningrad airspace, says the deviation was a one‑time safety‑driven exception caused by adverse weather conditions.

Turkish Airlines explained on Thursday that flight TK1424 from Tallinn to Istanbul on 12 July 2026 was planned in accordance with operational requirements, and Russian airspace was not part of the intended route.

"During the flight, the crew encountered adverse weather conditions along the planned route, including convective activity and thunderstorms. In coordination with air traffic control and in line with international aviation procedures, the aircraft performed a limited weather‑avoidance maneuver to ensure flight safety," the airline said in an e-mailed comment. "During this maneuver, the aircraft briefly entered Kaliningrad airspace before continuing toward its destination."

Short-term adjustment

Weather‑related route adjustments are common in aviation and may occur when operational conditions require it, the airline noted.

"Such decisions are made in real time by the crew in cooperation with relevant air traffic authorities, with passenger safety always the top priority."

Turkish Airlines confirmed that they do not normally use Russian airspace for EU flights. "The route change was a one‑time, short‑term operational adjustment caused by the specific weather conditions on that day."

"Route changes may occur only once the aircraft is airborne, as weather conditions constantly evolve and pilots make safety‑driven decisions in real time. The crew monitors weather radar throughout the flight and receives updated information from air traffic control. If hazardous weather is detected along the planned route, the crew is obliged to make safety‑focused decisions and may request alternative routing. In this case, altering the route was necessary to ensure passenger safety and a smooth flight."

Only suitable option

"Briefly entering Kaliningrad airspace was the only suitable option," the airline noted. "This TK1424 route adjustment was a one‑time, short‑term operational measure taken solely due to the weather conditions on that specific day."

Turkish Airlines said that the airline has not made similar route changes before or after on this flight path, confirming that it was an exceptional case driven by that day's weather.

Eesti Ekspress wrote on July 12, that Turkish Airlines aircraft changed its usual route and flew over the Kaliningrad region, although flights normally avoid Russian airspace.
