The authors also point out that Sukhum still has no monuments to Abkhazia’s first president, Vladislav Ardzinba, or to volunteers from the North Caucasus republics who fought alongside Abkhazia during the 1992–93 Georgian-Abkhaz war.

“If we intend to begin preserving our historical memory, we should start with them. Otherwise, not only the people of Abkhazia but also our friends in the North Caucasus and the parents of the fallen volunteers will not understand us,” the appeal says.

The signatories also argue that the issue has an important foreign policy dimension. Despite its strategic partnership with Russia, they say, Abkhazia is not at war with Ukraine.

“Our state has never carried out any mobilisation or organisational measures in connection with what Russia calls its ‘special military operation’. The relevant authorities have no information about either the total number of our citizens in the conflict zone or the terms under which they entered military service,” the appeal says.

They argue that officially recognising the participation of Abkhaz citizens in the fighting would provide diplomatic grounds for Ukraine and its regional allies, including Turkey, to regard Abkhazia as a party to the conflict. As a result, they say, “our citizens’ participation in the war would cease to be a matter of personal choice and instead become our collective choice.”

Although the appeal has been signed by only six people, its authors say they believe their views are widely shared across Abkhaz society.

“We are in contact with people from all walks of life and can say with confidence that thousands of residents of Sukhum and citizens of Abkhazia share our views and the arguments set out above.”

The signatories call on the president and the city authorities to act with prudence and wisdom.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

Monument to Abkhazians who fought in Ukraine

World.title: Turkey takes practical steps to restore rail link with Armenia
World.content:
Turkey restores Akyaka–Gyumri railway

Turkey has begun restoring the entire railway infrastructure along the Akyaka–Gyumri route, the section connecting it with Armenia. Preliminary estimates suggest the work will take two to three months to complete. Akyaka Mayor Erduger Toptas told this to a group of Armenian journalists visiting Turkey.

According to Toptas, the construction work now under way in Turkey signals preparations for reopening the Armenian-Turkish border. He said reopening the border would give Turkey another route to the Caucasus. It would also allow Armenia to establish transport links with Middle Eastern countries through Turkey.

Kadir Bozan, chairman of the Kars Chamber of Commerce and Industry, also told the Armenian journalists that freight traffic on the Akhalkalaki–Kars railway has increased by 400% in recent months. He did not specify whether Armenia uses the route for exports or imports.

However, on 24 May, Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan said that “the Akhalkalaki–Kars railway is now open for exports from Armenia and imports into Armenia.” He described the development as extremely important for the country’s economy.

Armenian journalists’ impressions from their visit to Turkey

According to official information, a group of Armenian journalists travelled to Turkey as part of a journalist exchange programme. The purpose of the visit was to observe progress on the work to reopen the railway on the Turkish side.

The journalists also wanted to see how Turkey’s railway infrastructure operates more broadly. In particular, they travelled by train from Kars to Akyaka. The 57-kilometre journey took just 50 minutes.

After returning, they wrote that Akyaka station lies only 18–20 kilometres from the Armenian city of Gyumri. That means the journey would take just 30–40 minutes. However, the closed border currently makes it impossible to travel from Akyaka to Gyumri.

Tender announced for Akyaka–Gyumri highway

Akyaka Mayor Erduger Toptas said Turkey plans to restore not only the railway but also the highway.

“The tender for the construction of the road from Akyaka to Gyumri has already been announced. We now expect work on that project to begin as well,” he said.

According to Toptas, these developments indicate that both governments are moving towards establishing good-neighbourly and friendly relations.

The mayor said reopening the Armenian-Turkish border and expanding bilateral economic cooperation would benefit both countries. He believes the two sides have opportunities to cooperate in both agriculture and industry.

The Armenian journalists also spoke with residents of Turkish settlements near the Armenian border. Most said they hope the border will reopen as soon as possible. They also believe it will create new economic opportunities for local communities on both sides of the border.

“We do not expect any obstacles to reopening the border”

Akyaka Mayor Erduger Toptas expressed optimism about the prospects for normalising relations between Armenia and Turkey. In his view, once Armenia and Azerbaijan normalise their relations, reopening the Armenian-Turkish border should not present any difficulties.

He said that, on the instructions of the Turkish president and under the coordination of the transport ministry, officials have begun preparatory work at the border crossing points ahead of the border’s reopening. Railway infrastructure also requires restoration. However, he said the closed border remains the main obstacle to resuming rail services.

At the beginning of 2026, Armenian media reported that the Armenian-Turkish border would open on 1 February to third-country nationals and holders of diplomatic passports. Armenia’s and Turkey’s special envoys for normalisation, Ruben Rubinyan and Serdar Kilic, reached that agreement in July 2022. The Margara border crossing on the Armenian side has stood ready to receive travellers since December 2023. Despite those agreements, however, Turkey has kept the border closed.

Even so, the two countries periodically announce positive steps. For example, from 1 January 2026, Armenia and Turkey simplified visa procedures for holders of diplomatic, special and service passports. They can now obtain a free electronic visa (e-visa) for short-term trips of up to 20 days.

Background

Since 2008, Armenia’s railway network has operated under a concession held by the South Caucasus Railway company, a wholly owned subsidiary of Russian Railways. The concession agreement runs for 30 years, with an option to extend it by another 10 years if both sides agree.

Armenian experts say freight traffic on the country’s railways has halved since 2008. Some routes have ceased operating, while the mandatory investment commitments have never materialised.

Despite this, Yerevan asked Moscow to restore the Gyumri–Akhurik and Yerask railway sections.

Rebuilding these lines would reconnect Armenia with the borders of Azerbaijan and Turkey. This is strategically important for Yerevan, which seeks to fully unblock regional transport links.

Russia has neither acted on Armenia’s request nor indicated a willingness to do so. At the same time, Moscow has said it does not intend to give up its railway concession.

Meanwhile, the Armenian government is considering revoking Russia’s concession and taking control of the railway network itself. It has also left open the possibility of transferring the concession to a third party.

At the beginning of July, Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan announced that Armenia had begun preparatory work to restore the Gyumri–Akhurik and Yerask railway sections.

“We will carry out this work ourselves. As for the remaining sections, we will continue working-level discussions, including with our Russian partners,” he said.

Turkey restores Akyaka–Gyumri railway

World.title: Parents of Australian facing possible death penalty in Syria question confession
World.content:
The family of a Gold Coast man facing a possible death penalty for allegedly murdering another Australian in Syria has gone public to express frustration at the lack of progress made by the federal government in the case.

Patrick Stevenson, 20, has been detained for nearly seven months in north-western Syria accused of the shooting murder of Abdullah Glen Charles Burgess, 40, from northern New South Wales.

Mr Stevenson's mother, Angela Bell, said Australian officials had told her diplomatic efforts had gone nowhere.

She told the ABC she was disappointed by her dealings with the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade (DFAT).

Patrick Stevenson travelled to Syria late last year. (Supplied)

"They say … that their policy is that he shouldn't have been travelling to Syria … and that's where the conversation gets stuck," she told the ABC's 7.30 program.

"They use the word 'limited' a lot. They don't use the word failure, but basically the sense is they … have limited capacity to help in this situation."

The ABC has established that Mr Burgess was a tree lopper from the village of Eltham, near Lismore, who spent months in Afghanistan before settling in Syria last year with his Australian wife and their daughters.

Abdullah Glen Charles Burgess was shot dead in the town of Darkush on December 31, 2025. (Supplied)

According to Syrian authorities, Mr Burgess was shot dead in his home in the town of Darkush in Idlib province on December 31, while his wife and daughters were in another room.

Mr Stevenson was arrested nearby soon afterwards and later charged with premeditated murder, an offence punishable by death in Syria.

Syrian authorities allege he confessed to firing at least eight shots from an AK-47 at Mr Burgess.

But his family and Australian legal team say they do not know how the alleged confession was obtained and have raised serious concerns about whether he will receive a fair trial.

"Not a single document has come from Syria explaining the charges," Ms Bell said.

"There's no paperwork, there's no access to Patrick."

No Australian government representative has visited Mr Stevenson in prison, attended his court hearings or independently assessed his welfare.

Clay Stevenson says his son's health has deteriorated severely. (ABC News: Sissy Reyes)

Last week, Mr Stevenson's father, Clay, travelled to Syria carrying his son's Australian medical records and a psychiatric report for the court.

He visited Mr Stevenson in Sarmada prison and attended a court hearing on Sunday — the first time a member of the family had seen him since he secretly left Australia last October.

His parents say his mental health has deteriorated severely in detention.

Mr Stevenson has learning disorders, ADHD and probable autism spectrum disorder, according to a 2025 psychiatric report.

He travelled to Syria late last year and came to the attention of counterterrorism police after becoming radicalised, an ABC investigation has established.

Do you know more? Contact Sean Rubinsztein-Dunlop on Signal: @seanrdunlop.01 and on Protonmail: seanrdunlop@protonmail.com

on Signal: and on Protonmail: Please use this form to get in contact with the ABC Investigations team, or if you require more secure communication, please choose an option on the confidential tips page

The family's Australian lawyer, Bernadette Zaydan, said the alleged confession raised "alarm bells" because it was unclear how it had been obtained.

"Was it given under duress? Was it given in writing? Was it given orally?" she said.

"We have grave concerns for his welfare."

Ms Zaydan urged the federal government to press for Mr Stevenson to receive a transparent trial before an independent court, rather than one associated with Syria's administration or armed forces.

Canberra struggling to gain access

The ABC understands Australia has made representations about Mr Stevenson's case, but DFAT told his family last month that the Syrian government had shown little engagement.

Correspondence seen by the ABC shows the department repeatedly told the family it could not obtain information from Syrian authorities and had no access to the country's detention facilities.

Australia has no embassy or consulate in Syria, severely limiting the consular assistance it can provide.

Canberra has also been unable to independently monitor the investigation into Mr Burgess's death.

After the ABC revealed the case, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said on Thursday that Australia was providing support to both families.

"Legal processes will take their course overseas, of course, and that is appropriate," he said.

"I feel for the family of the person who's lost their life, and we're connected to them and providing support for them.

"We're also providing support for the family of the man who's been charged."

But Canberra has struggled to establish relations with Syria's new government, unlike allies including the United States and France.

Australia continues to impose sanctions on Hayat Tahrir al-Sham, the militant group from which Syria's new leadership emerged, and lists it as a terrorist organisation.

The group, which formally dissolved last year, was previously affiliated with Al Qaeda.

Parents discovered police were investigating son

Mr Stevenson left Australia on a flight to Bali on October 10 before travelling to Syria.

His parents said they had no idea he had left the country.

"I was shocked to find out that he was there," Clay Stevenson said.

"It's just like, 'Wow, what's going through his head to be in Syria and who helped him get there?'"

Patrick Stevenson's parents said he told them he intended to study at a Syrian university and hoped to find a wife.

They tried desperately to convince him to return home.

Patrick Stevenson is facing a possible death penalty in Syria. (Supplied)

The family said they discovered he was overseas only after officers from the Queensland Police Security and Counter-Terrorism Command contacted them.

His parents said officers searched his bedroom at his father's home and questioned them about extremist material he had allegedly posted in a group chat.

"He was talking to someone in a group chat that the Australian government were investigating and Patrick had come up as peripheral to another investigation," Ms Bell said.

She said ASIO later questioned her about her son's associations on the Gold Coast.

Mr Stevenson converted to Islam during his final year of high school in 2023, according to his family.

Patrick Stevenson converted to Islam in his final year of high school in 2023. (Supplied)

By last year, he was showing signs of radicalisation, including sharing speeches by Anwar al-Awlaki, the US-born Al Qaeda cleric and propagandist killed in a US drone strike in Yemen in 2011.

He also volunteered with Muslim Youth GC (MYGC), a youth group connected to the Worongary Mosque on the Gold Coast.

The group's leader, Abdul Rahman Nasiri, said neither it nor any other local organisation had supported Mr Stevenson's journey and he was free to make his own choices.

"We created MYGC to help young people [both Muslim and non-Muslim] steer away and overcome the negative challenges they face daily and give them the correct understanding of Islam, free from the stereotypes and misinformation that can appear online or in the media," he said in a written statement.

Case referred to civilian court

DFAT advised Mr Stevenson's family that Syrian authorities initially treated the shooting as an accident.

They later investigated whether he was affiliated with the Islamic State terrorist group.

According to information provided to the family, that investigation ended in February when authorities referred the case to the civilian criminal courts as a murder prosecution, rather than as a terrorism case.

The prosecution is likely to test Syria's fractured legal system as the country attempts to rebuild its institutions after 14 years of civil war.

Syrian legal sources told the ABC that it could take up to a year for the court to reach a verdict.

Any death sentence imposed by an ordinary criminal court would have to be reviewed by the Court of Cassation, considered by a clemency committee and approved by Syria's president before it could be carried out.

Patrick Stevenson travelled to Syria late last year. (Supplied)

Quiet man who avoided the camera

Those who knew Mr Burgess described him as quiet, devout and reluctant to be photographed.

"He was a very soft-spoken, gentle sort of guy," said Shahz Rana, a former president of the North Coast Muslim Association.

"Not too talkative, just used to keep to himself, but was still nice and polite to others."

Mr Rana said the news of his death had shocked the community.

"It was a little bit surprising that he was in Syria, but it was shocking news and I feel sad for him," he said.

Mr Rana said Mr Burgess told community members in about 2024 that his family was moving to Malaysia to live in a Muslim community and learn more about the faith.

He was unaware the family had spent at least six months travelling through Taliban-ruled Afghanistan before moving to Darkush, near Syria's border with Türkiye.

It is not known what brought the family to Syria. The ABC does not suggest they had links to extremist groups.

People who knew the two men said Mr Burgess took Mr Stevenson under his wing and that they became close before the shooting.

Widow could spare Stevenson's life

Mr Stevenson's fate may ultimately rest with a third Australian: Mr Burgess's widow, Amatullah Laurie Duniam.

Under the Syrian legal system, she could spare him execution by granting forgiveness, potentially in exchange for a payment of blood money, known as diya.

Ms Duniam and other members of Mr Burgess's family declined to speak to the ABC.

World.title: 'Take them seriously': CFMEU administrator on Setka threats
World.content:
CFMEU administrator Michael Crosby has opened up on threats from John Setka, cast doubt on a statement made by former Victorian premier Jacinta Allan and questioned the value of royal commissions during an extensive 7.30 interview.

Mr Crosby was appointed to the role in May following the resignation of its previous administrator, Mark Irving.

At the time, Mr Crosby said he was committed to changing the culture of the union, which in 2024 was placed into administration by the Albanese government following revelations it had been infiltrated by organised crime.

Mr Irving had said he had received death threats during his tenure.

Mr Crosby says he too has received threats, a first for him, from former CFMEU boss John Setka.

"I take them seriously," Mr Crosby told 7.30.

"There's not much I can do about it. The police have taken out the Victorian equivalent of an AVO.

"I'm basically ignoring it and moving on.

"I think about the work that we're doing in this union, [and] I'm incredibly proud of the people who have come into this union to reform it."

John Setka is accused of threatenig CFMEU administrator Michael Crosby. (AAP: Stefan Postles)

Asked if he would take a meeting with Mick Gatto, who had wanted one with his predecessor, Mr Crosby said he would not.

"Why would I associate with anybody like that and give him credibility?" Mr Crosby said.

Mr Crosby said in his view the union had done well to weed out corruption since it went into administration, telling 7.30 that he believed criminal elements no longer held sway.

"They have very little grip on the union," Mr Crosby said.

"We've moved off 27 leaders, 150 staff members of various kinds have gone away. We've got a whole new team in there rebuilding that union from the ground up."

Scepticism on royal commission

With corruption and criminality having been major problems for the CFMEU, Mr Crosby was adamant that corruption had also been responsible for a blowout in costs on major Victorian projects.

The CFMEU is being rebuilt "from the ground up", Michael Crosby says. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

That was something former premier Jacinta Allan had refused to admit, when she blamed inflation rather than CFMEU corruption for the skyrocketing costs on Victoria's Big Build.

"That's difficult to accept," Mr Crosby told 7.30.

Mr Crosby said criminality had generally caused the cost of construction in Australia to be more expensive.

"Inevitably … somebody is clipping the ticket on the way through," he said.

Former Victorian premier Jacinta Allan blamed cost blow outs on Victoria's Big Build on inflation. (AAP: Joel Carrett)

"Some of the corruption is about who gets to do the work, and these are rich contracts because they're big projects.

"If you can get that job, then you get paid by the government to do that."

Mr Crosby said that process was a major problem for the construction industry to reckon with.

"Criminality comes out of the way in which the industry is organised," he said.

"Governments hand over control of a particular infrastructure project to a head contractor, the head contractor then hands over control to subcontractors, and then they get labour hire agencies in.

"Right through that, that's where supervision breaks down, and you get these criminals coming in, subverting the union, corrupting the union and its leadership, but lining their pockets all the way through."

New Victorian premier Ben Carroll has called a royal commission into the construction sector in the state. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

A major question for any royal commission into construction, as called for by new Victorian Premier Ben Carroll, is if it can fix the major issues around corruption in the sector.

It is something that Mr Crosby is unsure of.

"Will [we] cooperate with the royal commission? Absolutely," he said.

"I am sceptical about royal commissions. There's been four into the CFMEU [and] they've all failed."

Watch 7.30, Mondays to Thursdays 7:30pm on ABC iview and ABC TV

World.title: Toy library makes statement grieving loss of Helena Wright and children
World.content:
A South Australian toy library has expressed sadness following the deaths of a mother and her two children, which police are treating as a murder-suicide.

The bodies of Helena Wright and her 23-month-old daughter were retrieved from waters off Cape Northumberland in SA's south-east on Monday.

The search for her three-month-old son was formally called off by South Australian Police on Wednesday afternoon, after receiving advice the child could not have survived.

Ms Wright was a volunteer committee member at the Mount Gambier Toy Library, which issued a statement on Thursday.

"Mt Gambier Toy Library is deeply saddened by the tragic loss of a member of our committee and her children. Our thoughts are with their family, friends and everyone affected by this devastating event," it said. "Our volunteer committee and toy library community are grieving and supporting one another."

Police on Wednesday confirmed Ms Wright had attended a local police station on Sunday and officers had attended her home to conduct a welfare check on Monday morning following a call from a friend. Her car was found later that morning at Cape Northumberland.

The three deaths have shaken the Port MacDonnell community, which has rallied around locals who volunteered to help the police search.

The matter is now the subject of a coronial investigation.

World.title: 'Sadness' falls across coastal community after double murder-suicide
World.content:
Residents of a South Australian coastal town rocked by a double murder-suicide say a "sadness" has fallen across the tight-knit community.

Helena Wright, 36, and her 23-month-old daughter were pulled from the ocean near Port MacDonnell on Monday, with Ms Wright's two-month-old son still missing.

Helicopters and planes flew over the scene on Monday while boats scoured the ocean nearby searching for the boy.

Weather hampered search efforts on Tuesday and Wednesday, limiting searchers to foot patrols along the coastline.

Police made the call to end the formal search for the baby boy as of Wednesday afternoon, saying he could not have survived almost three days in the conditions.

Police are treating the death of Helena Wright and her two children as a murder-suicide. (Supplied)

Also on Wednesday, police said Ms Wright had attended a local police station the day before the deaths.

Police conducted a welfare check at her home at Compton, near Mount Gambier, just hours before the public found Ms Wright's vehicle running near the cliffs at Cape Northumberland.

Country Fire Service Kingsley Group officer Grant Fensom's team is based in Port MacDonnell, and he helped with rescue efforts.

He said volunteers told police the best chance of finding Ms Wright and her children was on Monday during the more favourable weather conditions.

"The locals, let alone the SES and the police, did their absolute best to locate them on the first day, which obviously you know resulted in two people being found and not the third," Mr Fensom said.

"The last two days it has been hard, been wet, it's been windy, and the sea has definitely been rough.

Police say they are continuing to search for the missing baby boy. (ABC News: Guido Salazar)

" So it's been a trying time knowing that you can't get out there and actually probably continue a search to give some closure to some people. "

Mr Fensom said the incident was hard on a town that prided itself on being welcoming.

"So to have something happen in our town is hard because people want to think that they can always help someone out that's in need," he said.

Strength in speaking up

Salt cafe owner Mel Lewis donated more than 30 meals to those on the ground as police and SES volunteers from around the state descended on Port MacDonnell to aid the search.

Mel Lewis says the deaths have taken a toll on the tight-knit town. (ABC South East SA: Aiden McNamara)

She said the entire town felt a "sadness".

"People are coming together, maybe connecting a little bit more, reaching out to family, friends, hugging their children a little bit tighter," she said.

Ms Lewis said it was important the town took the time to support one another.

"It shows more strength to reach out and ask for help than to not," she said.

"I know personally to do that, and it is very, very tough, but we have a lot of services around for us to be able to reach out.

"But even just your friends and your family, but like I said, it just shows so much more strength asking for help than not."

Emergency services volunteer Roger Bobolka said the impact spread beyond those on the ground aiding the search effort.

Roger Bobulka said the incident would "stick" with locals. (ABC South East SA: Aiden McNamara)

"You can talk to anyone in town now and you can tell they've been impacted in some way because it's not the sort of thing you can just shut off and push aside and move on," he said.

"It's the sort of thing that hangs around for quite some time and it will for the community.

"I mean it's happened in a fairly prominent location within Port MacDonnell, so you can't get away from it."

Shoreline monitoring continues

Police Commissioner Grant Stevens told 891 ABC Adelaide officers would continue to monitor the shoreline for the missing baby boy despite ceasing the formal search.

"We will continue searching the shoreline in the coming days in the hope of being able to recover the little infant, but we're not holding a lot of hope in that regard," he said.

He said the deaths of children were "distressing" not only for police but for the community.

Commissioner Grant Stevens says the incident is distressing. (ABC News)

"It's heartbreaking to think we can't find the little infant, that sits heavily on the shoulders of the people involved, and it's not just police," he said.

The bodies of Helena Wright and her 23-month-old daughter were recovered from the ocean. (ABC News: Guido Salazar)

The commissioner added the case was now part of a coronial investigation and would not elaborate on any interactions Ms Wright had with police.

"That evidence [to the coroner] will include all of the activities involving Helena and her interactions with police, any other services in the days leading up to what we are now describing as a murder-suicide," he said.

World.title: Nauru officially changes name to Naoero
World.content:
Nauru has officially changed its name to Naoero, the Micronesian nation's government has announced.

A constitutional amendment to rename the country passed parliament in May, following a proposal tabled by President David Adeang in January.

Mr Adeang said at the time that the name Nauru had been recognised internationally since the island's independence, the proposed change sought to "more faithfully honour our nation's heritage, our language, and our identity".

However, a national referendum was expected to follow to complete the constitutional procedures.

"The Republic of Naoero is the new official designation for what was previously known as Nauru. The abbreviated form will be Naoero, with the code updated to NRO, and the people will be referred to as dei-Naoero," the government said in a statement.

Nauru's parliament passed a constitutional amendment to change the name in May. (AFP: Mike Leyral)

It added that Mr Adeang delivered his opening message to parliament on July 20 and addressed the decision to return the country to its traditional name, Naoero, "following extensive discussions".

"The decision not to pursue a referendum was reached after thoughtful deliberation that Naoero is not a new name seeking acceptance by the people.

"It is already the identity of the people, is on the national coat of arms, and spoken in the community; and importantly is allowed by the Constitution.

"While a referendum is intended to determine the will of the people, the name Naoero has never been lost, but rather waiting to be fully embraced."

The government said a bill to amend the constitution to allow the name change was tabled in January. It was followed by a layover period of 90 days and the unanimous vote in favour by the members of parliament.

Speaker Marcus Stephen certified the amendment on May 13 to enact the name change.

"International organisations and countries have formally been notified of the change and have begun making the transition," the government statement said.

"Naoero is the beginning of renewed national pride, and a new chapter founded on unity, responsibility, patriotism, better health, education, and sustainable development.

" The future of Naoero will be built by learning from the mistakes of the past and using their experience to make wiser decisions for the generations to come. "

The United Nations said Nauru had informed it about changing its name to Republic of Naoero on June 26.

This story was first published on rnz.co.nz

World.content:

And who steps up? Nick Daicos. He hit the boundary throw-in hard to gather at pace and lace out a left-foot centering pass to Jack Crisp. But the veteran could not convert from 45 metres out.

Guess what happens? The ball goes down the other end for former Pie Ollie Henry to dribble it through from just inside 50. It was an ugly kick by Henry, with a beautiful result if you’re a Cats fan.

World.title: Roosters shatter NRL records in 82-12 thrashing of Cowboys
World.content:
Well, that was something.

An embarrassing result for the Cowboys, who could still play finals football this season (although that fact isn’t a great look for the NRL either after tonight).

The Roosters have looked like an underachieving powerhouse for much of this season, but they lived up to their potential tonight and produced the highest-scoring game of any team in the NRL era.

It’s been 91 years since any team has scored 80 points in a game. Sam Walker has also matched the individual record for most points in a game in the NRL era, with 36.

World.content:
Thursday’s hearings have ended with questions about the government’s handling of domestic and family violence services, a portfolio that has faced immense scrutiny in recent weeks.

Addressing criticism of DFV funding cuts head on, after it was revealed the LNP had wiped $40 million from services, Camm accused her Labor opponents of running a media scare campaign.

Families, Seniors, Disability Services, Child Safety and Prevention of Domestic and Family Violence Minister Amanda Camm along with her DG Belinda Drew. Julius Dennis

But there has been a “reallocation” of funds, with Director-General Belinda Drew admitting $10.5 million to provide support and counselling services for victim-survivors of domestic violence had been diverted to other programs.

World.content:
Married At First Sight groom and Australian weightlifter Ridge Barredo has vowed to return to the Commonwealth Games after suffering a minor knee injury that ended his campaign in heartbreaking fashion.

Barredo failed to complete the men’s 110kg competition after collapsing in agony on his third and final clean and jerk attempt at 190kg.

Ridge Barredo of Team Australia celebrates during the Men’s 110kg Weightlifting. Getty Images

“I heard a pop on the third attempt. I tried to give it my all,” Barredo said. “I’ll get some scans but, hopefully, it’s not too serious. It’s a first for me ... which was a bit scary.

World.title: Launching a myth
World.content:
“When, as one does, fact checking Homer’s Odyssey, I find that 1196 ships sailed to Troy. Helen, the face that launched 1196 ships doesn’t have the same ring,” reckons Jane Stranger of Erskineville. “Clearly the PR gurus and brand managers of the time thought so, too.”

Barry Lamb of Eastwood’s suggested names for the Australian Underwater Hockey team (C8) are so elite that they could utilise any of them. Take your pick from, The Scubaroos, The Flipperoos, The Scudding Neptunes or The Munned Stullets.

Philip Cooney of Wentworth Falls suggests The Hockeyrays, though that could result in a complaint from the Australian women’s water polo team, The Stingers.

“Your correspondent found the film Jedda traumatising as a young child,” notes Mary Julian of Glebe. “I was also at the opening in 1959 and was probably fearful, too, but I managed another look at the movie recently. What amazed me were the perfect English accents, dubbed, for all indigenous and non-indigenous actors, except, of course Chips Rafferty. Chips used his own Aussie voice.”

Speaking of Australian cinema, Nola Tucker of Kiama thinks there’s one film that could perform another type of screening: “My Japanese grandson-in-law, Yuji, used to assess possible new friends by their attitude to The Castle [SMH, July 29]. Like the film, and they’re fine; don’t like it, not welcome. Seems a good enough standard to go by.”

World.content:
We’re into the last 10 minutes of the game, so it’s getting desperate for the Pies.

And who steps up? Nick Daicos. He hit the boundary throw-in hard to gather at pace and lace out a left-foot centering pass to Jack Crisp. But the veteran could not convert from 45 metres out.

Guess what happens? The ball goes down the other end for former Pie Ollie Henry to dribble it through from just inside 50. It was an ugly kick by Henry, with a beautiful result if you’re a Cats fan.

Cats are up by 25 points.

World.title: Roosters shatter NRL records in 82-12 thrashing of Cowboys
World.content:
Well, that was something.

An embarrassing result for the Cowboys, who could still play finals football this season (although that fact isn’t a great look for the NRL either after tonight).

The Roosters have looked like an underachieving powerhouse for much of this season, but they lived up to their potential tonight and produced the highest-scoring game of any team in the NRL era.

It’s been 91 years since any team has scored 80 points in a game. Sam Walker has also matched the individual record for most points in a game in the NRL era, with 36.

World.title: Queensland parliament as it happened: Education, arts, women and child safety up at budget estimates
World.content:
Thursday’s hearings have ended with questions about the government’s handling of domestic and family violence services, a portfolio that has faced immense scrutiny in recent weeks.

Addressing criticism of DFV funding cuts head on, after it was revealed the LNP had wiped $40 million from services, Camm accused her Labor opponents of running a media scare campaign.

Families, Seniors, Disability Services, Child Safety and Prevention of Domestic and Family Violence Minister Amanda Camm along with her DG Belinda Drew. Julius Dennis

“There has been no reduction in funding to our frontline domestic violence services,” she said.

But there has been a “reallocation” of funds, with Director-General Belinda Drew admitting $10.5 million to provide support and counselling services for victim-survivors of domestic violence had been diverted to other programs.

World.title: Commonwealth Games 2026 LIVE: Sad end for former MAFS star who injures leg during last lift; Jenneke powers into hurdles semis
World.content:
Married At First Sight groom and Australian weightlifter Ridge Barredo has vowed to return to the Commonwealth Games after suffering a minor knee injury that ended his campaign in heartbreaking fashion.

Barredo failed to complete the men’s 110kg competition after collapsing in agony on his third and final clean and jerk attempt at 190kg.

Ridge Barredo of Team Australia celebrates during the Men’s 110kg Weightlifting. Getty Images

“I heard a pop on the third attempt. I tried to give it my all,” Barredo said. “I’ll get some scans but, hopefully, it’s not too serious. It’s a first for me ... which was a bit scary.

World.title: Launching a myth
World.content:
“When, as one does, fact checking Homer’s Odyssey, I find that 1196 ships sailed to Troy. Helen, the face that launched 1196 ships doesn’t have the same ring,” reckons Jane Stranger of Erskineville. “Clearly the PR gurus and brand managers of the time thought so, too.”

Barry Lamb of Eastwood’s suggested names for the Australian Underwater Hockey team (C8) are so elite that they could utilise any of them. Take your pick from, The Scubaroos, The Flipperoos, The Scudding Neptunes or The Munned Stullets.

Philip Cooney of Wentworth Falls suggests The Hockeyrays, though that could result in a complaint from the Australian women’s water polo team, The Stingers.

“Your correspondent found the film Jedda traumatising as a young child,” notes Mary Julian of Glebe. “I was also at the opening in 1959 and was probably fearful, too, but I managed another look at the movie recently. What amazed me were the perfect English accents, dubbed, for all indigenous and non-indigenous actors, except, of course Chips Rafferty. Chips used his own Aussie voice.”

Speaking of Australian cinema, Nola Tucker of Kiama thinks there’s one film that could perform another type of screening: “My Japanese grandson-in-law, Yuji, used to assess possible new friends by their attitude to The Castle [SMH, July 29]. Like the film, and they’re fine; don’t like it, not welcome. Seems a good enough standard to go by.”

World.title: Stephen Fleming replaces Brendon McCullum as England Test coach
World.content:
England has named Stephen Fleming as its Men's Test head coach, replacing one New Zealander with another.

He fills the space left by Brendon McCullum, who was fired earlier this month following a string of poor results and several off-field incidents.

In an announcement on Thursday night (NZT), the England and Wales Cricket Board also named Joe Root as returning captain.

Fleming, who played 111 Tests for New Zealand between 1994 and 2008, stepped down as Chennai Super Kings (CSK) head coach earlier this month after 18 years with the Indian Premier League franchise.

"Fleming is one of the most highly regarded coaches in world cricket," the board said.

"As a player Fleming was New Zealand's longest-serving (80 Tests) and most successful Test captain (28 wins). He played for Middlesex, Yorkshire and Nottinghamshire where also enjoyed success in captaining Notts to a drought-breaking County Championship title in 2005."

It said Fleming was chosen unanimously "following a rigorous process, which involved numerous high-quality candidates".

England's next series is against Pakistan next month. Marcus Trescothick will serve as interim head coach, with Fleming due to start in time for the winter tour to South Africa.

"This is to allow Fleming to spend time with his family in New Zealand after leaving his long-term association with CSK earlier this month. Fleming is set to fly to the UK later this summer."

Fleming said he was "incredibly excited" to be appointed to "one of the most prestigious coaching positions in world cricket".

"I am looking forward to working with the players and bedding in the gains made by Brendon McCullum and Ben Stokes. Of course, the ambition is always to win now. But equally, it's about ensuring the team is well placed for the medium and long-term future. There is a lot of young talent in and around the team and our aim is to help them fulfil their potential as world-class cricketers," he said.

England’s captain Harry Brook (L) interacts with team head coach Brendon McCullum on March 4, 2026. PUNIT PARANJPE / AFP

"I'm particularly looking forward to working with Joe Root as Captain - a generational talent who has achieved so much already. There is still plenty more to come from him, and I'm excited to support him so he can enjoy and thrive in the role in what is a different context to his first stint.

"I'm also excited to work with Harry Brook. The best players are never finished products, and helping Harry continue to develop his extraordinary talent and his leadership will be an important part of this journey.

"I know what it feels like to have the weight of leadership and international cricket take their toll, and when that happened to me, my love for the game was rekindled by going to Notts and winning the County Championship. English cricket gave that to me and it is a privilege to have this chance to give something back."

McCullum, who played under Fleming in the Black Caps, will remain England's white ball coach and the pair will be required to work closely together.

World.title: Climber who survived 200m fall on Mount Aspiring should buy Lotto ticket, rescuers say
World.content:
A climber who survived a big fall down a steep, icy face on Mount Aspiring should buy a Lotto ticket, his rescuers say.

Emergency services launched a highly technical, high-altitude rescue on Tuesday night after the man's climbing companion hiked three hours to call for help, presuming his friend was dead.

The pair had summited Aspiring's south face and were descending via a steep snow and ice ridge known as The Ramp on Bonar Glacier.

Helicopters Otago chief executive Graeme Gale said climber fell just after dark at about 7pm.

"The message that I got was that he had fallen approximately 200 metres and his companion felt it was unsurvivable," he said.

The fallen climber had all of the pair's gear, including their locator beacon, Gale said.

With no way to signal for help, the second climber spent about three hours trekking back towards the summit in freezing conditions, searching for cellphone coverage.

Once the call for help came through, Gale said Wakatipu Alpine Cliff Rescue teams met Helicopters Otago crews in Queenstown to co-ordinate a response.

"We had some pretty sketchy co-ordinates of where it was, taken from the cellphone by the police. Police did a great job co-ordinating it and then we started pulling our guys together," he said.

With the climbers at nearly 3000m, wind building and poor weather pushing in from the west, the helicopter had to be stripped and made as light as possible.

Gale said crews used night vision goggles to track down the climber who had called for help.

"We could land on the edge of the ice shelf and pick him up and so we were able to hover load - with one skid on the edge - and got him in," he said.

The crew then decided to investigate a light source they had spotted "a couple of thousand feet below".

"They thought it was possibly other climbers on the mountain but it turned out to be this guy's companion and he was actually on his feet, although he'd had injuries," he said.

"Once again, we didn't need to winch, which was great. We were able to put a skid down, just hoverload again, and one of the alpine [cliff rescue team] guys got out and escorted him back into the helicopter."

Once the call for help came through, Wakatipu Alpine Cliff Rescue teams met Helicopters Otago crews in Queenstown to co-ordinate a response. Supplied / Screenshot

Gale was not sure the climber would have survived the night in frigid conditions if rescuers had not reached him.

He said the rescue was "the best of the best outcome" crews could have hoped for.

"It could have been catastrophic for him," Gale said.

"He was standing on a high shelf, on a slope on the mountain itself, so pretty lucky that he had gone into a crevasse and pretty lucky he hadn't had other injuries that would have been life-threatening. He was in remarkably good shape for the fall that he'd had. I reckon he should go and buy a lottery ticket for Saturday night."

Second rescue from The Ramp in a month

Wakatipu Alpine Cliff Rescue Team co-ordinator Russ Tilsley said it followed another even more technical rescue on 30 June on the same section of Mount Aspiring.

That rescue also took place late at night and involved two climbers who had ascended the south face, he said.

"These guys had basically been out too long and I think they were very tired. They abseiled down into an area where they got stuck in and they couldn't get out," he said.

"They were frostbitten, tired and had run out of food."

While winter was typically a quiet time for the rescue team, there seemed to be more and more people undertaking winter climbing missions, Tilsley said.

Summitting Mount Aspiring from the nearest walk-in Department of Conservation hut, French Ridge Hut, was a "big thing to do in a day", he said.

"To go up, climb and come back again is probably a 24-hour mission."

Earlier Sergeant Darren Cranfield from Wānaka Police described Tuesday's rescue as a timely reminder of the risks of alpine areas.

"Conditions in the mountains can change rapidly and even experienced climbers can find themselves in dangerous situations," he said.

World.title: New $2 million blood bank opens in Wellington, major upgrade on old facilities
World.content:
The New Zealand Blood Service says the capital's new blood bank - officially opened by the Health Minister on Wednesday - couldn't come soon enough.

The service at Wellington Regional Hospital plays a critical role in delivering life-saving donor blood to patients and according to staff, the new facility is a major upgrade.

NZ Blood Service chief executive Sam Cliffe said the almost 50-year-old former laboratory was "hopelessly not fit-for-purpose".

"The light fittings were so old we couldn't get new bulbs ... it was virtually impossible to clean. The staff did an amazing job of continuing to operate a very safe and reliable service."

New 'state of the art' blood bank opens in Wellington Checkpoint Download MP3 3m

She said the new space had been a long time coming and a couple of years ago things reached a crisis point.

"It could have been quite a dangerous situation in that we could have had our accreditation removed and we wouldn't have been able to provide a full service blood bank," she said.

That didn't happen. Health New Zealand found a solution, Cliffe said and the team was "utterly delighted" with it.

She said the facility was built for under $2 million "on time and on budget".

Sam Cliffe says the old laboratory was old and not fit for purpose. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

Wellington blood bank team leader Dan Gyles said he felt a mixture of relief and excitement at Wednesday's opening after pushing for a new lab for close to 16 years.

"It means everything. We now have space to do the job that we should have been doing all along. We have, despite the previous conditions, managed to maintain a safe service, but that was all it was."

He said they now had the space to implement laboratory practices around wearing gowns and protective gear, where required. "Rather than having tea breaks on our knees in the corner."

The laboratory, which includes pneumatic tubes that send and receive blood to and from the wards, multiple blood fridges, freezers storing plasma at minus 35 degrees, and room-temperature storage cabinets that keep platelets "jiggling," is three times the size of the old lab - built to meet expected future demand.

The new Wellington blood bank offices was built for $2 million and came in on time and one budget. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

Gyles said the extra space also meant a second blood grouping and screening machine, which was a game changer for the dozen staff that keep the service running around the clock.

Mel Homer received multiple blood transfusions during treatment for blood cancer. Supplied

"These do our grunt work, so this is where the patient samples are loaded up and we determine their blood group ... and then we do a red cell antibody screen."

The process ensured the blood was compatible with the patient who received it, he said.

Gyles said the blood bank was the behind-the-scenes critical step between people donating blood and patients receiving a transfusion - the majority of which were cancer patients, like Mel Homer.

Homer has received multiple blood transfusions over the past year while undergoing treatment for acute myeloid leukaemia, a blood cancer.

"They basically nuke your whole system, it's like scorched earth and you have no immune system and the idea is that they also kill off the cancer cells, and hopefully they don't grow back."

She said the treatment saw her haemoglobin and white blood cell count drop and her platelets - the clotting component - tank.

"You can't function properly so you need blood transfusions to top you up to a level so you can start healing."

In addition to red blood transfusions, Homer also needed platelets to reduce the risk of brain bleeds - but there were only two donors whose platelets were compatible, she said.

"It was life-saving." She said every time she used it - which was multiple times - she would think, "I'm so grateful".

The frozen blood product has to be thawed before it can be used. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

The blood bank also had to be ready for emergencies, Gyles said. Plasma was most often used for bleeding patients, patients in theatre, or trauma patients, he said.

It took about 15 minutes for the frozen blood product to thaw in a jiggling bath at 37C, he said.

"A bleeding patient - they need it quickly. So we've got some pre-thawed ahead of time."

Megan Piercy required an emergency blood transfusion after suffering from a post-partum haemorrhage. Supplied

Two years ago, Megan Piercy became a bleeding patient when she suffered a post-partum haemorrhage following the birth of her son.

"It was all kinds of bells and whistles from there. I had lost ... just over two litres at once."

She said given the emergency situation, she received blood from the universal donor type, however, samples of her blood were also sent off for testing in case she needed something more specific.

Piercy said the transfusion was crucial.

As a passionate blood donor herself, she knew the importance of it, she said. "I just never expected to be on the receiving end of it."

Michelle Sutherland, interim group director of operations for Capital, Coast and Hutt Valley, said the new blood bank was an important investment in the region's health services.

"Having this purpose-built facility on site strengthens our ability to deliver timely, safe and high-quality care for patients who need blood transfusions and other specialist services," she said.

Cliffe said patients, however, shouldn't notice the difference between Wellington's new blood bank and its predecessor.

"We've continued to maintain the same level of service delivery under incredibly trying conditions. [For] the people of Wellington this should be seamless."

Health Minister Simeon Brown cutting the ribbon to open the new Wellington Blood Bank. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

She said the new facility - in addition to future-proofing the service - provided the space for it to resume practical laboratory training for pathology professionals in the Pacific.

World.title: Police crack down on drug dealing in Wairoa
World.content:
A specialised police unit is cracking down on drug dealing in Wairoa, with six people arrested so far.

Four men and two women aged between 19 and 44 have been charged with drug dealing, firearms and dishonesty offences.

Police said eight search warrants were executed by specialist police staff and the Eastern District Gang Disruption Unit within three days.

Senior Sergeant Nathan Snell said the operation focused on the impacts of drug supply into the community.

"Police recognise the burden drug use and addiction has on the community and are committed to holding those involved in its supply to account," he said.

World.title: Defence Force training infrastructure in 'World War II era', new documents reveal
World.content:
The Defence Force is on its biggest push ever to get more combat ready and lethal at the same time its training infrastructure is in "World War II era", according to newly released documents.

Proactively released Cabinet papers from April and May outline the big deficit.

"The infrastructure to support training of recruits, in particular, is not in a position to meet existing ... demand in an effective way," said one 12-page paper that asked for, and got, a start to planning for an upgrade to how recruits are trained.

"Much of the infrastructure required to train NZDF personnel, like classrooms or rifle ranges, is World War II era, and is increasingly ineffective, and creating a potential for unsafe training environments.

"Investment is needed to avoid future failure."

The paper asked Cabinet to back a business case for fixing this, and Budget 2026 put in $23m.

However, this only funds a design phase out to 2029-30.

That means an actual fix of systems and infrastructure together appears at least three years away.

Defence Minister Chris Penk said there have been many years of under-investment into the Defence Force and this government is working to fix the consequences.

"We've begun the process of doing so to ensure training can be delivered safely, effectively and at the scale required into the future."

The Defence Capability Plan suggested investments over the next 15 years including into recruitment, retention and training, he said in a statement.

The paper said one upgraded rifle range would be added meantime, but one or two other short-term moves "to add resilience to a significantly degraded capability" were blanked out.

'Failing condition makes it difficult to train'

The deficiencies are a big hurdle to Defence's must-have in its new workforce strategy "to grow more soldiers, sailors and aviators, with urgency" and more tech-savvy ones as drone, cyber and electronic warfare take over.

Instead, "poor infrastructure in failing condition makes it difficult to train and retain people."

An example is old manual target practice ranges not suitable for modern weapons. Two other examples were blanked out.

The wider context is grim:

The state of bases and facilities was a key reason given at scrutiny week in June for the land combat readiness falling to 45 percent at the end of 2025.

Defence has admitted its training systems are degraded too much to rapidly boost battlefield adaptability and agility.

NZDF's ways of managing its existing assets do not meet Treasury standards, and it is slow to get contracts for projects signed up.

Eroded by old gear and slow take-up of new tech, 60 percent of the army's land training system had got to the end of its life, said the May Cabinet paper.

Recruits 'most pressing'

The whole system relied in the first place on recruit training but this was significantly degraded and the "most pressing" thing needing fixing.

That fix would focus on Waiouru camp and line up with Australia, which was putting almost a billion dollars into recruit training, as well as looking to the US, UK and Singapore.

The paper that Penk lodged with Cabinet showed the ministers - Judith Collins was Defence Minister at the time - walking a line between "capability and affordability", even after Defence got a $9 billion fillip in new spending over four years from 2025.

So they narrowed in on a new recruit training system and curriculum which was the "minimum viable capability needed in the short term", and would need to integrate with Australia, other partners and other government services.

"Australian designs will be used where possible" in the detailed business case that is now being worked on.

'Future growth' option not chosen

A third more ambitious option that catered for "future growth and the introduction of new and emerging ... capabilities" did not make the cut.

Budget 2026 also had funding for an undisclosed amount for a new 'virtual training' facility at Linton camp near Palmerston North.

Defence has a huge estate, huge budgets and a chequered track record running it all.

The latest available Treasury report on how NZDF was doing with its big capital investments said it was no longer reporting a significant underspend (which can indicate projects hitting delays). Its actual spend on projects at $406m, and its spending on repairs and maintenance at $193m, at that stage were only a bit behind forecast.

However, Defence spending on specialist equipment and on data/digital was running well behind forecast.

The report for the September-December 2025 quarter showed it took about a year for procurement processes to get to the point of signing contracts, among the slower on the major public agencies covered by the Treasury investment reports.

Its asset registers and asset management plans were not up to scratch according to the latest gauge in June 2025. An update for 2026 won't be publicly available for months.

Labour's defence spokesperson Damien O'Connor said it supported the direction of the Defence Capability Plan.

"Personnel is the most acute issue facing NZDF. Labour sees this as a priority and will get advice on ensuring training capacity is built when in government," he said.
